As by your high imperial Majesty / I had in charge at my depart for France, / As procurator to your excellence, / To marry Princess Margaret for your grace, / So, in the famous ancient city Tours, / In presence of the Kings of France and Sicil, / The Dukes of Orleans, Calaber, Bretagne, and Alencon, / Seven earls, twelve barons, and twenty reverend bishops, / I have perform'd my task and was espous'd, / And humbly now upon my bended knee, / In sight of England and her lordly peers, / Deliver up my title in the queen / To your most gracious hands, that are the substance / Of that great shadow I did represent: / The happiest gift that ever marquess gave, / The fairest queen that ever king receiv'd.

Your Majesty, when I left for France you ordered me, as your representative, to marry Princess Margaret on your behalf. So in the famous old city of Tours, before the Kings of France and Sicily, the Dukes of Orleans, Calabria, Brittany and Alencon, seven earls, twelve barons and twenty bishops, I carried out my task and married her for you. Now, kneeling humbly before England and her lords, I hand over my claim to the queen into your gracious hands. You are the real man of whom I was only the stand-in. It is the happiest gift a marquess ever gave, and the most beautiful queen a king ever received.

Suffolk, arise.—Welcome, Queen Margaret. / I can express no kinder sign of love / Than this kind kiss.—O Lord, that lends me life, / Lend me a heart replete with thankfulness! / For thou hast given me in this beauteous face / A world of earthly blessings to my soul, / If sympathy of love unite our thoughts.

Stand up, Suffolk. Welcome, Queen Margaret. I can show my love no more kindly than with this kiss. O Lord who gives me life, give me a heart full of thanks! In this lovely face you have given my soul a whole world of earthly blessings, if our thoughts are joined in love.

Great King of England and my gracious lord, / The mutual conference that my mind hath had, / By day, by night, waking and in my dreams, / In courtly company or at my beads, / With you, mine alder-liefest sovereign, / Makes me the bolder to salute my king / With ruder terms, such as my wit affords / And over-joy of heart doth minister.

Great King of England, my gracious lord, I have talked with you in my mind day and night, awake and dreaming, at court and at my prayers, my dearest sovereign. That makes me bold enough to greet you in plain words, as well as my wit and my overjoyed heart allow.

Her sight did ravish, but her grace in speech, / Her words yclad with wisdom's majesty, / Makes me from wondering fall to weeping joys; / Such is the fulness of my heart's content.— / Lords, with one cheerful voice welcome my love.
Her looks delighted me, but her graceful speech, dressed in wise and royal words, turns my wonder into tears of joy, my heart is so full. Lords, all welcome my love with one cheerful voice.
[Kneeling] Long live Queen Margaret, England's / happiness!
(Kneeling) Long live Queen Margaret, England's joy!
My Lord Protector, so it please your grace, / Here are the articles of contracted peace / Between our sovereign and the French king Charles, / For eighteen months concluded by consent.
My Lord Protector, if it please you, here are the articles of the peace agreed between our king and the French king Charles, a truce settled for eighteen months.

[Reads] 'Imprimis, It is agreed between the French king / Charles and William de la Pole, Marquess of Suffolk, ambassador / for Henry King of England, that the said Henry shall espouse the / Lady Margaret, daughter unto Reignier King of Naples, Sicilia, / and Jerusalem, and crown her Queen of England ere the thirtieth / of May next ensuing. Item, that the duchy of Anjou and the / county of Maine shall be released and delivered to the king her / father'—

(Reading) "First, it is agreed between Charles, King of France, and William de la Pole, Marquess of Suffolk, ambassador for Henry King of England, that Henry shall marry Lady Margaret, daughter of Reignier King of Naples, Sicily and Jerusalem, and crown her Queen of England before the thirtieth of May. Also, that the duchy of Anjou and the county of Maine shall be released and handed over to her father—"
Pardon me, gracious lord; / Some sudden qualm hath struck me at the heart / And dimm'd mine eyes, that I can read no further.
Forgive me, my lord. A sudden sickness has struck my heart and blurred my eyes, so that I can't read any more.
Uncle of Winchester, I pray, read on.

[Reads] 'Item, It is further agreed between them, / that the duchies of Anjou and Maine shall be released and / delivered over to the king her father, and she sent over of the / King of / England's own proper cost and charges, without having any dowry.'

(Reading) "Also, it is further agreed that the duchies of Anjou and Maine shall be released and handed over to her father, and that she shall be brought over at the King of England's own cost, without any dowry."

They please us well.—Lord marquess, kneel down. / We here create thee the first duke of Suffolk, / And girt thee with the sword.—Cousin of York, / We here discharge your grace from being regent / I' the parts of France, till term of eighteen months / Be full expir'd.—Thanks, uncle Winchester, / Gloster, York, Buckingham, Somerset, / Salisbury, and Warwick; / We thank you all for this great favour done / In entertainment to my princely queen. / Come, let us in, and with all speed provide / To see her coronation be perform'd.

They please us well. Lord Marquess, kneel. We make you the first Duke of Suffolk and fasten on your sword. Cousin York, we relieve you of your post as regent in France until eighteen months are over. Thank you, Uncle Winchester, Gloucester, York, Buckingham, Somerset, Salisbury and Warwick, for this great kindness in welcoming my queen. Come, let's go in and quickly arrange her coronation.

Brave peers of England, pillars of the state, / To you Duke Humphrey must unload his grief, / Your grief, the common grief of all the land. / What! did my brother Henry spend his youth, / His valour, coin, and people, in the wars? / Did he so often lodge in open field, / In winter's cold and summer's parching heat, / To conquer France, his true inheritance? / And did my brother Bedford toil his wits / To keep by policy what Henry got? / Have you yourselves, Somerset, Buckingham, / Brave York, Salisbury, and victorious Warwick, / Receiv'd deep scars in France and Normandy? / Or hath mine uncle Beaufort and myself, / With all the learned counsel of the realm, / Studied so long, sat in the council-house / Early and late, debating to and fro / How France and Frenchmen might be kept in awe, / And had his highness in his infancy / Crowned in Paris in despite of foes? / And shall these labours and these honours die? / Shall Henry's conquest, Bedford's vigilance, / Your deeds of war, and all our counsel die? / O peers of England, shameful is this league! / Fatal this marriage, cancelling your fame, / Blotting your names from books of memory, / Razing the characters of your renown, / Defacing monuments of conquer'd France, / Undoing all, as all had never been!

Noble lords of England, pillars of the state, I must unload my grief on you, Duke Humphrey's grief, which is the grief of the whole country. What! Did my brother Henry the Fifth spend his youth, courage, money and men in the wars? Did he so often camp in open fields in winter cold and summer heat to conquer France, his rightful inheritance? Did my brother Bedford wear out his brains to keep by clever policy what Henry won? Have you yourselves, Somerset, Buckingham, brave York, Salisbury and victorious Warwick, taken deep wounds in France and Normandy? Have my uncle Beaufort and I, with the realm's wisest counsellors, sat in council early and late, arguing how to keep France and the French in fear, and had the king crowned in Paris as a child in spite of his enemies? And shall all this work and honour die? Henry's conquest, Bedford's watchfulness, your fighting and all our counsel? O lords of England, this treaty is shameful! This marriage is fatal: it cancels your fame, blots your names out of history, erases the record of your glory, defaces the monuments of conquered France, and undoes everything as if it had never been!
Nephew, what means this passionate discourse, / This peroration with such circumstance? / For France, 't is ours; and we will keep it still.
Nephew, what is this emotional speech, this long-winded oration? As for France, it's ours, and we will keep it.

Ay, uncle, we will keep it if we can, / But now it is impossible we should. / Suffolk, the new-made duke that rules the roast, / Hath given the duchy of Anjou and Maine / Unto the poor King Reignier, whose large style / Agrees not with the leanness of his purse.

Yes, uncle, we'll keep it if we can, but now it's impossible. Suffolk, the new duke who runs everything, has given Anjou and Maine to poor King Reignier, whose grand titles don't match his thin purse.
Now, by the death of Him that died for all, / These counties were the keys of Normandy!— / But wherefore weeps Warwick, my valiant son?
By Christ who died for us all, those counties were the keys to Normandy! But why is Warwick, my brave son, weeping?

For grief that they are past recovery; / For, were there hope to conquer them again, / My sword should shed hot blood, mine eyes no tears. / Anjou and Maine! myself did win them both, / Those provinces these arms of mine did conquer; / And are the cities that I got with wounds / Deliver'd up again with peaceful words? / Mort Dieu!

In grief that they can never be won back. If there were hope of conquering them again, my sword would shed hot blood, not my eyes tears. Anjou and Maine! I won them both myself; these arms conquered those provinces. Are cities I won with wounds handed back with peaceful words? God's death!

For Suffolk's duke, may he be suffocate, / That dims the honour of this warlike isle! / France should have torn and rent my very heart, / Before I would have yielded to this league. / I never read but England's kings have had / Large sums of gold and dowries with their wives; / And our King Henry gives away his own, / To match with her that brings no vantages.

As for Suffolk's dukedom, may he be suffocated, since he dims the honour of this warlike island! France should have torn out my heart before I agreed to this treaty. I've only ever read that England's kings got big sums of gold and dowries with their wives, and our King Henry gives away his own land to marry a woman who brings no advantage.
A proper jest, and never heard before, / That Suffolk should demand a whole fifteenth / For costs and charges in transporting her! / She should have staid in France, and starv'd in France, / Before—
A fine joke, never heard before: Suffolk demands a fifteenth of the nation's wealth as a tax to pay for bringing her over! She should have stayed in France and starved in France before—
My Lord of Gloster, now ye grow too hot; / It was the pleasure of my lord the King.
My Lord of Gloucester, you're getting too heated. This was the king's wish.

My Lord of Winchester, I know your mind; / 'T is not my speeches that you do mislike, / But 't is my presence that doth trouble ye. / Rancour will out. / Proud prelate, in thy face / I see thy fury; if I longer stay, / We shall begin our ancient bickerings.— / Lordings, farewell; and say, when I am gone, / I prophesied France will be lost ere long.

My Lord of Winchester, I know what you think. It's not my speeches you dislike but my presence that troubles you. Hatred will show itself. Proud churchman, I see your fury in your face; if I stay longer we'll start our old quarrels again. Lords, farewell, and say when I'm gone that I foretold France will soon be lost.

So, there goes our protector in a rage. / 'T is known to you he is mine enemy, / Nay, more, an enemy unto you all, / And no great friend, I fear me, to the king. / Consider, lords, he is the next of blood, / And heir apparent to the English crown. / Had Henry got an empire by his marriage, / And all the wealthy kingdoms of the west, / There's reason he should be displeas'd at it. / Look to it, lords. / Let not his smoothing words / Bewitch your hearts; be wise and circumspect. / What though the common people favour him, / Calling him 'Humphrey, the good Duke of Gloster,' / Clapping their hands, and crying with loud voice, / 'Jesu maintain your royal excellence!' / With 'God preserve the good Duke Humphrey!' / I fear me, lords, for all this flattering gloss, / He will be found a dangerous protector.

So there goes our Protector in a rage. You know he is my enemy, and an enemy to all of you too, and, I fear, no great friend to the king. Remember, lords, he is next in blood and heir to the English crown. If Henry had won an empire and all the rich western kingdoms by his marriage, Gloucester would still have reason to be displeased. Watch out, lords. Don't let his smooth words bewitch you; be wise and careful. Even if the common people love him, calling him "Humphrey, the good Duke of Gloucester", clapping and shouting "Jesus keep your royal excellence!" and "God save the good Duke Humphrey!", I fear, lords, that for all this flattering show he will prove a dangerous Protector.

Why should he, then, protect our sovereign, / He being of age to govern of himself?— / Cousin of Somerset, join you with me, / And all together, with the Duke of Suffolk, / We'll quickly hoise Duke Humphrey from his seat.

Then why should he protect our king, when the king is old enough to rule for himself? Cousin Somerset, join with me, and together with the Duke of Suffolk we'll soon heave Duke Humphrey out of his place.
This weighty business will not brook delay; / I'll to the Duke of Suffolk presently.
This important business won't wait. I'll go to the Duke of Suffolk at once.

Cousin of Buckingham, though Humphrey's pride / And greatness of his place be grief to us, / Yet let us watch the haughty cardinal; / His insolence is more intolerable / Than all the princes in the land beside; / If Gloster be displac'd, he 'll be protector.

Cousin Buckingham, though Humphrey's pride and great position annoy us, we must also watch the arrogant cardinal. His insolence is harder to bear than that of all the other princes in the land. If Gloucester is removed, he'll be Protector.
Or thou or I, Somerset, will be protector, / Despite Duke Humphrey or the cardinal.
Either you or I will be Protector, Somerset, in spite of Duke Humphrey or the cardinal.

Pride went before, ambition follows him. / While these do labour for their own preferment, / Behoves it us to labour for the realm. / I never saw but Humphrey Duke of Gloster / Did bear him like a noble gentleman. / Oft have I seen the haughty cardinal, / More like a soldier than a man o' the church, / As stout and proud as he were lord of all, / Swear like a ruffian and demean himself / Unlike the ruler of a commonweal.— / Warwick my son, the comfort of my age, / Thy deeds, thy plainness, and thy housekeeping, / Hath won the greatest favour of the commons, / Excepting none but good Duke Humphrey;— / And, brother York, thy acts in Ireland, / In bringing them to civil discipline, / Thy late exploits done in the heart of France, / When thou wert regent for our sovereign, / Have made thee fear'd and honour'd of the people.— / Join we together, for the public good, / In what we can, to bridle and suppress / The pride of Suffolk and the cardinal, / With Somerset's and Buckingham's ambition, / And, as we may, cherish Duke Humphrey's deeds / While they do tend the profit of the land.

Pride went first; ambition follows it. While these men work for their own advancement, we must work for the kingdom. I have never seen Humphrey Duke of Gloucester behave other than as a noble gentleman. I have often seen the arrogant cardinal, more like a soldier than a churchman, as bold and proud as if he owned everything, swear like a thug and behave unlike a ruler of the state. Warwick, my son, comfort of my old age, your deeds, your honesty and your generous hospitality have won the commons' greatest love, second only to good Duke Humphrey. And brother York, your work in Ireland bringing it to order, and your recent exploits in the heart of France as regent, have made the people fear and honour you. Let's join together for the public good to check and hold down the pride of Suffolk and the cardinal, and the ambition of Somerset and Buckingham, and, as far as we can, support Duke Humphrey's actions while they serve the country.
So God help Warwick, as he loves the land / And common profit of his country!
God help Warwick as surely as he loves the country and the common good!
[Aside] And so says York, for he hath greatest cause.
(Aside) And so says York, for he has the greatest reason.
Then let's make haste away, and look unto the main.
Then let's hurry and look to the main business.

Unto the main! O father, Maine is lost; / That Maine which by main force Warwick did win, / And would have kept so long as breath did last! / Main chance, father, you meant; but I meant Maine, / Which I will win from France, or else be slain.

The main! Father, Maine is lost, the Maine that Warwick won by main force and would have held as long as he had breath! You meant the main chance, father, but I meant Maine, and I will win it back from France or die.

Anjou and Maine are given to the French; / Paris is lost; the state of Normandy / Stands on a tickle point now they are gone. / Suffolk concluded on the articles, / The peers agreed; and Henry was well pleas'd / To changes two dukedoms for a duke's fair daughter. / I cannot blame them all: what is't to them? / 'T is thine they give away, and not their own. / Pirates may make cheap pennyworths of their pillage, / And purchase friends, and give to courtesans, / Still revelling like lords till all be gone; / Whileas the silly owner of the goods / Weeps over them and wrings his hapless hands / And shakes his head and trembling stands aloof, / While all is shar'd and all is borne away, / Ready to starve and dare not touch his own. / So York must sit and fret and bite his tongue, / While his own lands are bargain'd for and sold. / Methinks the realms of England, France, and Ireland / Bear that proportion to my flesh and blood / As did the fatal brand Althaea burn'd / Unto the prince's heart of Calydon. / Anjou and Maine both given unto the French! / Cold news for me, for I had hope of France, / Even as I have of fertile England's soil. / A day will come when York shall claim his own; / And therefore I will take the Nevils' parts, / And make a show of love to proud Duke Humphrey, / And when I spy advantage, claim the crown, / For that 's the golden mark I seek to hit. / Nor shall proud Lancaster usurp my right, / Nor hold the sceptre in his childish fist, / Nor wear the diadem upon his head, / Whose church-like humours fits not for a crown. / Then, York, be still awhile till time do serve; / Watch thou and wake when others be asleep, / To pry into the secrets of the state; / Till Henry, surfeiting in joys of love, / With his new bride and England's dear-bought queen, / And Humphrey with the peers be fallen at jars. / Then will I raise aloft the milk-white rose, / With whose sweet smell the air shall be perfum'd, / And in my standard bear the arms of York, / To grapple with the house of Lancaster; / And, force perforce, I 'll make him yield the crown / Whose bookish rule hath pull'd fair England down.

Anjou and Maine are given to the French. Paris is lost, and the state of Normandy is on a knife edge now they're gone. Suffolk settled the terms, the lords agreed, and Henry was happy to swap two dukedoms for a duke's pretty daughter. I can't blame them all; what does it matter to them? It's yours they're giving away, York, not their own. Pirates can sell their loot cheaply, buy friends and give to whores, partying like lords till it's all gone, while the poor owner of the goods weeps over them, wrings his hands, shakes his head and stands back trembling while everything is shared out and carried off, starving and not daring to touch his own. So York must sit, fret and bite his tongue while his own lands are bargained away and sold. England, France and Ireland seem as bound up with my flesh and blood as the fatal log that Althaea burned was with the life of the prince of Calydon. Anjou and Maine both given to the French! Cold news for me, for I had hopes of France, just as I have of fertile England. A day will come when York will claim what's his. So I'll take the Nevilles' side, pretend to love proud Duke Humphrey, and when I see my chance, claim the crown, for that's the golden target I aim at. Proud Lancaster won't steal my right, or hold the sceptre in his childish fist, or wear the crown on his head, when his churchy temper is unfit for a crown. So, York, keep quiet for a while until the time is right. Stay awake while others sleep, and pry into the secrets of the state, until Henry is glutted with love for his new bride, England's expensive queen, and Humphrey and the lords are at odds. Then I'll raise the white rose high, whose sweet smell will perfume the air, carry the arms of York on my banner to wrestle with the house of Lancaster, and by force make him give up the crown whose bookish rule has dragged fair England down.

Why droops my lord, like over-ripen'd corn, / Hanging the head at Ceres' plenteous load? / Why doth the great Duke Humphrey knit his brows, / As frowning at the favours of the world? / Why are thine eyes fix'd to the sullen earth, / Gazing on that which seems to dim thy sight? / What see'st thou there? King Henry's diadem, / Enchas'd with all the honours of the world? / If so, gaze on, and grovel on thy face, / Until thy head be circled with the same. / Put forth thy hand, reach at the glorious gold. / What, is't too short? I'll lengthen it with mine, / And, having both together heav'd it up, / We'll both together lift our heads to heaven, / And never more abase our sight so low / As to vouchsafe one glance unto the ground.

Why does my lord droop like over-ripe corn, its head bowed under the weight of the harvest? Why does great Duke Humphrey frown as if the world's favours displeased him? Why are your eyes fixed on the gloomy ground, staring at something that seems to darken your sight? What do you see there? King Henry's crown, set with all the world's honours? If so, keep gazing, and crawl on your face until that crown circles your head. Reach out your hand to the glorious gold. What, is it too short? I'll lengthen it with mine, and when we've lifted it up together, we'll both raise our heads to heaven and never again lower our eyes so far as to glance at the ground.

O Nell, sweet Nell, if thou dost love thy lord, / Banish the canker of ambitious thoughts; / And may that thought when I imagine ill / Against my king and nephew, virtuous Henry, / Be my last breathing in this mortal world! / My troublous dreams this night doth make me sad.

O Nell, sweet Nell, if you love your husband, get rid of these cankerous ambitious thoughts. And if I ever think ill against my king and nephew, virtuous Henry, may that thought be my last breath in this world! My troubled dreams last night have made me sad.
What dream'd my lord? Tell me, and I'll requite it / With sweet rehearsal of my morning's dream.
What did you dream, my lord? Tell me, and I'll repay you with a sweet account of my dream this morning.

Methought this staff, mine office-badge in court, / Was broke in twain;—by whom I have forgot, / But, as I think, it was by the cardinal,— / And on the pieces of the broken wand / Were plac'd the heads of Edmund Duke of Somerset / And William de la Pole, first duke of Suffolk. / This was my dream; what it doth bode, God knows.

I dreamed that this staff, my badge of office at court, was broken in two, by whom I've forgotten, but I think it was the cardinal. And on the broken pieces were placed the heads of Edmund Duke of Somerset and William de la Pole, first Duke of Suffolk. That was my dream; God knows what it means.

Tut, this was nothing but an argument / That he that breaks a stick of Gloster's grove / Shall lose his head for his presumption. / But list to me, my Humphrey, my sweet duke: / Methought I sat in seat of majesty / In the cathedral church of Westminster / And in that chair where kings and queens are crown'd, / Where Henry and Dame Margaret kneel'd to me / And on my head did set the diadem.

Nonsense, that only meant that anyone who breaks a stick in Gloucester's grove will lose his head for his cheek. But listen to me, my Humphrey, my sweet duke. I dreamed I sat on the throne in Westminster Abbey, in the chair where kings and queens are crowned, and Henry and Margaret knelt to me and set the crown on my head.

Nay, Eleanor, then must I chide outright. / Presumptuous dame, ill-nurtur'd Eleanor, / Art thou not second woman in the realm, / And the protector's wife, belov'd of him? / Hast thou not worldly pleasure at command, / Above the reach or compass of thy thought? / And wilt thou still be hammering treachery, / To tumble down thy husband and thyself / From top of honour to disgrace's feet? / Away from me, and let me hear no more!

No, Eleanor, now I must scold you plainly. Arrogant woman, badly brought up Eleanor! Aren't you the second lady in the kingdom, the Protector's wife, and loved by him? Don't you have every worldly pleasure at your command, beyond what you can even imagine? And will you still keep forging treason, to throw your husband and yourself down from the height of honour to the feet of disgrace? Leave me, and let me hear no more!
What, what, my lord! are you so choleric / With Eleanor for telling but her dream? / Next time I'll keep my dreams unto myself, / And not be check'd.
What, my lord! Are you so angry with Eleanor just for telling her dream? Next time I'll keep my dreams to myself and not be told off.
Nay, be not angry; I am pleas'd again.
No, don't be angry; I'm happy again.
My lord protector, 't is his highness' pleasure / You do prepare to ride unto Saint Alban's, / Whereas the king and queen do mean to hawk.
My Lord Protector, his Highness wants you to prepare to ride to St Albans, where the king and queen intend to go hawking.
I go.—Come, Nell, thou wilt ride with us?
I'm going. Come, Nell, will you ride with us?
Yes, my good lord, I'll follow presently.
Yes, my good lord, I'll follow shortly.

Follow I must; I cannot go before / While Gloster bears this base and humble mind. / Were I a man, a duke, and next of blood, / I would remove these tedious stumbling-blocks / And smooth my way upon their headless necks; / And, being a woman, I will not be slack / To play my part in Fortune's pageant.— / Where are you there? Sir John! nay, fear not, man, / We are alone; here's none but thee and I.

I must follow; I can't go in front while Gloucester has such a low, humble mind. If I were a man, a duke and next in line to the throne, I'd remove these tiresome obstacles and smooth my way over their headless necks. And though I'm a woman, I won't be slow to play my part in Fortune's show. Who's there? Sir John! Don't be afraid, man, we're alone; there's nobody but you and me.
What say'st thou? majesty! I am but grace.
What did you say? Majesty! I'm only "your grace".
But, by the grace of God, and Hume's advice, / Your grace's title shall be multiplied.
But by the grace of God and Hume's advice, your grace's title will be raised higher.
What say'st thou, man? hast thou as yet conferr'd / With Margery Jourdain, the cunning witch, / With Roger Bolingbroke, the conjurer? / And will they undertake to do me good?
What do you say, man? Have you met with Margery Jourdain, the clever witch, and Roger Bolingbroke, the conjurer? Will they do what I want?
This they have promised,—to show your highness / A spirit rais'd from depth of underground, / That shall make answer to such questions / As by your Grace shall be propounded him.
They have promised this: to show your highness a spirit raised from deep underground, which will answer whatever questions your grace puts to it.

It is enough; I'll think upon the questions. / When from Saint Alban's we do make return, / We'll see these things effected to the full. / Here, Hume, take this reward; make merry, man, / With thy confederates in this weighty cause.

That's enough. I'll think about the questions. When we come back from St Albans, we'll see this carried out fully. Here, Hume, take this reward. Enjoy yourself, man, with your partners in this important business.

Hume must make merry with the duchess' gold, / Marry, and shall. But, how now, Sir John Hume! / Seal up your lips, and give no words but mum; / The business asketh silent secrecy. / Dame Eleanor gives gold to bring the witch; / Gold cannot come amiss, were she a devil. / Yet have I gold flies from another coast. / I dare not say, from the rich cardinal / And from the great and new-made Duke of Suffolk, / Yet I do find it so; for, to be plain, / They, knowing Dame Eleanor's aspiring humour, / Have hired me to undermine the duchess / And buzz these conjurations in her brain. / They say ' A crafty knave does need no broker;' / Yet am I Suffolk and the cardinal's broker. / Hume, if you take not heed, you shall go near / To call them both a pair of crafty knaves. / Well, so its stands; and thus, I fear, at last / Hume's knavery will be the duchess' wrack, / And her attainture will be Humphrey's fall. / Sort how it will, I shall have gold for all.

Hume is to enjoy himself with the duchess's gold? Indeed he will. But careful, Sir John Hume! Seal your lips and say nothing but "mum"; this business needs silence. Dame Eleanor gives gold to bring the witch; gold is always welcome, even from a devil. But I also have gold coming from another direction. I daren't say from the rich cardinal and the great new Duke of Suffolk, but that's how it is. To be plain, knowing Dame Eleanor's ambitious temper, they've hired me to bring down the duchess and fill her head with these conjurings. They say "a clever rogue doesn't need an agent", yet I'm Suffolk's and the cardinal's agent. Hume, if you're not careful you'll end up calling them both a pair of clever rogues. Well, that's how it stands, and I fear in the end Hume's trickery will wreck the duchess, and her disgrace will be Humphrey's fall. However it turns out, I'll get gold from everyone.
My masters, let's stand close; my lord protector / will come this way by and by, and then we may deliver our / supplications in the quill.
Friends, let's stand close together. My Lord Protector will come this way soon, and then we can hand in our petitions in one go.
Marry, the Lord protect him, for he's a good / man! Jesu bless him!
Indeed, the Lord protect him, for he's a good man! Jesus bless him!
Here 'a comes, methinks, and the queen with him. / I'll be the first, sure.
Here he comes, I think, and the queen with him. I'll be first, for sure.
Come back, fool; this is the Duke of Suffolk and / not my lord protector.
Come back, fool; this is the Duke of Suffolk, not my Lord Protector.
How now, fellow! wouldst any thing with me?
Well, fellow, do you want something from me?
I pray, my lord, pardon me; I took ye for my lord / protector.
I beg your pardon, my lord; I mistook you for my Lord Protector.
[Reading] 'To my Lord Protector!' Are your supplications / to his lordship? Let me see them; what is thine?
(Reading) "To my Lord Protector!" Are your petitions for him? Let me see them. What's yours?
Mine is, an 't please your grace, against John / Goodman, my lord cardinal's man, for keeping my house and lands, / and wife and all, from me.
Mine, if it please your grace, is against John Goodman, my lord cardinal's servant, for keeping my house, my land, my wife and everything from me.
Thy wife too! that's some wrong, indeed.—What's / yours?—What's here! [Reads] 'Against the Duke of Suffolk for / enclosing / the commons of Melford.'—How now, sir knave!
Your wife too! That is a real wrong. What's yours? What's this! (Reading) "Against the Duke of Suffolk, for fencing off the common land of Melford." What, you rascal!
Alas, sir, I am but a poor petitioner of our / whole township.
Sorry, sir, I'm only a poor petitioner speaking for our whole town.
[Giving his petition] Against my master, Thomas Horner, / for saying that the Duke of York was rightful heir to the crown.
(Giving his petition) Against my master, Thomas Horner, for saying that the Duke of York was the rightful heir to the crown.
What say'st thou? did the Duke of York say he was / rightful heir to the crown?
What are you saying? Did the Duke of York say he was rightful heir to the crown?
That my master was? no, forsooth; my master said that he / was, and that the king was an usurper.
That my master was? No, truly; my master said that York was, and that the king was a usurper.
Who is there? [Enter Servant] Take this fellow in, and / send for his master with a pursuivant presently.—We'll hear more / of your matter before the king.
Who's there? (Enter Servant) Take this fellow inside, and send an officer to fetch his master at once. We'll hear more about this in front of the king.
And as for you, that love to be protected / Under the wings of our protector's grace, / Begin your suits anew and sue to him.
And as for you, who like to be protected under the wings of our Protector, start your petitions again and take them to him.
Away, base cullions!—Suffolk, let them go.
Get out, you scum! Suffolk, let them go.

My Lord of Suffolk, say, is this the guise, / Is this the fashion in the court of England? / Is this the government of Britain's isle, / And this the royalty of Albion's king? / What, shall King Henry be a pupil still / Under the surly Gloster's governance? / Am I a queen in title and in style, / And must be made a subject to a duke? / I tell thee, Pole, when in the city Tours / Thou ran'st a tilt in honour of my love / And stol'st away the ladies' hearts of France, / I thought King Henry had resembled thee / In courage, courtship, and proportion; / But all his mind is bent to holiness, / To number Ave-Maries on his beads, / His champions are the prophets and apostles, / His weapons holy saws of sacred writ, / His study is his tilt-yard, and his loves / Are brazen images of canoniz'd saints. / I would the college of the cardinals / Would choose him pope and carry him to Rome, / And set the triple crown upon his head; / That were a state fit for his holiness.

My Lord of Suffolk, tell me, is this the custom, the fashion at the English court? Is this how Britain is governed, and this the royalty of England's king? What, is King Henry to stay a schoolboy under surly Gloucester's control? Am I a queen in title and name, only to be made a duke's subject? I tell you, Pole, when you jousted in Tours in honour of my love and stole the hearts of the French ladies, I thought King Henry would be like you in courage, courtliness and looks. But his mind is all set on holiness, counting Hail Marys on his rosary. His champions are the prophets and apostles, his weapons holy sayings from scripture, his study is his jousting ground, and his loves are bronze statues of saints. I wish the college of cardinals would elect him pope, carry him off to Rome and put the triple crown on his head. That would be a position to suit his holiness.
Madam, be patient; as I was cause / Your highness came to England, so will I / In England work your grace's full content.
Madam, be patient. As I was the reason you came to England, so I will make sure you are fully satisfied in England.
Beside the haughty protector, have we Beaufort / The imperious churchman, Somerset, Buckingham, / And grumbling York; and not the least of these / But can do more in England than the king.
Besides the arrogant Protector, we have Beaufort, the domineering churchman, Somerset, Buckingham and grumbling York, and even the least of them has more power in England than the king.
And he of these that can do most of all / Cannot do more in England than the Nevils; / Salisbury and Warwick are no simple peers.
And the most powerful of them can do no more in England than the Nevilles. Salisbury and Warwick are no ordinary lords.

Not all these lords do vex me half so much / As that proud dame, the lord protector's wife. / She sweeps it through the court with troops of ladies, / More like an empress than Duke Humphrey's wife. / Strangers in court do take her for the queen; / She bears a duke's revenues on her back, / And in her heart she scorns our poverty. / Shall I not live to be aveng'd on her? / Contemptuous base-born callat as she is, / She vaunted 'mongst her minions t' other day, / The very train of her worst wearing gown / Was better worth than all my father's land / Till Suffolk gave two dukedoms for his daughter.

None of these lords annoys me half as much as that proud woman, the Protector's wife. She sweeps through the court with crowds of ladies, more like an empress than Duke Humphrey's wife. Foreigners at court take her for the queen. She wears a duke's income on her back, and in her heart she sneers at our poverty. Won't I live to get revenge on her? The contemptuous, low-born slut boasted among her favourites the other day that the train of her worst gown was worth more than all my father's land, until Suffolk gave two dukedoms for his daughter.

Madam, myself have lim'd a bush for her, / And plac'd a quire of such enticing birds / That she will light to listen to the lays, / And never mount to trouble you again. / So, let her rest; and, madam, list to me, / For I am bold to counsel you in this. / Although we fancy not the cardinal, / Yet must we join with him and with the lords / Till we have brought Duke Humphrey in disgrace. / As for the Duke of York, this late complaint / Will make but little for his benefit. / So, one by one, we'll weed them all at last, / And you yourself shall steer the happy helm.

Madam, I've set a trap for her, smeared a bush with birdlime and placed a choir of such tempting birds there that she'll land to listen to their songs and never fly up to trouble you again. So leave her alone, and listen to me, madam, for I'm bold enough to advise you. Though we don't like the cardinal, we must join with him and the lords until we've brought Duke Humphrey into disgrace. As for the Duke of York, this recent accusation won't do him much good. So one by one we'll weed them all out at last, and you yourself will steer the ship of state.
For my part, noble lords, I care not which; / Or Somerset or York, all's one to me.
For my part, noble lords, I don't mind which, Somerset or York; it's all the same to me.
If York have ill demean'd himself in France, / Then let him be denay'd the regentship.
If York has behaved badly in France, then let him be refused the regentship.
If Somerset be unworthy of the place, / Let York be regent; I will yield to him.
If Somerset is unworthy of the post, let York be regent; I'll give way to him.
Whether your grace be worthy, yea or no, / Dispute not that; York is the worthier.
Whether your grace is worthy or not, don't argue about it: York is the worthier.
Ambitious Warwick, let thy betters speak.
Ambitious Warwick, let your betters speak.
The cardinal's not my better in the field.
The cardinal is not my better on the battlefield.
All in this presence are thy betters, Warwick.
Everyone here is your better, Warwick.
Warwick may live to be the best of all.
Warwick may live to be the best of all.
Peace, son!—and show some reason, Buckingham, / Why Somerset should be preferr'd in this.
Quiet, son! And Buckingham, give some reason why Somerset should be preferred.
Because the king, forsooth, will have it so.
Because the king, of course, wants it so.
Madam, the King is old enough himself / To give his censure; these are no women's matters.
Madam, the king is old enough to give his own judgement. These are not women's affairs.
If he be old enough, what needs your grace / To be protector of his excellence?
If he's old enough, why does your grace need to be his Protector?
Madam, I am protector of the realm, / And, at his pleasure, will resign my place.
Madam, I am Protector of the kingdom, and I will resign my post when he wishes.

Resign it then, and leave thine insolence. / Since thou wert king—as who is king but thou?— / The commonwealth hath daily run to wrack; / The Dauphin hath prevail'd beyond the seas; / And all the peers and nobles of the realm / Have been as bondmen to thy sovereignty.

Then resign it, and stop your insolence. Since you became king, for who is king but you?, the state has been going to ruin every day. The Dauphin has won abroad, and all the lords of the realm have been like slaves under your rule.
The commons hast thou rack'd; the clergy's bags / Are lank and lean with thy extortions.
You have squeezed the common people, and the clergy's purses are thin and empty from your demands.
Thy sumptuous buildings and thy wife's attire / Have cost a mass of public treasury.
Your expensive buildings and your wife's clothes have cost a fortune of public money.
Thy cruelty in execution / Upon offenders hath exceeded law, / And left thee to the mercy of the law.
Your cruelty in punishing criminals has gone beyond the law, and leaves you at the law's mercy.
Thy sale of offices and towns in France, / If they were known, as the suspect is great, / Would make thee quickly hop without thy head.—
Your sale of offices and towns in France, if it were known, and it is strongly suspected, would soon have you hopping about without your head.
Give me my fan. What minion! can ye not?
Give me my fan. What, you hussy! Can't you?
I cry your mercy, madam; was it you?
I beg your pardon, madam; was it you?
Was 't I! yea, I it was, proud Frenchwoman. / Could I come near your beauty with my nails, / I'd set my ten commandments in your face.
Was it me? Yes, it was me, you proud Frenchwoman. If I could get near your pretty face with my nails, I'd write my ten commandments on it.
Sweet aunt, be quiet; 't was against her will.
Sweet aunt, be quiet. She didn't mean it.
Against her will! good king, look to 't in time; / She'll hamper thee and dandle thee like a baby. / Though in this place most master wear no breeches, / She shall not strike Dame Eleanor unreveng'd.
Didn't mean it! Good king, watch out in time. She'll tie you up and dandle you like a baby. Though the person who wears the trousers here is no man, she won't strike Dame Eleanor without revenge.
Lord cardinal, I will follow Eleanor, / And listen after Humphrey, how he proceeds. / She's tickled now; her fume needs no spurs, / She'll gallop far enough to her destruction.
Lord Cardinal, I'll follow Eleanor and keep an ear on what Humphrey does. She's stirred up now; her temper needs no spurs; she'll gallop far enough to her own ruin.

Now, lords, my choler being overblown / With walking once about the quadrangle, / I come to talk of commonwealth affairs. / As for your spiteful false objections, / Prove them, and I lie open to the law; / But God in mercy so deal with my soul / As I in duty love my king and country! / But, to the matter that we have in hand: / I say, my sovereign, York is meetest man / To be your regent in the realm of France.

Now, lords, my anger has blown over after one walk around the courtyard, and I've come to talk about state business. As for your spiteful false charges, prove them and I'll answer to the law. But may God treat my soul as mercifully as I dutifully love my king and country! But to the matter in hand: I say, my sovereign, York is the best man to be your regent in France.
Before we make election, give me leave / To show some reason, of no little force, / That York is most unmeet of any man.
Before we choose, let me give a strong reason why York is the most unfit man of all.

I'll tell thee, Suffolk, why I am unmeet: / First, for I cannot flatter thee in pride; / Next, if I be appointed for the place, / My Lord of Somerset will keep me here, / Without discharge, money, or furniture, / Till France be won into the Dauphin's hands. / Last time, I danc'd attendance on his will / Till Paris was besieg'd, famish'd, and lost.

I'll tell you why I'm unfit, Suffolk. First, because I can't flatter your pride. Next, if I'm appointed, my Lord of Somerset will keep me waiting here without commission, money or equipment until France falls into the Dauphin's hands. Last time I hung about at his pleasure until Paris was besieged, starved and lost.
That can I witness; and a fouler fact / Did never traitor in the land commit.
I can swear to that, and no traitor in this land ever did a fouler deed.
Image of pride, why should I hold my peace?
You picture of pride, why should I keep quiet?
Because here is a man accus'd of treason. / Pray God the Duke of York excuse himself!
Because here is a man accused of treason. Pray God the Duke of York can clear himself!
Doth any one accuse York for a traitor?
Does anyone accuse York of being a traitor?
What mean'st thou, Suffolk? tell me, what are these?
What do you mean, Suffolk? Tell me, who are these?

Please it your majesty, this is the man / That doth accuse his master of high treason. / His words were these: that Richard Duke of York / Was rightful heir unto the English crown, / And that your majesty was an usurper.

If it please your Majesty, this is the man who accuses his master of high treason. His words were that Richard Duke of York was the rightful heir to the English crown and that your Majesty was a usurper.
Say, man, were these thy words?
Tell me, man, did you say this?
An 't shall please your majesty, I never said nor / thought any such matter; God is my witness, I am / falsely accused by the villain.
If it please your Majesty, I never said or thought any such thing. God is my witness, this villain accuses me falsely.
By these ten bones, my lords, he did speak them to / me in the garret one night, as we were scouring my Lord of / York's armour.
By these ten fingers, my lords, he said it to me one night in the attic while we were cleaning my Lord of York's armour.
Base dunghill villain and mechanical, / I'll have thy head for this thy traitor's speech.— / I do beseech your royal majesty, / Let him have all the rigour of the law.
Low, filthy, working-class villain, I'll have your head for this treasonous talk. I beg your royal Majesty, give him the full force of the law.

Alas, my lord, hang me if ever I spake the words. My / accuser is my prentice; and when I did correct him for his fault / the other day, he did vow upon his knees he would be even with / me. I have good witness of this; therefore I beseech your / majesty, do not cast away an honest man for a villain's / accusation.

Alas, my lord, hang me if I ever said those words. My accuser is my apprentice, and when I punished him for a fault the other day, he swore on his knees he'd get even with me. I have good witnesses to this, so I beg your Majesty not to throw away an honest man on a villain's accusation.
Uncle, what shall we say to this in law?
Uncle, what does the law say about this?

This doom, my lord, if I may judge: / Let Somerset be Regent o'er the French, / Because in York this breeds suspicion; / And let these have a day appointed them / For single combat in convenient place, / For he hath witness of his servant's malice. / This is the law, and this Duke Humphrey's doom.

This is my judgement, my lord. Let Somerset be regent over France, since this case puts York under suspicion. And let these two be given a day for single combat in a suitable place, since the master has witnesses to his servant's malice. This is the law, and Duke Humphrey's judgement.
I humbly thank your royal Majesty.
I humbly thank your royal Majesty.
And I accept the combat willingly.
And I accept the combat willingly.
Alas, my lord, I cannot fight; for God's sake, pity my case. / The spite of man prevaileth against me. O Lord, have mercy / upon me! I shall never be able to fight a blow! O Lord, my heart!
Alas, my lord, I can't fight! For God's sake, pity me. Man's spite is beating me. O Lord, have mercy on me! I'll never be able to strike a blow! O Lord, my heart!
Sirrah, or you must fight or else be hang'd.
Fellow, you must either fight or be hanged.
Away with them to prison; and the day of combat shall / be the last of the next month.—Come, Somerset, we'll see thee / sent away.
Take them away to prison, and the day of combat will be the last day of next month. Come, Somerset, we'll see you off.
Come, my masters; the duchess, I tell you, expects / performance of your promises.
Come, gentlemen, the duchess, I tell you, expects you to keep your promises.
Master Hume, we are therefore provided; / will her ladyship behold and hear our exorcisms?
Master Hume, we're ready for that. Will her ladyship watch and listen to our conjuring?
Ay, what else? fear you not her courage.
Yes, what else? Don't worry about her courage.

I have heard her reported to be a woman of an invincible spirit: / but it shall be convenient, Master Hume, that you be by her / aloft while we be busy below; and so, I pray you go, in God's / name, and leave us.—[Exit Hume] Mother Jourdain, be you / prostrate and grovel on the earth.—John Southwell, read you; and / let us to our work.

I've heard she is a woman of unbeatable spirit. But it would be best, Master Hume, if you were up above with her while we're busy down here. So please go, in God's name, and leave us. (Exit Hume) Mother Jourdain, lie flat and grovel on the ground. John Southwell, you read, and let's get to work.
Well said, my masters; and welcome all. To this gear / the sooner the better.
Well said, gentlemen, and welcome all. Let's get on with this business, the sooner the better.

Patience, good lady, wizards know their times: / Deep night, dark night, the silent of the night, / The time of night when Troy was set on fire, / The time when screech-owls cry and ban-dogs howl / And spirits walk and ghosts break up their graves, / That time best fits the work we have in hand. / Madam, sit you and fear not; whom we raise, / We will make fast within a hallow'd verge.

Patience, good lady; wizards know their hours. Deep night, dark night, the silence of the night, the hour when Troy was set on fire, when screech owls cry and watchdogs howl, when spirits walk and ghosts burst from their graves: that time best suits our work. Madam, sit down and don't be afraid. Whatever we raise, we'll hold fast inside a holy circle.
Asmath, / By the eternal God, whose name and power / Thou tremblest at, answer that I shall ask; / For till thou speak thou shalt not pass from hence.
Asmath, by the eternal God whose name and power make you tremble, answer what I ask, for until you speak you shall not leave here.
Ask what thou wilt. That I had said and done!
Ask what you like. I wish I'd answered and was done!
[Reads] 'First of the king: what shall / of him become?'
(Reading) "First, about the king: what will become of him?"
The duke yet lives that Henry shall depose, / But him outlive and die a violent death.
The duke is still alive who will depose Henry, but Henry will outlive him, and the duke will die a violent death.
'What fates await the Duke of Suffolk?'
"What fate awaits the Duke of Suffolk?"
By water shall he die and take his end.
He will die by water and meet his end.
[Reads] 'What shall befall the Duke of Somerset?'
(Reading) "What will happen to the Duke of Somerset?"
Let him shun castles; / Safer shall he be upon the sandy plains / Than where castles mounted stand. / Have done, for more I hardly can endure.
Let him avoid castles. He will be safer on the sandy plains than where castles stand on hills. Finish, for I can hardly bear any more.
Descend to darkness and the burning lake! / False fiend, avoid!
Go down to darkness and the burning lake! Lying devil, be gone!

Lay hands upon these traitors and their trash.— / Beldam, I think we watch'd you at an inch. / What, madam, are you there? the king and commonweal / Are deeply indebted for this piece of pains; / My lord protector will, I doubt it not, / See you well guerdon'd for these good deserts.

Arrest these traitors and their junk. Old hag, I think we watched you closely. What, madam, are you there? The king and the country owe you a great deal for this effort. My Lord Protector, I'm sure, will see you well rewarded for these good services.
Not half so bad as thine to England's king, / Injurious duke, that threatest where's no cause.
Not half as well as you deserve from England's king, insulting duke, threatening where there's no cause.
True, madam, none at all; what call you this?— / Away with them! let them be clapp'd up close, / And kept asunder.—You, madam, shall with us.— / Stafford, take her to thee.—
True, madam, no cause at all. What do you call this? Take them away! Lock them up tight and keep them apart. You, madam, will come with us. Stafford, take charge of her.
We'll see your trinkets here all forthcoming.— / All, away!
We'll make sure all your trinkets here are produced as evidence. Everyone, away!

Lord Buckingham, methinks you watch'd her well; / A pretty plot, well chosen to build upon! / Now, pray, my lord, let's see the devil's writ. / What have we here? / [Reads] 'The duke yet lives that Henry shall depose. / But him outlive and die a violent death.' / Why, this is just / 'Aio te, Aeacida, Romanos vincere posse.' / Well, to the rest: / 'Tell me what fate awaits the Duke of Suffolk? / By water shall he die and take his end. / What shall betide the Duke of Somerset? / Let him shun castles; / Safer shall he be upon the sandy plains / Than where castles mounted stand.'— / Come, come, my lords; / These oracles are hardly attain'd, / And hardly understood. / The king is now in progress towards Saint Alban's, / With him the husband of this lovely lady. / Thither go these news, as fast as horse can carry them; / A sorry breakfast for my lord protector.

Lord Buckingham, I think you watched her well. A nice plot, a good one to build on! Now, my lord, let's see the devil's writing. What have we here? (Reading) "The duke is still alive who will depose Henry, but Henry will outlive him, and the duke will die a violent death." Why, this is exactly like the old oracle "I say that you, son of Aeacus, the Romans can conquer", which could mean either. Well, the rest: "Tell me what fate awaits the Duke of Suffolk? He will die by water and meet his end. What will happen to the Duke of Somerset? Let him avoid castles; he will be safer on the sandy plains than where castles stand on hills." Come, come, my lords, these oracles are hard to get and hard to understand. The king is now on his way to St Albans, and with him this lovely lady's husband. This news must go there as fast as a horse can carry it. A sad breakfast for my Lord Protector.
Your Grace shall give me leave, my / Lord of York, / To be the post, in hope of his reward.
Your grace will allow me, my Lord of York, to be the messenger, in hope of his reward.
At your pleasure, my good lord.— / Who's within there, ho!
As you please, my good lord. Who's in there?
Invite my Lords of Salisbury and Warwick / To sup with me to-morrow night. Away!
Invite my Lords of Salisbury and Warwick to have supper with me tomorrow night. Go!
Believe me, lords, for flying at the brook, / I saw not better sport these seven years' day; / Yet, by your leave, the wind was very high, / And, ten to one, old Joan had not gone out.
Believe me, lords, for hawking at water birds I haven't seen better sport in seven years. Though, if I may say so, the wind was very high, and ten to one old Joan wouldn't have flown at all.
But what a point, my lord, your falcon made, / And what a pitch she flew above the rest! / To see how God in all His creatures works! / Yea, man and birds are fain of climbing high.
But what a position your falcon took, my lord, and how high she flew above the rest! See how God works in all His creatures! Yes, men and birds both love to climb high.
No marvel, an it like your majesty, / My lord protector's hawks do tower so well; / They know their master loves to be aloft, / And bears his thoughts above his falcon's pitch.
No wonder, if it please your Majesty, my Lord Protector's hawks fly so high. They know their master loves to be up high and carries his thoughts above his falcon's flight.
My lord, 't is but a base ignoble mind / That mounts no higher than a bird can soar.
My lord, it's a low, mean mind that rises no higher than a bird can fly.
I thought as much; he would be above the clouds.
I thought so; he'd like to be above the clouds.
Ay, my lord cardinal? how think you by that? / Were it not good your grace could fly to heaven?
Yes, my lord cardinal? What do you mean by that? Wouldn't it be good if your grace could fly to heaven?
The treasure house of everlasting joy.
Thy heaven is on earth; thine eyes and thoughts / Beat on a crown, the treasure of thy heart, / Pernicious protector, dangerous peer, / That smooth'st it so with king and commonweal.
Your heaven is on earth. Your eyes and thoughts are fixed on a crown, your heart's treasure, you harmful Protector, you dangerous lord, who flatter your way so smoothly with king and country.
What, cardinal, is your priesthood grown peremptory? / Tantaene animis coelestibus irae? / Churchmen so hot? good uncle, hide such malice; / With such holiness can you do it?
What, cardinal, has your priesthood become so bossy? "Is there such anger in heavenly minds?" Churchmen so hot-tempered? Good uncle, hide such malice. Can you do it, being so holy?
No malice, sir; no more than well becomes / So good a quarrel and so bad a peer.
No malice, sir; no more than suits so good a quarrel against so bad a lord.
Why, as you, my lord, / An 't like your lordly lord-protectorship.
Why, like you, my lord, if it please your lordly Lord Protectorship.
Why, Suffolk, England knows thine insolence.
Why, Suffolk, all England knows your insolence.
I prithee, peace, good queen, / And whet not on these furious peers; / For blessed are the peacemakers on earth.
Please, peace, good queen, and don't stir up these furious lords, for blessed are the peacemakers on earth.
Let me be blessed for the peace I make / Against this proud protector, with my sword!
Then let me be blessed for the peace I make with my sword against this proud Protector!
[Aside to Cardinal] Faith, holy uncle, would 't / were come to that!
(Aside to Cardinal) Truly, holy uncle, I wish it would come to that!
[Aside to Gloster] Marry, when thou dar'st.
(Aside to Gloucester) Indeed, whenever you dare.
[Aside to Cardinal] Make up no factious numbers / for the matter; / In thine own person answer thy abuse.
(Aside to Cardinal) Don't gather a gang of supporters for this; answer for your insults in person.
[Aside to Gloster] Ay, where thou dar'st not peep; / an if thou dar'st, / This evening, on the east side of the grove.
(Aside to Gloucester) Yes, where you won't dare show your face; and if you do dare, this evening, on the east side of the wood.
Believe me, cousin Gloster, / Had not your man put up the fowl so suddenly, / We had had more sport.—[Aside to Gloster] Come with thy / two-hand sword.
Believe me, cousin Gloucester, if your servant hadn't flushed the bird so suddenly, we'd have had more sport. (Aside to Gloucester) Bring your two-handed sword.
[Aside to Gloster] Are ye advis'd? the east side / of the grove?
(Aside to Gloucester) Are you agreed? The east side of the wood?
[Aside to CARDINAL] Cardinal, I am with you.
(Aside to Cardinal) Cardinal, I'll be there.
Talking of hawking; nothing else, my lord.— / [Aside to Cardinal] Now, by God's mother, priest, / I'll shave your crown for this, / Or all my fence shall fail.
Talking about hawking, nothing else, my lord. (Aside to Cardinal) By God's mother, priest, I'll shave your tonsured head for this, or all my swordsmanship will fail.
[Aside to Gloster] Medice, teipsum— / Protector, see to 't well, protect yourself.
(Aside to Gloucester) "Physician, heal yourself." Protector, take care; protect yourself.
The winds grow high; so do your stomachs, lords. / How irksome is this music to my heart! / When such strings jar, what hope of harmony? / I pray, my lords, let me compound this strife.

The winds are getting high, and so are your tempers, lords. How painful this music is to my heart! When such strings clash, what hope is there of harmony? Please, my lords, let me settle this quarrel.
What means this noise? / Fellow, what miracle dost thou proclaim?
What's this noise? Fellow, what miracle are you announcing?
Come to the king, and tell him what miracle.
Come to the king and tell him what miracle.
Forsooth, a blind man at Saint Alban's shrine, / Within this half hour, hath receiv'd his sight; / A man that ne'er saw in his life before.
Truly, a blind man at St Alban's shrine has received his sight within the last half hour, a man who never saw in his life before.
Now, God be prais'd, that to believing souls / Gives light in darkness, comfort in despair!
God be praised, who gives light in darkness and comfort in despair to believers!
Here comes the townsmen on procession, / To present your highness with the man.
Here come the townspeople in procession to present the man to your highness.
Great is his comfort in this earthly vale, / Although by his sight his sin be multiplied.
Great is his comfort in this earthly valley, even though seeing may multiply his chances to sin.
Stand by, my masters. / Bring him near the king; / His highness' pleasure is to talk with him.
Stand aside, friends. Bring him near the king; his highness wants to talk with him.
Good fellow, tell us here the circumstance, / That we for thee may glorify the Lord. / What, hast thou been long blind and now restor'd?
Good fellow, tell us what happened, so that we can praise the Lord for you. Have you been blind long, and now been cured?
Born blind, an 't please your grace.
Born blind, if it please your grace.
His wife, an 't like your worship.
His wife, if it please your worship.
Hadst thou been his mother, thou couldst / have better told.
If you'd been his mother, you could have told us better.
At Berwick in the north, an 't like your grace.
At Berwick in the north, if it please your grace.
Poor soul, God's goodness hath been great to thee; / Let never day nor night unhallow'd pass, / But still remember what the Lord hath done.
Poor soul, God has been very good to you. Never let a day or night pass without giving thanks, but always remember what the Lord has done.
Tell me, good fellow, cam'st thou here by chance, / Or of devotion, to this holy shrine?
Tell me, good fellow, did you come to this holy shrine by chance, or out of devotion?
God knows, of pure devotion; being call'd / A hundred times and oftener, in my sleep, / By good Saint Alban, who said 'Simpcox, come, / Come, offer at my shrine, and I will help thee.'
God knows, out of pure devotion, having been called a hundred times and more in my sleep by good St Alban, who said, "Simpcox, come, come and make an offering at my shrine, and I'll help you."
Most true, forsooth; and many time and oft / Myself have heard a voice to call him so.
Very true, indeed; and many times I've heard a voice call him like that myself.
A fall off of a tree.
I fell out of a tree.
How long hast thou been blind?
How long have you been blind?
Oh, I was born that way, master!
What, and wouldst climb a tree?
What, and you climbed a tree?
But that in all my life, when I was a youth.
Only once in my life, when I was young.
Too true; and bought his climbing very dear.
Too true, and he paid dearly for that climb.
Mass, thou lov'dst plums well that wouldst venture so.
By the mass, you must have loved plums to take such a risk.
Alas, good master, my wife desir'd some damsons, / And made me climb, with danger of my life.
Alas, good master, my wife wanted some damsons and made me climb, at risk of my life.
A subtle knave! but yet it shall not serve.— / Let me see thine eyes.—Wink now;—now open them. / In my opinion yet thou seest not well.
A cunning rogue! But it won't work. Let me see your eyes. Shut them now; now open them. In my opinion you still don't see well.
Yes, master, clear as day, I thank God and Saint Alban.
Yes, master, clear as day, thanks to God and St Alban.
Say'st thou me so? What colour is this cloak of?
Is that so? What colour is this cloak?
Why, that's well said. What colour is my gown of?
Well said. What colour is my gown?
Why, then, thou know'st what colour jet is of?
Why, then, you know what colour jet is?
And yet, I think, jet did he never see.
And yet I think he never saw jet.
But cloaks and gowns before this day, a many.
But he's seen plenty of cloaks and gowns before today.
Never before this day in all his life.
Never before today in all his life.
Tell me, sirrah, what's my name?
Tell me, fellow, what's my name?
Saunder Simpcox, an if it please you, master.
Saunder Simpcox, if it please you, master.

Then, Saunder, sit there, the lyingest knave in / Christendom. If thou hadst been born blind, thou mightst as well / have known all our names as thus to name the several colours we / do wear. Sight may distinguish of colours; but suddenly to / nominate them all, it is impossible.—My lords, Saint Alban here / hath done a miracle; and would ye not think his cunning to be / great that could restore this cripple to his legs again?

Then, Saunder, sit there, the biggest liar in Christendom. If you'd been born blind, you could just as easily have known all our names as named the different colours we're wearing. Sight can tell colours apart, but to name them all suddenly is impossible. My lords, St Alban has done a miracle here; but wouldn't you think a man very clever who could restore this cripple to his legs?
Oh master, if only you could!
My masters of Saint Alban's, have you not beadles in / your town, and things called whips?
Gentlemen of St Albans, don't you have parish officers in your town, and things called whips?
Yes, my lord, if it please your grace.
Yes, my lord, if it please your grace.
Then send for one at once.
Sirrah, go fetch the beadle hither straight.
You there, go and fetch the beadle here straight away.
Now fetch me a stool hither by and by.—Now, sirrah, / if you mean to save yourself from whipping, leap me over this / stool and run away.
Now bring me a stool here quickly. Now, fellow, if you want to save yourself from a whipping, jump over this stool and run away.
Alas, master, I am not able to stand alone; / You go about to torture me in vain.
Alas, master, I can't even stand on my own. You're trying to torture me for nothing.
Well, sir, we must have you find your legs.— / Sirrah beadle, whip him till he leap over that same stool.
Well, sir, we must help you find your legs. Beadle, whip him till he jumps over that stool.
I will, my lord.—Come on, sirrah; off with your doublet / quickly.
I will, my lord. Come on, fellow, take off your jacket quickly.
Alas, master, what shall I do? I am not able to stand.
Alas, master, what shall I do? I can't stand.
O God, seest Thou this, and bearest so long?
O God, do you see this, and put up with it so long?
It made me laugh to see the villain run.
It made me laugh to see the villain run.
Follow the knave, and take this drab away.
Follow the rogue, and take this slut away.
Alas, sir, we did it for pure need!
Alas, sir, we did it out of sheer poverty!
Let them be whipped through every market-town / till they come to Berwick, from whence they came.
Let them be whipped through every market town until they get back to Berwick, where they came from.
Duke Humphrey has done a miracle to-day.
Duke Humphrey has done a miracle today.
True; made the lame to leap and fly away.
True: made the lame leap and run away.
But you have done more miracles than I; / You made in a day, my lord, whole towns to fly.
But you've done more miracles than I have. In a single day, my lord, you made whole towns run away.
What tidings with our cousin Buckingham?

Such as my heart doth tremble to unfold. / A sort of naughty persons, lewdly bent, / Under the countenance and confederacy / Of Lady Eleanor, the protector's wife, / The ringleader and head of all this rout, / Have practis'd dangerously against your state, / Dealing with witches and with conjurers, / Whom we have apprehended in the fact, / Raising up wicked spirits from underground, / Demanding of King Henry's life and death, / And other of your highness' privy-council, / As more at large your Grace shall understand.

News my heart trembles to reveal. A gang of wicked people, bent on evil, with the support and partnership of Lady Eleanor, the Protector's wife, the ringleader and head of the whole crew, have plotted dangerously against your state, dealing with witches and conjurers, whom we caught in the act raising evil spirits from underground and asking about King Henry's life and death, and about others of your highness's privy council, as your grace will hear in more detail.

[Aside to Gloster] And so, my lord protector, / by this means / Your lady is forthcoming yet at London. / This news, I think, hath turn'd your weapon's edge; / 'T is like, my lord, you will not keep your hour.
(Aside to Gloucester) And so, my Lord Protector, your lady is now in custody in London. This news, I think, has blunted your sword; it seems, my lord, you won't keep our appointment.
Ambitious churchman, leave to afflict my heart. / Sorrow and grief have vanquish'd all my powers; / And, vanquish'd as I am, I yield to thee, / Or to the meanest groom.
Ambitious churchman, stop tormenting my heart. Sorrow and grief have beaten all my strength, and beaten as I am, I give in to you, or to the lowest servant.
O God, what mischiefs work the wicked ones, / Heaping confusion on their own heads thereby!
O God, what harm the wicked do, heaping confusion on their own heads by it!
Gloster, see here the tainture of thy nest; / And look thyself be faultless, thou wert best.
Gloucester, look at the stain on your nest, and you'd better make sure you yourself are blameless.

Madam, for myself, to heaven I do appeal, / How I have lov'd my king and commonweal; / And, for my wife, I know not how it stands. / Sorry I am to hear what I have heard; / Noble she is; but if she have forgot / Honour and virtue, and convers'd with such / As like to pitch defile nobility, / I banish her my bed and company, / And give her as a prey to law and shame, / That hath dishonoured Gloster's honest name.

Madam, as for myself, I appeal to heaven to witness how I have loved my king and country. As for my wife, I don't know how things stand. I'm sorry to hear what I've heard. She is noble, but if she has forgotten honour and virtue and mixed with people who, like pitch, stain nobility, I banish her from my bed and company and hand her over to the law and to shame, since she has dishonoured Gloucester's honest name.

Well, for this night we will repose us here; / To-morrow toward London back again, / To look into this business thoroughly, / And call these foul offenders to their answers, / And poise the cause in justice' equal scales, / Whose beam stands sure, whose rightful cause prevails.

Well, we'll rest here tonight. Tomorrow we'll go back to London to look into this business thoroughly, call these foul offenders to answer, and weigh the case in the even scales of justice, whose beam stays steady and where the right side wins.

Now, my good Lords of Salisbury and Warwick, / Our simple supper ended, give me leave / In this close walk to satisfy myself, / In craving your opinion of my title, / Which is infallible, to England's crown.
Now, my good Lords of Salisbury and Warwick, our simple supper is over. Let me take this private walk to satisfy myself by asking your opinion of my claim to England's crown, which cannot be faulted.
My lord, I long to hear it at full.
My lord, I long to hear it in full.
Sweet York, begin; and if thy claim be good, / The Nevils are thy subjects to command.
Sweet York, begin; and if your claim is good, the Nevilles are your subjects to command.

Then thus: / Edward the Third, my lords, had seven sons: / The first, Edward the Black Prince, Prince of Wales; / The second, William of Hatfield; and the third, / Lionel Duke of Clarence; next to whom / Was John of Gaunt, the Duke of Lancaster; / The fifth was Edmund Langley, Duke of York; / The sixth was Thomas of Woodstock, Duke of Gloster; / William of Windsor was the seventh and last. / Edward the Black Prince died before his father / And left behind him Richard, his only son, / Who after Edward the Third's death reign'd as king; / Till Henry Bolingbroke, Duke of Lancaster, / The eldest son and heir of John of Gaunt, / Crown'd by the name of Henry the Fourth, / Seiz'd on the realm, depos'd the rightful king, / Sent his poor queen to France, from whence she came, / And him to Pomfret, where, as all you know, / Harmless Richard was murther'd traitorously.

Then here it is. Edward the Third, my lords, had seven sons. The first was Edward the Black Prince, Prince of Wales; the second, William of Hatfield; the third, Lionel Duke of Clarence; next came John of Gaunt, Duke of Lancaster; the fifth was Edmund Langley, Duke of York; the sixth was Thomas of Woodstock, Duke of Gloucester; William of Windsor was the seventh and last. Edward the Black Prince died before his father and left Richard, his only son, who reigned as king after Edward the Third's death, until Henry Bolingbroke, Duke of Lancaster, eldest son and heir of John of Gaunt, crowned as Henry the Fourth, seized the kingdom, deposed the rightful king, sent his poor queen back to France where she came from, and sent him to Pomfret, where, as you all know, harmless Richard was treacherously murdered.
Father, the duke hath told the truth; / Thus got the house of Lancaster the crown.
Father, the duke has told the truth. That's how the house of Lancaster got the crown.
Which now they hold by force and not by right; / For Richard, the first son's heir, being dead, / The issue of the next son should have reign'd.
Which they now hold by force and not by right. For since Richard, the first son's heir, was dead, the descendants of the next son should have reigned.
But William of Hatfield died without an heir.
But William of Hatfield died without an heir.

The third son, Duke of Clarence, from whose line / I claim the crown, had issue, Philippe, a daughter, / Who married Edmund Mortimer, Earl of March. / Edmund had issue, Roger Earl of March; / Roger had issue, Edmund, Anne, and Eleanor.

The third son, the Duke of Clarence, from whose line I claim the crown, had a daughter, Philippa, who married Edmund Mortimer, Earl of March. Edmund had a son, Roger, Earl of March; Roger had children Edmund, Anne and Eleanor.
This Edmund, in the reign of Bolingbroke, / As I have read, laid claim unto the crown; / And, but for Owen Glendower, had been king, / Who kept him in captivity till he died. / But to the rest.
This Edmund, in Bolingbroke's reign, as I've read, claimed the crown, and would have been king but for Owen Glendower, who kept him prisoner until he died. But go on.

His eldest sister, Anne, / My mother, being heir unto the crown, / Married Richard Earl of Cambridge, who was son / To Edmund Langley, Edward the Third's fifth son. / By her I claim the kingdom; she was heir / To Roger Earl of March, who was the son / Of Edmund Mortimer, who married Philippe, / Sole daughter unto Lionel Duke of Clarence. / So, if the issue of the elder son / Succeed before the younger, I am king.

His eldest sister, Anne, my mother, heir to the crown, married Richard Earl of Cambridge, son of Edmund Langley, Edward the Third's fifth son. Through her I claim the kingdom. She was heir to Roger Earl of March, son of Edmund Mortimer, who married Philippa, only daughter of Lionel Duke of Clarence. So if the descendants of the elder son come before the younger, I am king.

What plain proceeding is more plain than this? / Henry doth claim the crown from John of Gaunt, / The fourth son; York claims it from the third. / Till Lionel's issue fails, his should not reign; / It fails not yet, but flourishes in thee / And in thy sons, fair slips of such a stock.— / Then, father Salisbury, kneel we together; / And in this private plot be we the first / That shall salute our rightful sovereign / With honour of his birthright to the crown.

What could be plainer than this? Henry claims the crown from John of Gaunt, the fourth son; York claims it from the third. Until Lionel's line dies out, Gaunt's should not reign. It hasn't died out but flourishes in you and your sons, fine shoots from such a stem. So, father Salisbury, let's kneel together, and in this private place be the first to salute our rightful sovereign and honour his birthright to the crown.
Long live our sovereign Richard, England's king!
Long live our sovereign Richard, England's king!

We thank you, lords. But I am not your king / Till I be crown'd, and that my sword be stain'd / With heart-blood of the house of Lancaster; / And that's not suddenly to be perform'd, / But with advice and silent secrecy. / Do you as I do in these dangerous days,— / Wink at the Duke of Suffolk's insolence, / At Beaufort's pride, at Somerset's ambition, / At Buckingham, and all the crew of them, / Till they have snar'd the shepherd of the flock, / That virtuous prince, the good Duke Humphrey; / 'T is that they seek, and they in seeking that / Shall find their deaths, if York can prophesy.

Thank you, lords. But I'm not your king until I'm crowned and my sword is stained with the heart's blood of the house of Lancaster. That can't be done suddenly, but with careful planning and silent secrecy. In these dangerous days, do as I do: turn a blind eye to the Duke of Suffolk's insolence, Beaufort's pride, Somerset's ambition, Buckingham and their whole crew, until they have trapped the shepherd of the flock, that virtuous prince, good Duke Humphrey. That's what they're after, and in getting it they'll find their own deaths, if York can foretell anything.
My lord, break we off; we know your mind at full.
My lord, let's stop here; we know your mind fully.
My heart assures me that the Earl of Warwick / Shall one day make the Duke of York a king.
My heart tells me that the Earl of Warwick will one day make the Duke of York a king.
And, Nevil, this I do assure myself: / Richard shall live to make the Earl of Warwick / The greatest man in England but the king.
And Neville, I promise myself this: Richard will live to make the Earl of Warwick the greatest man in England after the king.

Stand forth, Dame Eleanor Cobham, Gloster's wife. / In sight of God and us, your guilt is great; / Receive the sentence of the law for sins / Such as by God's book are adjudg'd to death.— / You four, from hence to prison back again, / From thence unto the place of execution. / The witch in Smithfield shall be burn'd to ashes, / And you three shall be strangled on the gallows.— / You, madam, for you are more nobly born, / Despoiled of your honour in your life, / Shall, after three days' open penance done, / Live in your country here in banishment, / With Sir John Stanley, in the Isle of Man.

Step forward, Dame Eleanor Cobham, Gloucester's wife. In the sight of God and us, your guilt is great. Receive the law's sentence for sins that God's book judges worthy of death. You four, go back to prison from here, and from there to the place of execution. The witch will be burned to ashes in Smithfield, and you three will be hanged on the gallows.
