You, madam, because you are more nobly born, will lose your honour for the rest of your life, and after three days of public penance will live in banishment within this country, in the Isle of Man, in Sir John Stanley's charge.
Welcome is banishment; welcome were my death.
Banishment is welcome; death would be welcome.
Eleanor, the law, thou seest, hath judged thee; / I cannot justify whom the law condemns.—
Eleanor, you see the law has judged you; I can't defend someone the law condemns.

Mine eyes are full of tears, my heart of grief. / Ah, Humphrey, this dishonour in thine age / Will bring thy head with sorrow to the ground!— / I beseech your majesty, give me leave to go; / Sorrow would solace, and mine age would ease.

My eyes are full of tears, my heart of grief. Ah, Humphrey, this disgrace in your old age will bring your head down to the grave with sorrow! I beg your Majesty to let me go; my grief wants comfort and my age wants rest.

Stay, Humphrey Duke of Gloster. / Ere thou go, / Give up thy staff; Henry will to himself / Protector be, and God shall be my hope, / My stay, my guide, and lantern to my feet. / And go in peace, Humphrey, no less belov'd / Than when thou wert protector to thy king.

Wait, Humphrey Duke of Gloucester. Before you go, hand over your staff. Henry will be his own Protector, and God will be my hope, my support, my guide and the lamp for my feet. And go in peace, Humphrey, loved no less than when you were your king's Protector.
I see no reason why a king of years / Should be to be protected like a child.— / God and King Henry govern England's realm. / Give up your staff, sir, and the king his realm.
I see no reason why a grown-up king needs to be protected like a child. God and King Henry govern England. Give up your staff, sir, and give the king his kingdom.

My staff? Here, noble Henry, is my staff. / As willingly do I the same resign / As e'er thy father Henry made it mine; / And even as willingly at thy feet I leave it / As others would ambitiously receive it. / Farewell, good king; when I am dead and gone, / May honourable peace attend thy throne!

My staff? Here, noble Henry, is my staff. I give it up as willingly as your father Henry ever gave it to me, and I leave it at your feet as gladly as others would greedily take it. Farewell, good king. When I'm dead and gone, may honourable peace surround your throne!

Why, now is Henry king, and Margaret queen; / And Humphrey Duke of Gloster scarce himself, / That bears so shrewd a maim; two pulls at once— / His lady banish'd, and a limb lopp'd off. / This staff of honour raught, there let it stand / Where it best fits to be, in Henry's hand.

Why, now Henry is king and Margaret queen, and Humphrey Duke of Gloucester hardly himself after such a wound; two blows at once, his wife banished and a limb cut off. Now this staff of honour has been taken, let it stay where it belongs, in Henry's hand.
Thus droops this lofty pine and hangs his sprays; / Thus Eleanor's pride dies in her youngest days.
So this tall pine droops and hangs its branches; so Eleanor's pride dies while it's still young.

Lords, let him go.—Please it your majesty, / This is the day appointed for the combat; / And ready are the appellant and defendant, / The armourer and his man, to enter the lists, / So please your highness to behold the fight.

Lords, let him go. If it please your Majesty, this is the day set for the combat, and the accuser and defendant, the armourer and his man, are ready to enter the lists, if your highness wishes to watch the fight.
Ay, good my lord; for purposely therefore / Left I the court, to see this quarrel tried.
Yes, my good lord; I left the court on purpose to see this quarrel settled.
O' God's name, see the lists and all things fit. / Here let them end it; and God defend the right!
In God's name, see that the lists and everything are ready. Let them end it here, and God defend the right!
I never saw a fellow worse bested, / Or more afraid to fight, than is the appellant, / The servant of his armourer, my lords.
I never saw anyone in a worse state or more afraid to fight than the accuser, the armourer's servant, my lords.
Here, neighbour Horner, I drink to you in a cup of / sack; and fear not, neighbour, you shall do well enough.
Here, neighbour Horner, I drink to you in a cup of sherry; don't be afraid, neighbour, you'll do well enough.
And here, neighbour, here's a cup of charneco.
And here, neighbour, here's a cup of Portuguese wine.
And here's a pot of good double beer, neighbour; / drink, and fear not your man.
And here's a pot of good strong beer, neighbour. Drink, and don't be afraid of your man.
Let it come, i' faith, and I'll pledge you all; and a / fig for Peter!
Bring it on, truly, and I'll drink to you all; and a fig for Peter!
Here, Peter, I drink to thee; and be not afraid.
Here, Peter, I drink to you; don't be afraid.
Be merry, Peter, and fear not thy master: fight / for credit of the prentices.
Cheer up, Peter, and don't fear your master. Fight for the honour of the apprentices.

I thank you all; drink, and pray for me, I pray you, for I / think I have taken my last draught in this world.—Here, Robin, / an if I die, I give thee my apron;—and, Will, thou shalt have my / hammer;—and here, Tom, take all the money that I have.—O Lord / bless me! I pray God! for I am never able to deal with my master, / he hath learnt so much fence already.

Thank you all. Drink, and pray for me, please, for I think I've had my last drink in this world. Here, Robin, if I die, I give you my apron; and Will, you can have my hammer; and here, Tom, take all the money I have. O Lord bless me! I pray God! For I'll never be able to beat my master; he's learned so much swordplay already.
Come, leave your drinking and fall to blows.— / Sirrah, what's thy name?
Come, stop drinking and start fighting. You, what's your name?
Thump! then see thou thump thy master well.
Thump! Then make sure you thump your master well.

Masters, I am come hither, as it were, upon my man's instigation, / to prove him a knave and myself an honest man; and touching the / Duke of York, I will take my death, I never meant him any ill, / nor the / king, nor the queen;—and therefore, Peter, have at thee with a / downright / blow!

Gentlemen, I've come here because my man forced me to, to prove him a rogue and myself an honest man. As for the Duke of York, I'll swear on my life I never meant him any harm, nor the king, nor the queen. And so, Peter, take this straight blow!
Dispatch; this knave's tongue begins to double.— / Sound, trumpets, alarum to the combatants!
Hurry up; this rogue's tongue is starting to slur. Sound the trumpets, call the fighters to battle!
Hold, Peter, hold! I confess, I confess treason.
Stop, Peter, stop! I confess, I confess treason.
Take away his weapon.—Fellow, thank God, and the good / wine in thy master's way.
Take away his weapon. Fellow, thank God, and the good wine that got in your master's way.
O God, have I overcome mine enemies in this presence? O / Peter, thou hast prevail'd in right!
O God, have I beaten my enemy in front of all these people? O Peter, you've won because you were in the right!

Go, take hence that traitor from our sight, / For by his death we do perceive his guilt; / And God in justice hath reveal'd to us / The truth and innocence of this poor fellow, / Which he had thought to have murther'd wrongfully.— / Come, fellow, follow us for thy reward.

Go, take that traitor out of our sight, for by his death we see his guilt. God has justly shown us the truth and innocence of this poor fellow, whom he meant to have wrongly killed. Come, fellow, follow us for your reward.

Thus sometimes hath the brightest day a cloud, / And after summer evermore succeeds / Barren winter, with his wrathful nipping cold; / So cares and joys abound, as seasons fleet. / Sirs, what's o'clock?

So even the brightest day sometimes has a cloud, and after summer always comes barren winter with its fierce biting cold. So sorrows and joys come and go like the passing seasons. Men, what time is it?

Ten is the hour that was appointed me / To watch the coming of my punish'd duchess. / Uneath may she endure the flinty streets, / To tread them with her tender-feeling feet.— / Sweet Nell, ill can thy noble mind abrook / The abject people gazing on thy face / With envious looks, laughing at thy shame, / That erst did follow thy proud chariot-wheels / When thou didst ride in triumph through the streets.— / But, soft! I think she comes; and I'll prepare / My tear-stain'd eyes to see her miseries.

Ten is the hour I was told to wait for my punished duchess to come by. She can hardly bear to walk on the stony streets with her tender feet. Sweet Nell, your noble mind can hardly endure the low people staring at your face with spiteful looks and laughing at your shame, who once followed your proud chariot wheels when you rode through the streets in triumph. But wait! I think she's coming, and I'll ready my tear-stained eyes to see her misery.
So please your Grace, we'll take her from the / sheriff.
If it please your grace, we'll take her from the sheriff.
No, stir not for your lives; let her pass by.
No, don't move, on your lives. Let her pass.

Come you, my lord, to see my open shame? / Now thou dost penance too. Look how they gaze! / See how the giddy multitude do point, / And nod their heads, and throw their eyes on thee! / Ah, Gloster, hide thee from their hateful looks, / And, in thy closet pent up, rue my shame, / And ban thine enemies, both mine and thine!

Have you come, my lord, to see my public shame? Now you're doing penance too. Look how they stare! See how the fickle crowd points and nods and casts their eyes on you! Ah, Gloucester, hide from their hateful looks, shut yourself in your room, mourn my shame, and curse your enemies, both mine and yours!
Be patient, gentle Nell; forget this grief.
Be patient, gentle Nell; forget this grief.

Ah, Gloster, teach me to forget myself! / For whilst I think I am thy married wife, / And thou a prince, protector of this land, / Methinks I should not thus be led along, / Mail'd up in shame, with papers on my back, / And follow'd with a rabble that rejoice / To see my tears and hear my deep-fet groans. / The ruthless flint doth cut my tender feet, / And when I start, the envious people laugh / And bid me be advised how I tread. / Ah, Humphrey, can I bear this shameful yoke? / Trow'st thou that e'er I'll look upon the world, / Or count them happy that enjoy the sun? / No; dark shall be my light and night my day; / To think upon my pomp shall be my hell. / Sometimes I'll say, I am Duke Humphrey's wife, / And he a prince and ruler of the land; / Yet so he rul'd and such a prince he was / As he stood by whilst I, his forlorn duchess, / Was made a wonder and a pointing-stock / To every idle rascal follower. / But be thou mild and blush not at my shame, / Nor stir at nothing till the axe of death / Hang over thee, as, sure, it shortly will; / For Suffolk, he that can do all in all / With her that hateth thee and hates us all, / And York, and impious Beaufort, that false priest, / Have all lim'd bushes to betray thy wings, / And, fly thou how thou canst, they'll tangle thee; / But fear not thou until thy foot be snar'd, / Nor never seek prevention of thy foes.

Ah, Gloucester, teach me to forget who I am! For while I think I'm your married wife and you are a prince, Protector of this land, I feel I shouldn't be led along like this, wrapped in shame, with papers on my back listing my crimes, followed by a mob who love to see my tears and hear my deep groans. The cruel stones cut my tender feet, and when I flinch, the spiteful people laugh and tell me to watch my step. Ah, Humphrey, can I bear this shameful yoke? Do you think I'll ever look at the world again, or think those who enjoy the sun are happy? No; darkness will be my light, and night my day; to remember my grandeur will be my hell. Sometimes I'll say I am Duke Humphrey's wife, and he a prince and ruler of the land. Yet he ruled so, and was such a prince, that he stood by while I, his miserable duchess, was made a spectacle and a laughing stock for every idle rascal. But you be gentle and don't blush at my shame, and don't stir until the axe of death hangs over you, as it surely will soon. For Suffolk, who can do anything with her who hates you and all of us, and York, and wicked Beaufort, that false priest, have all set traps for your wings, and however you fly, they'll tangle you. But don't be afraid till your foot is caught, and never try to forestall your enemies.

Ah, Nell, forbear! thou aimest all awry. / I must offend before I be attainted; / And had I twenty times so many foes, / And each of them had twenty times their power, / All these could not procure me any scath / So long as I am loyal, true, and crimeless. / Wouldst have me rescue thee from this reproach? / Why, yet thy scandal were not wip'd away, / But I in danger for the breach of law. / Thy greatest help is quiet, gentle Nell. / I pray thee, sort thy heart to patience; / These few days' wonder will be quickly worn.

Ah, Nell, stop! You're completely wrong. I must commit a crime before I can be condemned. If I had twenty times as many enemies and each had twenty times their power, they couldn't do me any harm as long as I'm loyal, true and innocent. Would you have me rescue you from this disgrace? Your scandal still wouldn't be wiped away, and I'd be in danger for breaking the law. Your best help is quiet, gentle Nell. Please, settle your heart to patience; this nine days' wonder will soon wear off.
I summon your grace to his majesty's parliament, / Holden at Bury the first of this next month.
I summon your grace to his Majesty's parliament, held at Bury on the first of next month.
And my consent ne'er ask'd herein before! / This is close dealing.—Well, I will be there.—
And my consent was never asked before this! This is secret dealing. Well, I'll be there.
My Nell, I take my leave;—and, master sheriff, / Let not her penance exceed the king's commission.
My Nell, I take my leave. And master sheriff, don't let her penance go beyond what the king ordered.
An 't please your grace, here my commission stays, / And Sir John Stanley is appointed now / To take her with him to the Isle of Man.
If it please your grace, my orders end here, and Sir John Stanley is now appointed to take her with him to the Isle of Man.
Must you, Sir John, protect my lady here?
Are you, Sir John, to guard my lady here?
So am I given in charge, may 't please your grace.
That is my charge, if it please your grace.
Entreat her not the worse in that I pray / You use her well. / The world may laugh again, / And I may live to do you kindness if / You do it her; and so, Sir John, farewell!
Don't treat her worse because I beg you to treat her well. The world may smile on me again, and I may live to do you a kindness if you do her one. And so, Sir John, farewell!
What, gone, my lord, and bid me not farewell!
What, going, my lord, without saying goodbye!
Witness my tears, I cannot stay to speak.
My tears are my witness; I can't stay to speak.

Art thou gone too? all comfort go with thee! / For none abides with me; my joy is death, / Death, at whose name I oft have been afeard, / Because I wish'd this world's eternity.— / Stanley, I prithee, go, and take me hence; / I care not whither, for I beg no favour, / Only convey me where thou art commanded.

Are you gone too? All comfort go with you! For none stays with me. My only joy is death, death whose name I've often feared because I wanted to stay in this world forever. Stanley, please go and take me away. I don't care where, for I ask no favour; just take me where you're ordered.
Why, madam, that is to the Isle of Man; / There to be us'd according to your state.
Why, madam, that's to the Isle of Man, to be treated there as befits your rank.
That's bad enough, for I am but reproach; / And shall I then be us'd reproachfully?
That's bad enough, for I am nothing but disgrace. Shall I be treated disgracefully, then?
Like to a duchess, and Duke Humphrey's lady; / According to that state you shall be us'd.
Like a duchess, and Duke Humphrey's wife; you'll be treated according to that rank.
Sheriff, farewell, and better than I fare, / Although thou hast been conduct of my shame.
Sheriff, farewell, and may you fare better than I do, though you've been the escort of my shame.
It is my office; and, madam, pardon me.
It is my job; and madam, forgive me.
Ay, ay, farewell; thy office is discharg'd.— / Come, Stanley, shall we go?
Yes, yes, farewell; your job is done. Come, Stanley, shall we go?
Madam, your penance done, throw off this sheet, / And go we to attire you for our journey.
Madam, now your penance is done, throw off this sheet, and let's go and dress you for our journey.
My shame will not be shifted with my sheet; / No, it will hang upon my richest robes / And show itself, attire me how I can. / Go, lead the way; I long to see my prison.
My shame won't be changed with my sheet. No, it will hang on my richest robes and show itself however I dress. Go, lead the way; I long to see my prison.
I muse my Lord of Gloster is not come; / 'Tis not his wont to be the hindmost man, / Whate'er occasion keeps him from us now.
I'm surprised my Lord of Gloucester hasn't come. It's not like him to be the last, whatever is keeping him from us now.

Can you not see? or will ye not observe / The strangeness of his alter'd countenance? / With what a majesty he bears himself, / How insolent of late he is become, / How proud, how peremptory, and unlike himself? / We know the time since he was mild and affable, / And if we did but glance a far-off look, / Immediately he was upon his knee, / That all the court admir'd him for submission; / But meet him now, and be it in the morn / When every one will give the time of day, / He knits his brow, and shows an angry eye, / And passeth by with stiff unbowed knee, / Disdaining duty that to us belongs. / Small curs are not regarded when they grin, / But great men tremble when the lion roars; / And Humphrey is no little man in England. / First note that he is near you in descent, / And should you fall, he is the next will mount. / Me seemeth then it is no policy, / Respecting what a rancorous mind he bears / And his advantage following your decease, / That he should come about your royal person / Or be admitted to your highness' council. / By flattery hath he won the commons' hearts, / And when he please to make commotion / 'T is to be fear'd they all will follow him. / Now 't is the spring and weeds are shallow-rooted; / Suffer them now, and they'll o'ergrow the garden / And choke the herbs for want of husbandry. / The reverent care I bear unto my lord / Made me collect these dangers in the duke. / If it be fond, can it a woman's fear; / Which fear if better reasons can supplant, / I will subscribe and say I wrong'd the duke.— / My Lord of Suffolk, Buckingham, and York, / Reprove my allegation if you can, / Or else conclude my words effectual.

Can't you see, or won't you notice, how strangely his face has changed? How majestically he carries himself, how insolent he's become lately, how proud, how bossy, how unlike himself? We remember when he was mild and friendly, and if we even glanced at him from far off, he was immediately on his knee, so that the whole court admired his humility. But meet him now, even in the morning when everyone says good day, and he frowns, gives an angry look, and walks past with a stiff knee that won't bow, scorning the respect he owes us. Little dogs aren't noticed when they snarl, but great men tremble when the lion roars, and Humphrey is no little man in England. First, remember that he is close to you by birth, and if you fell, he would be the next to rise. So it seems to me unwise, considering his bitter mind and what he'd gain from your death, that he should come near your royal person or be allowed into your highness's council. He has won the commons' hearts by flattery, and when he chooses to stir up trouble, it's to be feared they'll all follow him. Now it's spring and the weeds have shallow roots; leave them now, and they'll overgrow the garden and choke the plants for lack of care. The loving concern I have for my lord made me gather these dangers in the duke. If it's foolish, call it a woman's fear; and if better reasons can replace that fear, I'll agree and say I wronged the duke. My Lords of Suffolk, Buckingham and York, disprove my charge if you can, or else agree my words are right.

Well hath your highness seen into this duke; / And, had I first been put to speak my mind, / I think I should have told your grace's tale. / The duchess by his subornation, / Upon my life, began her devilish practices; / Or, if he were not privy to those faults, / Yet, by reputing of his high descent, / As next the king he was successive heir, / And such high vaunts of his nobility, / Did instigate the bedlam brain-sick duchess / By wicked means to frame our sovereign's fall. / Smooth runs the water where the brook is deep, / And in his simple show he harbours treason. / The fox barks not when he would steal the lamb.— / No, no, my sovereign; Gloster is a man / Unsounded yet and full of deep deceit.

Your highness has seen right into this duke, and if I'd been asked to speak first, I think I would have said the same. On my life, the duchess began her devilish practices because he encouraged her. Or if he didn't know of those crimes, still, by boasting of his high birth, that he was next heir after the king, and by bragging so much about his nobility, he egged on the mad, brain-sick duchess to plot our sovereign's fall by wicked means. Still waters run deep, and under his simple appearance he hides treason. The fox doesn't bark when it means to steal the lamb. No, no, my sovereign, Gloucester is a man not yet sounded out, and full of deep deceit.
Did he not, contrary to form of law, / Devise strange deaths for small offences done?
Didn't he, against the proper process of law, invent cruel deaths for small crimes?
And did he not, in his protectorship, / Levy great sums of money through the realm / For soldiers' pay in France, and never sent it? / By means whereof the towns each day revolted.
And didn't he, as Protector, raise large sums across the country to pay the soldiers in France and never send it? That's why towns there revolted every day.
Tut, these are petty faults to faults unknown, / Which time will bring to light in smooth Duke Humphrey.
Nonsense, these are small faults compared with the hidden ones that time will bring to light in smooth Duke Humphrey.

My lords, at once: the care you have of us, / To mow down thorns that would annoy our foot, / Is worthy praise; but, shall I speak my conscience, / Our kinsman Gloster is as innocent / From meaning treason to our royal person / As is the sucking lamb or harmless dove. / The duke is virtuous, mild, and too well given / To dream on evil or to work my downfall.

My lords, to answer you all at once: your care for us, cutting down thorns that might hurt our feet, deserves praise. But to speak my conscience, our kinsman Gloucester is as innocent of meaning treason to us as a suckling lamb or a harmless dove. The duke is virtuous, gentle, and too good-natured to dream of evil or plot my downfall.

Ah, what's more dangerous than this fond affiance! / Seems he a dove? his feathers are but borrow'd, / For he's disposed as the hateful raven; / Is he a lamb? his skin is surely lent him, / For he's inclin'd as is the ravenous wolf. / Who cannot steal a shape that means deceit? / Take heed, my lord; the welfare of us all / Hangs on the cutting short that fraudful man.

Ah, what's more dangerous than this foolish trust! Does he seem a dove? His feathers are only borrowed, for he has the nature of the hateful raven. Is he a lamb? His skin is surely lent to him, for he has the instincts of the greedy wolf. Who can't put on a disguise to deceive? Be careful, my lord; all our safety depends on cutting that cheat down.
All health unto my gracious sovereign!
Good health to my gracious sovereign!
Welcome, Lord Somerset. What news from France?
Welcome, Lord Somerset. What news from France?
That all your interest in those territories / Is utterly bereft you; all is lost.
That all your claims in those lands are completely taken from you. Everything is lost.
Cold news, Lord Somerset; but God's will be done!
Cold news, Lord Somerset; but God's will be done!

[Aside] Cold news for me, for I had hope of France / As firmly as I hope for fertile England. / Thus are my blossoms blasted in the bud, / And caterpillars eat my leaves away; / But I will remedy this gear ere long / Or sell my title for a glorious grave.

(Aside) Cold news for me, for I hoped for France as firmly as I hope for fertile England. So my blossoms are blighted in the bud, and caterpillars eat away my leaves. But I'll put this business right before long, or trade my claim for a glorious grave.
All happiness unto my lord the king! / Pardon, my liege, that I have staid so long.
All happiness to my lord the king! Forgive me, my lord, for being so late.
Nay, Gloster, know that thou art come too soon, / Unless thou wert more loyal than thou art. / I do arrest thee of high treason here.
No, Gloucester, you've come too soon, unless you were more loyal than you are. I arrest you here for high treason.

Well, Suffolk, thou shalt not see me blush, / Nor change my countenance for this arrest; / A heart unspotted is not easily daunted. / The purest spring is not so free from mud / As I am clear from treason to my sovereign. / Who can accuse me? wherein am I guilty?

Well, Suffolk, you won't see me blush or change my expression at this arrest; an unstained heart is not easily scared. The purest spring is not as free of mud as I am free of treason against my sovereign. Who accuses me? What am I guilty of?
'T is thought, my lord, that you took bribes of France, / And, being protector, stay'd the soldiers' pay, / By means whereof his highness hath lost France.
It's said, my lord, that you took bribes from France, and as Protector held back the soldiers' pay, and that's how his highness has lost France.

Is it but thought so? what are they that think it? / I never robb'd the soldiers of their pay, / Nor ever had one penny bribe from France. / So help me God, as I have watch'd the night, / Ay, night by night, in studying good for England! / That doit that e'er I wrested from the king, / Or any groat I hoarded to my use, / Be brought against me at my trial-day! / No; many a pound of mine own proper store, / Because I would not tax the needy commons, / Have I dispursed to the garrisons, / And never ask'd for restitution.

Is it only "said"? Who says it? I never robbed the soldiers of their pay, nor took one penny in bribes from France. So help me God, as I have stayed awake night after night working for England's good! Let any coin I ever squeezed from the king, or any penny I hoarded for myself, be brought against me on the day of my trial! No; many pounds of my own money I've paid out to the garrisons, because I wouldn't tax the poor commons, and I never asked to be paid back.
It serves you well, my lord, to say so much.
It suits you well, my lord, to say so much.
I say no more than truth, so help me God!
I say nothing but the truth, so help me God!
In your protectorship you did devise / Strange tortures for offenders never heard of, / That England was defam'd by tyranny.
As Protector you invented strange, unheard-of tortures for criminals, so that England got a name for tyranny.

Why, 't is well known that, whiles I was protector, / Pity was all the fault that was in me; / For I should melt at an offender's tears, / And lowly words were ransom for their fault. / Unless it were a bloody murtherer, / Or foul felonious thief that fleec'd poor passengers, / I never gave them condign punishment. / Murther indeed, that bloody sin, I tortur'd / Above the felon or what trespass else.

Why, everyone knows that while I was Protector, my only fault was pity. I would melt at a criminal's tears, and humble words paid for their crime. Unless it was a bloody murderer or a foul thief who robbed poor travellers, I never gave the full punishment. Murder, that bloody sin, I did punish more than theft or any other crime.

My lord, these faults are easy, quickly answer'd; / But mightier crimes are laid unto your charge, / Whereof you cannot easily purge yourself. / I do arrest you in his highness' name, / And here commit you to my lord cardinal / To keep until your further time of trial.

My lord, these faults are slight and quickly answered; but greater crimes are charged against you, which you can't easily clear yourself of. I arrest you in his highness's name, and hand you over to my lord cardinal to keep until your trial.
My Lord of Gloster, 't is my special hope / That you will clear yourself from all suspect; / My conscience tells me you are innocent.
My Lord of Gloucester, I truly hope you will clear yourself of all suspicion. My conscience tells me you are innocent.

Ah, gracious lord, these days are dangerous. / Virtue is chok'd with foul ambition, / And charity chas'd hence by rancour's hand; / Foul subornation is predominant, / And equity exil'd your highness' land. / I know their complot is to have my life, / And if my death might make this island happy / And prove the period of their tyranny, / I would expend it with all willingness; / But mine is made the prologue to their play, / For thousands more, that yet suspect no peril, / Will not conclude their plotted tragedy. / Beaufort's red sparkling eyes blab his heart's malice, / And Suffolk's cloudy brow his stormy hate; / Sharp Buckingham unburthens with his tongue / The envious load that lies upon his heart; / And dogged York, that reaches at the moon, / Whose overweening arm I have pluck'd back, / By false accuse doth level at my life.— / And you, my sovereign lady, with the rest, / Causeless have laid disgraces on my head / And with your best endeavour have stirr'd up / My liefest liege to be mine enemy.— / Ay, all of you have laid your heads together— / Myself had notice of your conventicles— / And all to make away my guiltless life. / I shall not want false witness to condemn me, / Nor store of treasons to augment my guilt; / The ancient proverb will be well effected,— / 'A staff is quickly found to beat a dog.'

Ah, gracious lord, these are dangerous days. Virtue is choked by foul ambition and charity driven out by hatred; foul bribery rules and justice is exiled from your land. I know their plot is to take my life. If my death could make this island happy and end their tyranny, I'd give it gladly. But mine is only the prologue to their play, for thousands more who don't yet suspect danger won't finish their planned tragedy. Beaufort's red, sparkling eyes give away his heart's malice, and Suffolk's cloudy frown his stormy hatred. Sharp-tongued Buckingham unloads the envy that weighs on his heart, and stubborn York, who reaches for the moon and whose overreaching arm I have pulled back, aims at my life with false accusations. And you, my sovereign lady, along with the rest, have heaped disgrace on my head for no reason and done your best to stir up my dearest lord to be my enemy. Yes, you've all put your heads together, I heard about your secret meetings, all to get rid of my innocent life. I won't lack false witnesses to condemn me, or invented treasons to add to my guilt. The old proverb will come true: "Any stick will do to beat a dog."

My liege, his railing is intolerable; / If those that care to keep your royal person / From treason's secret knife and traitor's rage / Be thus upbraided, chid, and rated at, / And the offender granted scope of speech, / 'T will make them cool in zeal unto your grace.

My lord, his abuse is unbearable. If those who care to keep your royal person safe from treason's hidden knife and traitors' rage are insulted, scolded and abused like this, and the offender is allowed to say what he likes, it will cool their zeal for your grace.
Hath he not twit our sovereign lady here / With ignominious words, though clerkly couch'd, / As if she had suborned some to swear / False allegations to o'erthrow his state?
Hasn't he taunted our sovereign lady here with disgraceful words, though cleverly phrased, as if she had bribed people to swear false charges to bring him down?
But I can give the loser leave to chide.
But I can allow the loser to complain.
Far truer spoke than meant; I lose, indeed. / Beshrew the winners, for they play'd me false! / And well such losers may have leave to speak.
Spoken more truly than you meant: I do lose indeed. Curse the winners, for they cheated me! And losers like that may well be allowed to speak.
He'll wrest the sense and hold us here all day.— / Lord Cardinal, he is your prisoner.
He'll twist our meaning and keep us here all day. Lord Cardinal, he is your prisoner.
Sirs, take away the Duke, and guard him sure.
Men, take the duke away, and guard him well.

Ah, thus King Henry throws away his crutch / Before his legs be firm to bear his body. / Thus is the shepherd beaten from thy side, / And wolves are gnarling who shall gnaw thee first. / Ah, that my fear were false! ah, that it were! / For, good King Henry, thy decay I fear.

Ah, so King Henry throws away his crutch before his legs are strong enough to carry his body. So the shepherd is beaten from your side, and wolves are snarling over who will bite you first. Ah, I wish my fear were false! I wish it were! For, good King Henry, I fear your ruin.
My lords, what to your wisdoms seemeth best, / Do or undo, as if ourself were here.
My lords, do or undo whatever seems best to your wisdom, as if we were here ourself.
What, will your highness leave the parliament?
What, will your highness leave the parliament?

Ay, Margaret; my heart is drown'd with grief, / Whose flood begins to flow within mine eyes, / My body round engirt with misery, / For what's more miserable than discontent?— / Ah, uncle Humphrey! in thy face I see / The map of honour, truth, and loyalty; / And yet, good Humphrey, is the hour to come / That e'er I prov'd thee false or fear'd thy faith. / What lowering star now envies thy estate, / That these great lords and Margaret our queen / Do seek subversion of thy harmless life? / Thou never didst them wrong nor no man wrong; / And as the butcher takes away the calf / And binds the wretch and beats it when it strays, / Bearing it to the bloody slaughter-house, / Even so remorseless have they borne him hence; / And as the dam runs lowing up and down, / Looking the way her harmless young one went, / And can do nought but wail her darling's loss, / Even so myself bewails good Gloster's case / With sad unhelpful tears, and with dimm'd eyes / Look after him, and cannot do him good, / So mighty are his vowed enemies. / His fortunes I will weep and 'twixt each groan / Say 'Who's a traitor? Gloster he is none.'

Yes, Margaret. My heart is drowned in grief, whose flood begins to pour from my eyes, and my body is wrapped in misery, for what is more miserable than unhappiness? Ah, uncle Humphrey! In your face I see the map of honour, truth and loyalty, and the hour has yet to come when I found you false or doubted your faith. What gloomy star now envies your fortune, that these great lords and our queen Margaret seek to destroy your harmless life? You never wronged them or any man. And as the butcher takes away the calf, ties up the poor thing and beats it when it strays, carrying it to the bloody slaughterhouse, so pitilessly have they carried him away. And as the mother cow runs up and down lowing, looking the way her harmless young one went, and can do nothing but wail for her darling, so I mourn good Gloucester's fate with sad, useless tears, and watch after him with dim eyes, unable to help him, his sworn enemies are so powerful. I'll weep for his fortunes, and between each groan say, "Who's a traitor? Gloucester is not."

Free lords, cold snow melts with the sun's hot beams. / Henry my lord is cold in great affairs, / Too full of foolish pity, and Gloster's show / Beguiles him as the mournful crocodile / With sorrow snares relenting passengers, / Or as the snake roll'd in a flowering bank, / With shining checker'd slough, doth sting a child / That for the beauty thinks it excellent. / Believe me, lords, were none more wise than I— / And yet herein I judge mine own wit good— / This Gloster should be quickly rid the world, / To rid us from the fear we have of him.

Noble lords, cold snow melts in the sun's hot rays. My lord Henry is cold in great matters, too full of foolish pity, and Gloucester's show of goodness fools him, as the weeping crocodile traps soft-hearted travellers with its sorrow, or as the snake coiled on a flowery bank, with its shining speckled skin, stings a child who thinks it lovely because of its beauty. Believe me, lords, if nobody were wiser than me, and in this I think my judgement good, this Gloucester would soon be got rid of, to rid us of the fear we have of him.
That he should die is worthy policy, / But yet we want a colour for his death, / 'T is meet he be condemn'd by course of law.
His death would be good policy, but we still need a pretext for it. It's right he should be condemned by the course of law.

But, in my mind, that were no policy. / The king will labour still to save his life; / The commons haply rise to save his life, / And yet we have but trivial argument, / More than mistrust, that shows him worthy death.

But in my view that would be bad policy. The king will keep working to save his life, the commons might rise to save it, and so far we have only trivial evidence, nothing beyond suspicion, to show he deserves death.
So that, by this, you would not have him die.
So by this, you'd rather he didn't die.
Ah, York, no man alive so fain as I!
Ah, York, no man alive wants it more than I!

'T is York that hath more reason for his death.— / But, my lord cardinal, and you, my Lord of Suffolk, / Say as you think, and speak it from your souls, / Were 't not all one an empty eagle were set / To guard the chicken from a hungry kite, / As place Duke Humphrey for the king's protector?

It's York who has more reason to want him dead. But my lord cardinal, and you, my Lord of Suffolk, say what you think, from your souls: wouldn't putting Duke Humphrey in charge as the king's Protector be like setting a hungry eagle to guard a chicken from a hungry hawk?
So the poor chicken should be sure of death.
Then the poor chicken would be sure to die.

Madam, 't is true; and were 't not madness, then, / To make the fox surveyor of the fold? / Who being accus'd a crafty murtherer, / His guilt should be but idly posted over, / Because his purpose is not executed. / No; let him die, in that he is a fox, / By nature prov'd an enemy to the flock, / Before his chaps be stain'd with crimson blood, / As Humphrey, prov'd by reasons, to my liege. / And do not stand on quillets how to slay him. / Be it by gins, by snares, by subtlety, / Sleeping or waking, 't is no matter how, / So he be dead; for that is good deceit / Which mates him first that first intends deceit.

Madam, that's true. And wouldn't it be madness, then, to make the fox guardian of the sheepfold? If he were accused of being a cunning murderer, his guilt shouldn't be idly passed over just because he hasn't carried out his plan yet. No, let him die because he's a fox, proven by nature to be an enemy to the flock, before his jaws are stained with blood, as Humphrey is proven by argument to be my lord's enemy. And don't quibble about how to kill him. By traps, by snares, by cunning, sleeping or awake, it doesn't matter how, as long as he's dead. For it's good deceit that checkmates the man who first planned to deceive.

Not resolute, except so much were done, / For things are often spoke and seldom meant; / But that my heart accordeth with my tongue,— / Seeing the deed is meritorious, / And to preserve my sovereign from his foe,— / Say but the word, and I will be his priest.

It's not bold unless it's done, for things are often said and seldom meant. But to show my heart agrees with my tongue, since the deed deserves credit and will protect my sovereign from his enemy, just say the word and I'll be his priest at his deathbed.

But I would have him dead, my Lord of Suffolk, / Ere you can take due orders for a priest. / Say you consent and censure well the deed, / And I'll provide his executioner, / I tender so the safety of my liege.
But I'd have him dead, my Lord of Suffolk, before you could be properly ordained a priest. Say you agree and approve the deed, and I'll provide his executioner, I care so much for my lord's safety.
Here is my hand, the deed is worthy doing.
Here's my hand; the deed is worth doing.
And I; and now we three have spoke it, / It skills not greatly who impugns our doom.
And I. And now that we three have said it, it hardly matters who disputes our verdict.

Great lords, from Ireland am I come amain, / To signify that rebels there are up / And put the Englishmen unto the sword. / Send succours, lords, and stop the rage betime, / Before the wound do grow uncurable; / For, being green, there is great hope of help.

Great lords, I've come at full speed from Ireland to report that rebels there have risen and are putting the English to the sword. Send help, lords, and stop the violence in time, before the wound becomes incurable; while it's fresh there's great hope of a cure.
A breach that craves a quick expedient stop! / What council give you in this weighty cause?
A breach that needs to be stopped quickly! What do you advise in this serious matter?
That Somerset be sent as regent thither. / 'T is meet that lucky ruler be employ'd; / Witness the fortune he hath had in France.
That Somerset be sent there as regent. It's right to use such a lucky ruler; look at the luck he's had in France.
If York, with all his far-fet policy, / Had been the regent there instead of me, / He never would have stay'd in France so long.
If York, with all his far-fetched cunning, had been regent there instead of me, he wouldn't have stayed in France as long as I did.

No, not to lose it all as thou hast done; / I rather would have lost my life betimes / Than bring a burden of dishonour home / By staying there so long till all were lost. / Show me one scar character'd on thy skin; / Men's flesh preserv'd so whole do seldom win.

No, not to lose it all as you have done. I'd rather have lost my life early than bring home a load of dishonour by staying until everything was lost. Show me one scar written on your skin; men who keep their flesh so whole rarely win.

Nay then, this spark will prove a raging fire, / If wind and fuel be brought to feed it with. / No more, good York.—Sweet Somerset, be still.— / Thy fortune, York, hadst thou been regent there, / Might happily have prov'd far worse than his.

Now then, this spark will become a raging fire if wind and fuel are added. No more, good York. Sweet Somerset, be quiet. If you'd been regent there, York, your luck might well have been far worse than his.
What, worse than nought? nay, then a shame take all!
What, worse than nothing? Then shame take everyone!
And, in the number, thee that wishest shame!
Including you, who wish shame on us!

My Lord of York, try what your fortune is. / The uncivil kerns of Ireland are in arms, / And temper clay with blood of Englishmen. / To Ireland will you lead a band of men, / Collected choicely, from each county some, / And try your hap against the Irishmen?

My Lord of York, try your own luck. The savage Irish foot soldiers are up in arms and mixing mud with English blood. Will you lead a band of men to Ireland, picked carefully from every county, and try your luck against the Irish?
I will, my lord, so please his majesty.
I will, my lord, if it please his Majesty.
Why, our authority is his consent, / And what we do establish he confirms.— / Then, noble York, take thou this task in hand.
Why, our authority is his consent, and what we decide, he confirms. So, noble York, take on this task.
I am content.—Provide me soldiers, lords, / Whiles I take order for mine own affairs.
I'm happy to. Lords, get soldiers ready for me while I put my own affairs in order.
A charge, Lord York, that I will see perform'd. / But now return we to the false Duke Humphrey.
A responsibility, Lord York, I'll make sure is carried out. But now back to the false Duke Humphrey.
No more of him; for I will deal with him / That henceforth he shall trouble us no more. / And so break off; the day is almost spent.— / Lord Suffolk, you and I must talk of that event.
No more about him, for I'll deal with him so that he won't trouble us any more. So let's end here; the day is almost over. Lord Suffolk, you and I must talk about that business.
My Lord of Suffolk, within fourteen days / At Bristol I expect my soldiers; / For there I'll ship them all for Ireland.
My Lord of Suffolk, I expect my soldiers at Bristol within fourteen days, for there I'll ship them all to Ireland.
I'll see it truly done, my Lord of York.
I'll see it faithfully done, my Lord of York.

Now, York, or never, steel thy fearful thoughts, / And change misdoubt to resolution. / Be that thou hop'st to be, or what thou art / Resign to death; it is not worth the enjoying. / Let pale-fac'd fear keep with the mean-born man, / And find no harbour in a royal heart. / Faster than spring-time showers comes thought on thought, / And not a thought but thinks on dignity. / My brain more busy than the labouring spider / Weaves tedious snares to trap mine enemies. / Well, nobles, well, 't is politicly done, / To send me packing with an host of men; / I fear me you but warm the starved snake, / Who, cherish'd in your breasts, will sting your hearts. / 'T was men I lack'd, and you will give them me; / I take it kindly, yet be well-assur'd / You put sharp weapons in a madman's hands. / Whiles I in Ireland nourish a mighty band, / I will stir up in England some black storm / Shall blow ten thousand souls to heaven or hell; / And this fell tempest shall not cease to rage / Until the golden circuit on my head, / Like to the glorious sun's transparent beams, / Do calm the fury of this mad-bred flaw. / And for a minister of my intent, / I have seduc'd a headstrong Kentishman, / John Cade of Ashford, / To make commotion, as full well he can, / Under the tide of John Mortimer. / In Ireland have I seen this stubborn Cade / Oppose himself against a troop of kerns, / And fought so long till that his thighs with darts / Were almost like a sharp-quill'd porpentine; / And, in the end being rescu'd, I have seen / Him caper upright like a wild Morisco, / Shaking the bloody darts as he his bells. / Full often, like a shag-hair'd crafty kern, / Hath he conversed with the enemy, / And undiscover'd come to me again / And given me notice of their villainies. / This devil here shall be my substitute; / For that John Mortimer, which now is dead, / In face, in gait, in speech, he doth resemble. / By this I shall perceive the commons' mind, / How they affect the house and claim of York. / Say he be taken, rack'd, and tortured, / I know no pain they can inflict upon him / Will make him say I mov'd him to those arms. / Say that he thrive, as 't is great like he will, / Why, then from Ireland come I with my strength / And reap the harvest which that rascal sow'd; / For Humphrey being dead, as he shall be, / And Henry put apart, the next for me.

Now, York, or never, harden your fearful thoughts and turn doubt into determination. Be what you hope to be, or give up what you are to death; it isn't worth keeping. Let pale-faced fear stay with low-born men and find no shelter in a royal heart. Thoughts come faster than spring showers, and every thought is about high rank. My brain, busier than the working spider, weaves elaborate traps for my enemies. Well, nobles, well; it's clever of you to send me off with an army. I fear you're just warming the frozen snake that, cherished in your bosoms, will sting your hearts. It was men I lacked, and you're giving them to me. I take it kindly, but be sure you're putting sharp weapons in a madman's hands. While I build up a mighty army in Ireland, I'll stir up some black storm in England that will blow ten thousand souls to heaven or hell, and this fierce storm won't stop raging until the golden circle on my head, like the sun's glorious bright rays, calms the fury of this mad gust. And as the agent of my plan, I've persuaded a headstrong man from Kent, John Cade of Ashford, to stir up a rising, as he well can, under the name of John Mortimer. In Ireland I've seen this stubborn Cade take on a troop of Irish soldiers and fight so long that his thighs were stuck with darts like a porcupine's quills. When he was finally rescued, I saw him leap about like a wild morris dancer, shaking the bloody darts as a dancer shakes his bells. Very often, disguised as a shaggy-haired, crafty Irish soldier, he has mixed with the enemy and come back to me undiscovered with news of their plots. This devil will be my stand-in, for he looks, walks and talks like John Mortimer, who is now dead. Through him I'll find out what the commons think, how they feel about the house of York and its claim. Say he's caught, racked and tortured; I know of no pain they can inflict that will make him say I put him up to this rising. Say he succeeds, as is very likely; why, then I'll come from Ireland with my army and reap the harvest that rascal sowed. For with Humphrey dead, as he will be, and Henry pushed aside, the crown comes next to me.
Run to my Lord of Suffolk; let him know / We have dispatch'd the duke, as he commanded.
Run to my Lord of Suffolk and tell him we've killed the duke, as he ordered.
O that it were to do! What have we done? / Didst ever hear a man so penitent?
Oh, if only it were still to do! What have we done? Did you ever hear a man so repentant?
Now, sirs, have you dispatch'd this thing?
Now, men, have you finished this business?
Ay, my good lord, he's dead.
Yes, my good lord, he's dead.

Why, that's well said. Go, get you to my house; / I will reward you for this venturous deed. / The king and all the peers are here at hand. / Have you laid fair the bed? Is all things well, / According as I gave directions?
Good, well said. Go to my house; I'll reward you for this daring deed. The king and all the lords are close by. Have you smoothed the bed? Is everything in order, as I told you?
Go, call our uncle to our presence straight; / Say we intend to try his grace to-day, / If he be guilty, as 't is published.
Go and call our uncle here at once. Tell him we mean to try his case today, if he is guilty, as people say.
I'll call him presently, my noble lord.
I'll call him at once, my noble lord.
Lords, take your places; and, I pray you all, / Proceed no straiter 'gainst our uncle Gloster / Than from true evidence of good esteem / He be approv'd in practice culpable.
Lords, take your seats, and I beg you all not to deal more harshly with our uncle Gloucester than true and reliable evidence proves he is guilty in fact.
God forbid any malice should prevail / That faultless may condemn a nobleman! / Pray God he may acquit him of suspicion!
God forbid that any malice should win and condemn an innocent nobleman! I pray God he can clear himself of suspicion!
I thank thee, Meg; these words content me much.—
Thank you, Meg; those words please me very much.
How now! why look'st thou pale? why tremblest thou? / Where is our uncle? what's the matter, Suffolk?
What's this! Why do you look pale? Why are you trembling? Where is our uncle? What's the matter, Suffolk?
Dead in his bed, my lord; Gloster is dead.
Dead in his bed, my lord. Gloucester is dead.
God's secret judgment!—I did dream to-night / The duke was dumb and could not speak a word.
God's secret judgement! I dreamed last night that the duke was dumb and couldn't speak a word.
How fares my lord?—Help, lords! the king is dead.
How is my lord? Help, lords! The king is dead.
Rear up his body; wring him by the nose.
Lift him up; pinch his nose.
Run, go, help, help!—O Henry, ope thine eyes!
Run, go, help, help! O Henry, open your eyes!
He doth revive again.—Madam, be patient.
He's coming round. Madam, be calm.
Comfort, my sovereign! gracious Henry, comfort!
Take comfort, my sovereign! Gracious Henry, take comfort!

What, doth my Lord of Suffolk comfort me? / Came he right now to sing a raven's note / Whose dismal tune bereft my vital powers, / And thinks he that the chirping of a wren, / By crying comfort from a hollow breast, / Can chase away the first-conceived sound? / Hide not thy poison with such sugar'd words; / Lay not thy hands on me; forbear, I say! / Their touch affrights me as a serpent's sting. / Thou baleful messenger, out of my sight! / Upon thy eye-balls murtherous tyranny / Sits in grim majesty, to fright the world. / Look not upon me, for thine eyes are wounding. / Yet do not go away; come, basilisk, / And kill the innocent gazer with thy sight, / For in the shade of death I shall find joy, / In life but double death, now Gloster's dead.

What, does my Lord of Suffolk comfort me? Did he just now come to croak like a raven, whose deadly tune took away my strength, and does he think that the chirping of a wren, crying "comfort" from a hollow heart, can drive away that first sound? Don't hide your poison with such sugary words. Don't touch me; stop, I say! Your hands frighten me like a snake's sting. You deadly messenger, out of my sight! Murderous tyranny sits in grim majesty on your eyeballs to frighten the world. Don't look at me, for your eyes wound. Yet don't go. Come, basilisk, and kill the innocent onlooker with your glance, for I'll find joy in the shadow of death, and only double death in life, now Gloucester is dead.

Why do you rate my Lord of Suffolk thus? / Although the duke was enemy to him, / Yet he most Christian-like laments his death; / And for myself, foe as he was to me, / Might liquid tears or heart-offending groans / Or blood-consuming sighs recall his life, / I would be blind with weeping, sick with groans, / Look pale as primrose with blood-drinking sighs, / And all to have the noble duke alive. / What know I how the world may deem of me? / For it is known we were but hollow friends. / It may be judg'd I made the duke away; / So shall my name with slander's tongue be wounded / And princes' courts be fill'd with my reproach. / This get I by his death. Ay me, unhappy! / To be a queen, and crown'd with infamy!

Why do you scold my Lord of Suffolk like this? Though the duke was his enemy, he mourns his death like a true Christian. And as for me, enemy though he was to me, if flowing tears or heartbreaking groans or life-draining sighs could bring him back, I'd blind myself weeping, sicken myself groaning, turn pale as a primrose with sighs, all to have the noble duke alive. How do I know what the world will think of me? For it's known we were only false friends. People may think I got rid of the duke, so my name will be wounded by slander and royal courts all over will be full of my disgrace. That's what I get from his death. Oh, how unhappy I am, to be a queen and crowned with shame!
Ah, woe is me for Gloster, wretched man!
Ah, woe is me for Gloucester, poor man!

Be woe for me, more wretched than he is. / What, dost thou turn away and hide thy face? / I am no loathsome leper; look on me. / What! art thou, like the adder, waxen deaf? / Be poisonous too and kill thy forlorn queen. / Is all thy comfort shut in Gloster's tomb? / Why, then, dame Margaret was ne'er thy joy. / Erect his statue and worship it, / And make my image but an alehouse sign. / Was I for this nigh wrack'd upon the sea, / And twice by awkward wind from England's bank / Drove back again unto my native clime? / What boded this but well forewarning wind / Did seem to say 'Seek not a scorpion's nest, / Nor set no footing on this unkind shore?' / What did I then, but curs'd the gentle gusts / And he that loos'd them forth their brazen caves, / And bid them blow towards England's blessed shore, / Or turn our stern upon a dreadful rock? / Yet Aeolus would not be a murtherer, / But left that hateful office unto thee. / The pretty-vaulting sea refus'd to drown me, / Knowing that thou wouldst have me drown'd on shore, / With tears as salt as sea, through thy unkindness. / The splitting rocks cower'd in the sinking sands / And would not dash me with their ragged sides, / Because thy flinty heart, more hard than they, / Might in thy palace perish Margaret. / As far as I could ken thy chalky cliffs, / When from thy shore the tempest beat us back, / I stood upon the hatches in the storm, / And when the dusky sky began to rob / My earnest-gaping sight of thy land's view, / I took a costly jewel from my neck— / A heart it was, bound in with diamonds— / And threw it towards thy land; the sea receiv'd it, / And so I wish'd thy body might my heart. / And even with this I lost fair England's view, / And bid mine eyes be packing with my heart, / And call'd them blind and dusky spectacles, / For losing ken of Albion's wished coast. / How often have I tempted Suffolk's tongue, / The agent of thy foul inconstancy, / To sit and witch me, as Ascanius did / When he to madding Dido would unfold / His father's acts commenc'd in burning Troy! / Am I not witch'd like her? or thou not false like him? / Ay me, I can no more! die, Margaret! / For Henry weeps that thou dost live so long.

Say woe for me, more wretched than he is. What, are you turning away and hiding your face? I'm not a disgusting leper; look at me. What! Have you gone deaf like the adder? Then be poisonous too and kill your abandoned queen. Is all your comfort shut up in Gloucester's tomb? Then Queen Margaret was never your joy. Put up his statue and worship it, and make my picture into a pub sign. Was it for this that I was nearly shipwrecked at sea, and twice driven back home from England's coast by contrary winds? What did that mean except that the warning wind seemed to say, "Don't seek a scorpion's nest; don't set foot on this unkind shore"? And what did I do but curse the gentle winds and the god who let them out of their caves, and order them to blow towards England's blessed shore or wreck us on a terrible rock? Yet Aeolus wouldn't be a murderer, but left that hateful job to you. The heaving sea refused to drown me, knowing you'd have me drowned on shore in tears as salt as the sea through your unkindness. The splitting rocks hid themselves in the sinking sands and wouldn't dash me with their jagged sides, so that your heart, harder than flint, could kill Margaret in your palace. As long as I could see your chalk cliffs, when the storm beat us back from your shore, I stood on deck in the storm, and when the dark sky began to rob my eager eyes of the sight of your land, I took a precious jewel from my neck, a heart set in diamonds, and threw it towards your land. The sea took it, and so I wished your body would take my heart. And with that I lost sight of fair England, told my eyes to go away with my heart, and called them blind, dim glasses for losing sight of England's longed-for coast. How often have I tempted Suffolk's tongue, the agent of your foul fickleness, to sit and charm me, as Ascanius did when he told the frantic Dido his father's deeds that began in burning Troy! Am I not bewitched like her? Or you not false like him? Oh, I can't go on! Die, Margaret! For Henry weeps that you live so long.

It is reported, mighty sovereign, / That good Duke Humphrey traitorously is murther'd / By Suffolk and the Cardinal Beaufort's means. / The commons, like an angry hive of bees / That want their leader, scatter up and down / And care not who they sting in his revenge. / Myself have calm'd their spleenful mutiny / Until they hear the order of his death.

Mighty sovereign, it's reported that good Duke Humphrey has been treacherously murdered by Suffolk and Cardinal Beaufort. The commons, like an angry hive of bees that have lost their leader, are swarming up and down and don't care whom they sting to avenge him. I've calmed their furious rioting until they hear how he died.
That he is dead, good Warwick, 't is too true; / But how he died God knows, not Henry. / Enter his chamber, view his breathless corpse, / And comment then upon his sudden death.
That he is dead, good Warwick, is too true; but how he died, God knows, not Henry. Go into his room, look at his lifeless body, and then explain his sudden death.
That shall I do, my liege.—Stay, Salisbury, / With the rude multitude till I return.
I will, my lord. Stay, Salisbury, with the rough crowd until I come back.

O Thou that judgest all things, stay my thoughts, / My thoughts, that labour to persuade my soul / Some violent hands were laid on Humphrey's life! / If my suspect be false, forgive me, God, / For judgment only doth belong to thee. / Fain would I go to chafe his paly lips / With twenty thousand kisses, and to drain / Upon his face an ocean of salt tears / To tell my love unto his dumb deaf trunk, / And with my fingers feel his hand unfeeling; / But all in vain are these mean obsequies; / And to survey his dead and earthy image, / What were it but to make my sorrow greater?

O You who judge all things, restrain my thoughts, which are trying to persuade my soul that violent hands were laid on Humphrey's life! If my suspicion is false, forgive me, God, for judgement belongs only to you. I'd gladly go and warm his pale lips with twenty thousand kisses, pour an ocean of salt tears on his face, tell my love to his dumb, deaf body, and feel his unfeeling hand with my fingers. But these poor funeral rites are all useless, and what would looking at his dead, earthly form do but make my sorrow greater?
Come hither, gracious sovereign, view this body.
Come here, gracious sovereign, and look at this body.
That is to see how deep my grave is made; / For with his soul fled all my worldly solace, / For seeing him I see my life in death.
That's like seeing how deep my grave is dug, for all my earthly comfort fled with his soul, and seeing him I see my life in death.

As surely as my soul intends to live / With that dread King that took our state upon him / To free us from his father's wrathful curse, / I do believe that violent hands were laid / Upon the life of this thrice-famed duke.
As surely as my soul hopes to live with that awesome King who took on human form to free us from his father's angry curse, I believe violent hands were laid on the life of this most famous duke.
A dreadful oath, sworn with a solemn tongue! / What instance gives Lord Warwick for his vow?
A dreadful oath, sworn solemnly! What evidence does Lord Warwick give for his oath?

See how the blood is settled in his face. / Oft have I seen a timely-parted ghost, / Of ashy semblance, meagre, pale, and bloodless, / Being all descended to the labouring heart, / Who, in the conflict that it holds with death, / Attracts the same for aidance 'gainst the enemy, / Which with the heart there cools and ne'er returneth / To blush and beautify the cheek again. / But see, his face is black and full of blood, / His eyeballs further out than when he liv'd, / Staring full ghastly like a strangled man; / His hair uprear'd, his nostrils stretch'd with struggling, / His hands abroad display'd, as one that grasp'd / And tugg'd for life and was by strength subdu'd. / Look, on the sheets his hair, you see, is sticking; / His well-proportion'd beard made rough and rugged, / Like to the summer's corn by tempest lodged. / It cannot be but he was murther'd here; / The least of all these signs were probable.

See how the blood has settled in his face. I've often seen a body whose soul left it naturally, ashen-looking, thin, pale and bloodless, because all the blood has gone down to the struggling heart, which in its fight with death draws the blood to help it against the enemy; there it cools with the heart and never returns to colour and beautify the cheek again. But look, his face is black and full of blood, his eyeballs bulge further than when he lived, staring hideously like a strangled man's; his hair stands on end, his nostrils stretched with struggling, his hands spread out like one who grabbed and fought for life and was overpowered. Look, you see his hair is stuck to the sheets, and his neat beard is rough and messy, like summer corn flattened by a storm. He must have been murdered here; the least of these signs would make it likely.
Why, Warwick, who should do the duke to death? / Myself and Beaufort had him in protection; / And we, I hope, sir, are no murtherers.
Why, Warwick, who would have killed the duke? Beaufort and I had him in our custody, and we, I hope, sir, are not murderers.
But both of you were vow'd Duke Humphrey's foes, / And you, forsooth, had the good duke to keep; / 'T is like you would not feast him like a friend, / And 't is well seen he found an enemy.
But you were both Duke Humphrey's sworn enemies, and you, indeed, had charge of the good duke. It's not likely you'd entertain him like a friend, and it's plain to see he met an enemy.
Then you, belike, suspect these noblemen / As guilty of Duke Humphrey's timeless death.
Then you suspect, apparently, that these noblemen are guilty of Duke Humphrey's untimely death.

Who finds the heifer dead and bleeding fresh / And sees fast by a butcher with an axe / But will suspect 't was he that made the slaughter? / Who finds the partridge in the puttock's nest / But may imagine how the bird was dead, / Although the kite soar with unbloodied beak? / Even so suspicious is this tragedy.

Who finds a young cow dead and freshly bleeding, and sees a butcher with an axe close by, but suspects that he did the killing? Who finds a partridge in a hawk's nest and can't imagine how the bird died, even if the hawk flies about with a clean beak? This tragedy is just as suspicious.
Are you the butcher, Suffolk? Where's your knife? / Is Beaufort term'd a kite? Where are his talons?
Are you the butcher, Suffolk? Where's your knife? Is Beaufort called a hawk? Where are his claws?

I wear no knife to slaughter sleeping men; / But here's a vengeful sword, rusted with ease, / That shall be scoured in his rancorous heart / That slanders me with murther's crimson badge.— / Say, if thou dar'st, proud Lord of Warwickshire, / That I am faulty in Duke Humphrey's death.

I don't carry a knife to slaughter sleeping men; but here's an avenging sword, rusty from lack of use, which will be cleaned in the spiteful heart of the man who slanders me with the bloody badge of murder. Say, if you dare, proud Lord of Warwickshire, that I'm guilty of Duke Humphrey's death.
What dares not Warwick, if false Suffolk dare him?
What won't Warwick dare, if false Suffolk dares him?
He dares not calm his contumelious spirit, / Nor cease to be an arrogant controller, / Though Suffolk dare him twenty thousand times.
He doesn't dare calm his insulting temper or stop being an arrogant critic, even if Suffolk dared him twenty thousand times.
Madam, be still,—with reverence may I say; / For every word you speak in his behalf / Is slander to your royal dignity.
Madam, be quiet, if I may say so with respect, for every word you speak for him is a slander on your royal dignity.

Blunt-witted lord, ignoble in demeanour! / If ever lady wrong'd her lord so much, / Thy mother took into her blameful bed / Some stern untutor'd churl, and noble stock / Was graft with crab-tree slip, whose fruit thou art, / And never of the Nevils' noble race.

Dim-witted lord, low-born in your manners! If any lady ever wronged her husband that much, your mother took some rough, ignorant peasant into her guilty bed, and a noble family tree was grafted with a crab-apple shoot, whose fruit you are, and you're no true son of the noble Nevilles.

But that the guilt of murther bucklers thee / And I should rob the deathsman of his fee, / Quitting thee thereby of ten thousand shames, / And that my sovereign's presence makes me mild, / I would, false murtherous coward, on thy knee / Make thee beg pardon for thy passed speech / And say it was thy mother that thou meant'st, / That thou thyself was born in bastardy; / And after all this fearful homage done, / Give thee thy hire and send thy soul to hell, / Pernicious blood-sucker of sleeping men!

If it weren't that your guilt of murder protects you, and I'd be robbing the executioner of his fee and so sparing you ten thousand shames, and that my sovereign's presence keeps me calm, I would, false murdering coward, make you beg pardon on your knees for what you've said, and say it was your own mother you meant, and that you yourself were born a bastard. And after all this frightened homage, I'd pay you your wages and send your soul to hell, you deadly bloodsucker of sleeping men!
Thou shalt be waking while I shed thy blood, / If from this presence thou dar'st go with me.
You'll be awake while I shed your blood, if you dare leave this room with me.
Away even now, or I will drag thee hence. / Unworthy though thou art, I'll cope with thee / And do some service to Duke Humphrey's ghost.
Let's go right now, or I'll drag you out. Unworthy though you are, I'll fight you, and do some service to Duke Humphrey's ghost.
What stronger breastplate than a heart untainted! / Thrice is he arm'd that hath his quarrel just, / And he but naked, though lock'd up in steel, / Whose conscience with injustice is corrupted.
What breastplate is stronger than an innocent heart? A man is armed three times over if his cause is just, and naked, though locked in steel armour, if his conscience is corrupted by injustice.
Why, how now, lords! your wrathful weapons drawn / Here in our presence! dare you be so bold? / Why, what tumultuous clamour have we here?
What's this, lords! Your angry swords drawn here in our presence! Do you dare be so bold? What's this uproar?
The traitorous Warwick with the men of Bury / Set all upon me, mighty sovereign.
Mighty sovereign, the traitor Warwick and the men of Bury all attacked me.

[To the Commons, entering] Sirs, stand apart; / the king shall know your mind.— / Dread lord, the commons send you word by me, / Unless false Suffolk straight be done to death, / Or banished fair England's territories, / They will by violence tear him from your palace / And torture him with grievous lingering death. / They say, by him the good Duke Humphrey died; / They say, in him they fear your highness' death; / And mere instinct of love and loyalty, / Free from a stubborn opposite intent, / As being thought to contradict your liking, / Makes them thus forward in his banishment. / They say, in care of your most royal person, / That if your highness should intend to sleep / And charge that no man should disturb your rest / In pain of your dislike or pain of death, / Yet, notwithstanding such a strait edict, / Were there a serpent seen, with forked tongue, / That slily glided towards your majesty, / It were but necessary you were wak'd, / Lest, being suffer'd in that harmful slumber, / The mortal worm might make the sleep eternal; / And therefore do they cry, though you forbid, / That they will guard you, whether you will or no, / From such fell serpents as false Suffolk is, / With whose envenomed and fatal sting, / Your loving uncle, twenty times his worth, / They say, is shamefully bereft of life.

(To the Commons, entering) Men, stand back; the king will know your mind. Dread lord, the commons send you word through me that unless false Suffolk is put to death at once or banished from England, they will tear him from your palace by force and torture him with a slow, painful death. They say good Duke Humphrey died because of him; they say they fear your highness's death from him; and pure love and loyalty, not any stubborn wish to oppose you or go against your wishes, makes them so eager for his banishment. They say, out of care for your royal person, that if your highness meant to sleep and ordered that no one should disturb you on pain of your displeasure or of death, still, despite such a strict order, if a snake with forked tongue were seen sliding slyly towards your majesty, you would have to be woken, in case, left in that dangerous sleep, the deadly serpent made your sleep eternal. And so they cry that, even if you forbid it, they will guard you, whether you want it or not, from such deadly snakes as false Suffolk, by whose poisonous, fatal sting, they say, your loving uncle, worth twenty of him, has been shamefully robbed of his life.
[Within] An answer from the king, my Lord of Salisbury!
(Within) An answer from the king, my Lord of Salisbury!

'T is like the commons, rude unpolish'd hinds, / Could send such message to their sovereign; / But you, my lord, were glad to be employ'd, / To show how quaint an orator you are. / But all the honour Salisbury hath won / Is that he was the lord ambassador / Sent from a sort of tinkers to the king.

It's likely that the commons, rough, uneducated peasants, could send such a message to their king! But you, my lord, were glad to be given the job, to show what an elegant speaker you are. But all the honour Salisbury has won is to be the lord ambassador sent to the king from a bunch of tinkers.
[Within] An answer from the king, or we will all break in!
(Within) An answer from the king, or we'll all break in!

Go, Salisbury, and tell them all from me, / I thank them for their tender loving care, / And had I not been cited so by them, / Yet did I purpose as they do entreat, / For, sure, my thoughts do hourly prophesy / Mischance unto my state by Suffolk's means; / And therefore, by His majesty I swear, / Whose far unworthy deputy I am, / He shall not breathe infection in this air / But three days longer, on the pain of death.

Go, Salisbury, and tell them all from me that I thank them for their tender, loving care; and even if they hadn't urged me, I meant to do what they ask, for my thoughts warn me every hour of harm to my state through Suffolk. And so I swear by His majesty, whose very unworthy deputy I am, that he won't breathe his infection in this air for more than three more days, on pain of death.
O Henry, let me plead for gentle Suffolk!
O Henry, let me plead for gentle Suffolk!

Ungentle queen, to call him gentle Suffolk! / No more, I say; if thou dost plead for him, / Thou wilt but add increase unto my wrath. / Had I but said, I would have kept my word, / But when I swear, it is irrevocable.— / If, after three days' space, thou here be'st found / On any ground that I am ruler of, / The world shall not be ransom for thy life.— / Come, Warwick, come, good Warwick, go with me; / I have great matters to impart to thee.

Ungentle queen, to call him gentle Suffolk! No more, I say. If you plead for him, you'll only add to my anger. If I had only said it, I would have kept my word; but when I swear, it can't be undone. If after three days you are found here on any land I rule, the whole world won't be enough ransom for your life. Come, Warwick, come, good Warwick, come with me; I have important things to tell you.

Mischance and sorrow go along with you! / Heart's discontent and sour affliction / Be playfellows to keep you company! / There's two of you; the devil make a third! / And threefold vengeance tend upon your steps!
Bad luck and sorrow go with you! May heartache and bitter suffering be your playmates and keep you company! There are two of you; may the devil make a third, and triple vengeance follow your steps!
Cease, gentle queen, these execrations, / And let thy Suffolk take his heavy leave.
Stop these curses, gentle queen, and let your Suffolk take his sad leave.
Fie, coward woman and soft-hearted wretch, / Has thou not spirit to curse thine enemy?
Shame, you cowardly woman, soft-hearted wretch! Haven't you the spirit to curse your enemy?

A plague upon them! wherefore should I curse them? / Would curses kill, as doth the mandrake's groan, / I would invent as bitter-searching terms, / As curst, as harsh and horrible to hear, / Deliver'd strongly through my fixed teeth, / With full as many signs of deadly hate, / As lean-fac'd Envy in her loathsome cave. / My tongue should stumble in mine earnest words; / Mine eyes should sparkle like the beaten flint; / Mine hair be fix'd an end, as one distract; / Ay, every joint should seem to curse and ban; / And even now my burthen'd heart would break, / Should I not curse them. Poison be their drink! / Gall, worse than gall, the daintiest that they taste! / Their sweetest shade a grove of cypress-trees! / Their chiefest prospect murthering basilisks! / Their softest touch as smart as lizards' stings! / Their music frightful as the serpent's hiss, / And boding screech-owls make the consort full! / All the foul terrors in dark-seated hell—

A plague on them! Why should I curse them? If curses could kill, like the mandrake's groan, I'd invent words as bitter and piercing, as savage, harsh and horrible to hear, spat through my clenched teeth with as many signs of deadly hate, as lean-faced Envy in her disgusting cave. My tongue would trip over my passionate words, my eyes would spark like struck flint, my hair would stand on end like a madman's; yes, every joint would seem to curse; and even now my heavy heart would break if I didn't curse them. May poison be their drink! Bitterness, worse than bitterness, the finest food they taste! Their sweetest shade a grove of funeral cypress trees! Their best view, killing basilisks! Their softest touch as painful as lizards' stings! Their music as frightening as a snake's hiss, with ominous screech owls to complete the band! All the foul terrors of deep, dark hell—
Enough, sweet Suffolk; thou torment'st thyself; / And these dread curses, like the sun 'gainst glass, / Or like an overcharged gun, recoil / And turns the force of them upon thyself.
Enough, sweet Suffolk; you're torturing yourself. These dreadful curses, like the sun reflected off glass or an overloaded gun, recoil and turn their force on you.

You bade me ban, and will you bid me leave? / Now, by the ground that I am banish'd from, / Well could I curse away a winter's night, / Though standing naked on a mountain top / Where biting cold would never let grass grow, / And think it but a minute spent in sport.

You told me to curse, and now you tell me to stop? By the ground I'm banished from, I could curse through a whole winter's night standing naked on a mountaintop where the biting cold would never let grass grow, and think it only a minute spent in fun.

O, let me entreat thee cease. Give me thy hand, / That I may dew it with my mournful tears; / Nor let the rain of heaven wet this place, / To wash away my woeful monuments. / O, could this kiss be printed in thy hand, / That thou mightest think upon these by the seal, / Through whom a thousand sighs are breath'd for thee! / So, get thee gone, that I may know my grief; / 'T is but surmis'd whiles thou art standing by, / As one that surfeits thinking on a want. / I will repeal thee, or, be well assur'd, / Adventure to be banished myself; / And banished I am, if but from thee. / Go; speak not to me, even now be gone.— / O, go not yet!—Even thus two friends condemn'd / Embrace and kiss and take ten thousand leaves, / Loather a hundred times to part than die. / Yet now farewell; and farewell life with thee!

Oh, please stop. Give me your hand, so I can wet it with my sad tears; and don't let heaven's rain wet this place and wash away the marks of my grief.
