Oh, if only this kiss could be printed on your hand, so you might remember, by this seal, the lips through which a thousand sighs are breathed for you! So go, so that I can fully feel my grief; while you're standing here I only imagine it, like someone who's full thinking about hunger. I'll have you called back, or, be sure of it, risk being banished myself; and I'm banished already, if only from you. Go; don't speak to me; go right now. Oh, don't go yet! This is how two condemned friends embrace and kiss and say goodbye ten thousand times, a hundred times less willing to part than to die. But now farewell, and farewell life with you!

Thus is poor Suffolk ten times banished; / Once by the king, and three times thrice by thee. / 'T is not the land I care for, wert thou thence; / A wilderness is populous enough, / So Suffolk had thy heavenly company; / For where thou art, there is the world itself, / With every several pleasure in the world, / And where thou art not, desolation. / I can no more; live thou to joy thy life, / Myself no joy in nought but that thou liv'st.

So poor Suffolk is banished ten times: once by the king and nine times by you. It's not the country I care about, if you weren't in it. A wilderness would be crowded enough if Suffolk had your heavenly company, for where you are is the whole world, with every pleasure in it, and where you are not is desolation. I can say no more. Live and enjoy your life; I'll have no joy in anything except that you are alive.
Whither goes Vaux so fast? what news, I prithee?
Where is Vaux going so fast? What news, please?

To signify unto his majesty / That Cardinal Beaufort is at point of death; / For suddenly a grievous sickness took him, / That makes him gasp and stare and catch the air, / Blaspheming God and cursing men on earth. / Sometime he talks as if Duke Humphrey's ghost / Were by his side, sometime he calls the king / And whispers to his pillow as to him / The secrets of his overcharged soul; / And I am sent to tell his majesty / That even now he cries aloud for him.

To tell his majesty that Cardinal Beaufort is about to die. A terrible sickness suddenly took him, making him gasp and stare and gulp at the air, blaspheming God and cursing men on earth. Sometimes he talks as if Duke Humphrey's ghost were beside him; sometimes he calls for the king and whispers to his pillow as if to him the secrets of his overburdened soul. I'm sent to tell his majesty that he's crying out for him right now.
Go tell this heavy message to the king.—
Go and give this sad message to the king.

Ay me! what is this world! what news are these! / But wherefore grieve I at an hour's poor loss, / Omitting Suffolk's exile, my soul's treasure? / Why only, Suffolk, mourn I not for thee, / And with the southern clouds contend in tears, / Theirs for the earth's increase, mine for my sorrows? / Now get thee hence. / The king, thou know'st, is coming; / If thou be found by me; thou art but dead.

Oh, what a world this is! What news this is! But why do I grieve over such a small loss as an hour's, and forget Suffolk's exile, my soul's treasure? Why don't I mourn only for you, Suffolk, and compete with the southern clouds in tears, theirs to make the earth grow, mine for my sorrows? Now go. The king, you know, is coming. If you're found with me, you're dead.

If I depart from thee, I cannot live; / And in thy sight to die, what were it else / But like a pleasant slumber in thy lap? / Here could I breathe my soul into the air, / As mild and gentle as the cradle-babe / Dying with mother's dug between its lips; / Where, from thy sight, I should be raging mad / And cry out for thee to close up mine eyes, / To have thee with thy lips to stop my mouth. / So shouldst thou either turn my flying soul, / Or I should breathe it so into thy body, / And then it liv'd in sweet Elysium. / To die by thee were but to die in jest; / From thee to die were torture more than death. / O, let me stay, befall what may befall!

If I leave you, I can't live; and to die in your sight, what would that be but like a pleasant sleep in your lap? Here I could breathe my soul into the air as gently as a baby in its cradle dying with its mother's breast between its lips; whereas out of your sight I'd go raving mad and cry for you to close my eyes, to have your lips close my mouth. So you'd either turn my soul back as it flew away, or I'd breathe it into your body, and then it would live in sweet paradise. To die beside you would only be to die in play; to die away from you would be torture worse than death. Oh, let me stay, whatever happens!

Away! though parting be a fretful corrosive, / It is applied to a deathful wound. / To France, sweet Suffolk; let me hear from thee, / For whereso'er thou art in this world's globe / I'll have an Iris that shall find thee out.
Go! Though parting is a painful remedy, it's applied to a deadly wound. To France, sweet Suffolk; let me hear from you. Wherever you are on this earth, I'll have a messenger who will find you.
And take my heart with thee.
And take my heart with you.
A jewel, lock'd into the wofull'st cask / That ever did contain a thing of worth. / Even as a splitted bark, so sunder we; / This way fall I to death.
A jewel locked in the saddest box that ever held anything precious. Like a ship split in two, we part; I fall this way to death.
How fares my lord? speak, Beaufort, to thy sovereign.
How are you, my lord? Speak to your sovereign, Beaufort.
If thou be'st Death, I'll give thee England's treasure, / Enough to purchase such another island, / So thou wilt let me live and feel no pain.
If you're Death, I'll give you England's treasure, enough to buy another island like it, if you'll let me live and feel no pain.
Ah, what a sign it is of evil life / Where death's approach is seen so terrible!
Ah, what a sign of an evil life it is when death's approach looks so terrible!
Beaufort, it is thy sovereign speaks to thee.
Beaufort, it's your sovereign speaking to you.

Bring me unto my trial when you will. / Died he not in his bed? where should he die? / Can I make men live, whether they will or no? / O, torture me no more! I will confess.— / Alive again? then show me where he is; / I'll give a thousand pound to look upon him. / He hath no eyes, the dust hath blinded them. / Comb down his hair; look, look! it stands upright, / Like lime-twigs set to catch my winged soul.— / Give me some drink; and bid the apothecary / Bring the strong poison that I bought of him.

Bring me to trial when you like. Didn't he die in his bed? Where else should he die? Can I make men live whether they want to or not? Oh, don't torture me any more! I'll confess. Alive again? Then show me where he is; I'll give a thousand pounds to see him. He has no eyes; the dust has blinded them. Comb down his hair; look, look, it's standing on end like sticky twigs set to catch my winged soul! Give me a drink, and tell the chemist to bring the strong poison I bought from him.

O Thou eternal Mover of the Heavens, / Look with a gentle eye upon this wretch! / O, beat away the busy meddling fiend / That lays strong siege unto this wretch's soul, / And from his bosom purge this black despair!
O eternal Mover of the heavens, look gently on this wretch! Oh, beat away the busy, meddling devil that is besieging this wretch's soul, and purge this black despair from his heart!
See how the pangs of death do make him grin!
See how the pains of death make him bare his teeth!
Disturb him not; let him pass peaceably.
Don't disturb him; let him die in peace.
Peace to his soul, if God's good pleasure be!— / Lord cardinal, if thou think'st on heaven's bliss, / Hold up thy hand, make signal of thy hope.— / He dies, and makes no sign.—O God, forgive him!
Peace to his soul, if it is God's will! Lord Cardinal, if you are thinking of heaven's bliss, raise your hand and give a sign of your hope. He dies and makes no sign. O God, forgive him!
So bad a death argues a monstrous life.
Such a bad death shows a monstrous life.
Forbear to judge, for we are sinners all.— / Close up his eyes and draw the curtain close; / And let us all to meditation.
Don't judge, for we are all sinners. Close his eyes and draw the bed curtains, and let us all go to pray.

The gaudy, blabbing, and remorseful day / Is crept into the bosom of the sea; / And now loud-howling wolves arouse the jades / That drag the tragic melancholy night, / Who, with their drowsy, slow, and flagging wings, / Clip dead men's graves and from their misty jaws / Breathe foul contagious darkness in the air. / Therefore bring forth the soldiers of our prize; / For, whilst our pinnace anchors in the Downs, / Here shall they make their ransom on the sand / Or with their blood stain this discolour'd shore.— / Master, this prisoner freely give I thee;— / And thou that art his mate, make boot of this;— / The other, Walter Whitmore, is thy share.

The bright, gossiping, pitying day has crept into the sea's embrace, and now loud-howling wolves wake the tired horses that pull the tragic, gloomy night, who with drowsy, slow, drooping wings hugs dead men's graves and breathes foul, infectious darkness from her misty jaws into the air. So bring out the soldiers we've captured, for while our small ship is anchored in the Downs, they'll pay their ransom here on the sand or stain this muddy shore with their blood. Master, I give you this prisoner freely; and you, his mate, take profit from this one; the other one, Walter Whitmore, is your share.
What is my ransom, master? let me know?
What's my ransom, master? Tell me.
A thousand crowns, or else lay down your head.
A thousand crowns, or else lay down your head.
And so much shall you give, or off goes yours.
And you'll give the same, or off goes yours.

What, think you much to pay two thousand crowns, / And bear the name and port of gentlemen?— / Cut both the villains' throats;—for die you shall. / The lives of those which we have lost in fight / Be counterpois'd with such a petty sum!

What, do you think two thousand crowns too much, when you have the name and bearing of gentlemen? Cut both the villains' throats; you shall die. Are the lives of the men we lost in the fight to be weighed against such a small sum!
I'll give it, sir; and therefore spare my life.
I'll pay it, sir, so spare my life.
And so will I, and write home for it straight.
And so will I, and I'll write home for it at once.
I lost mine eye in laying the prize aboard,— / [To Suffolk] And therefore, to revenge it, shalt thou die;— / And so should these, if I might have my will.
I lost my eye boarding the captured ship, (to Suffolk) and so, to avenge it, you will die; and so would these, if I had my way.
Be not so rash; take ransom, let him live.
Don't be so hasty. Take a ransom and let him live.
Look on my George; I am a gentleman. / Rate me at what thou wilt, thou shalt be paid.
Look at my George, the badge of the Garter; I'm a gentleman. Name your price, and you'll be paid.
And so am I; my name is Walter Whitmore. / How now! why start'st thou? What, doth death affright?
And so am I; my name is Walter Whitmore. What's this! Why do you jump? What, does death frighten you?

Thy name affrights me, in whose sound is death. / A cunning man did calculate my birth / And told me that by water I should die. / Yet let not this make thee be bloody-minded; / Thy name is Gaultier, being rightly sounded.

Your name frightens me; there's death in its sound. A fortune-teller cast my horoscope and told me I would die by water. But don't let this make you bloodthirsty; your name, pronounced correctly, is Gaultier.

Gaultier or Walter, which it is, I care not. / Never yet did base dishonour blur our name / But with our sword we wip'd away the blot; / Therefore, when merchant-like I sell revenge, / Broke be my sword, my arms torn and defac'd, / And I proclaim'd a coward through the world!

Gaultier or Walter, I don't care which. No low disgrace ever stained our name without our swords wiping the stain away. So if I ever sell revenge like a merchant, may my sword be broken, my coat of arms torn and defaced, and I proclaimed a coward across the world!
Stay, Whitmore; for thy prisoner is a prince, / The Duke of Suffolk, William de la Pole.
Wait, Whitmore, for your prisoner is a prince: the Duke of Suffolk, William de la Pole.
The Duke of Suffolk muffled up in rags!
The Duke of Suffolk wrapped up in rags!
Ay, but these rags are no part of the duke; / Jove sometime went disguis'd, and why not I?
Yes, but these rags are no part of the duke. Jove sometimes went in disguise, so why not I?
But Jove was never slain, as thou shalt be.
But Jove was never killed, as you will be.

Obscure and lowly swain, King Henry's blood, / The honourable blood of Lancaster, / Must not be shed by such a jaded groom. / Hast thou not kiss'd thy hand and held my stirrup? / Bare-headed plodded by my foot-cloth mule / And thought thee happy when I shook my head? / How often hast thou waited at my cup, / Fed from my trencher, kneel'd down at the board, / When I have feasted with Queen Margaret? / Remember it and let it make thee crest-fallen, / Ay, and allay thus thy abortive pride, / How in our voiding lobby hast thou stood / And duly waited for my coming forth. / This hand of mine hath writ in thy behalf, / And therefore shall it charm thy riotous tongue.

Low, obscure peasant, King Henry's blood, the honourable blood of Lancaster, must not be spilled by such a worn-out servant. Haven't you kissed your hand to me and held my stirrup? Walked bare-headed beside my richly covered mule and thought yourself lucky when I nodded to you? How often have you served my wine, eaten from my plate, knelt at the table when I feasted with Queen Margaret? Remember it, and let it humble you, yes, and so check your premature pride: how you stood in my hall waiting dutifully for me to come out. This hand of mine has written letters on your behalf, and so it will charm your unruly tongue into silence.
Speak, captain, shall I stab the forlorn swain?
Tell me, captain, shall I stab this wretched peasant?
First let my words stab him, as he hath me.
First let my words stab him, as his have stabbed me.
Base slave, thy words are blunt and so art thou.
Low slave, your words are blunt, and so are you.
Convey him hence, and on our long-boat's side / Strike off his head.
Take him away, and cut off his head on the side of our longboat.
Thou dar'st not, for thy own.
You don't dare, for fear of losing your own.

Pool! Sir Pool! lord! / Ay, kennel, puddle, sink, whose filth and dirt / Troubles the silver spring where England drinks. / Now will I dam up this thy yawning mouth / For swallowing the treasure of the realm; / Thy lips that kiss'd the queen shall sweep the ground; / And thou that smil'dst at good Duke Humphrey's death / Against the senseless winds shalt grin in vain, / Who in contempt shall hiss at thee again. / And wedded be thou to the hags of hell, / For daring to affy a mighty lord / Unto the daughter of a worthless king, / Having neither subject, wealth, nor diadem. / By devilish policy art thou grown great / And, like ambitious Sylla, overgorg'd / With gobbets of thy mother's bleeding heart. / By thee Anjou and Maine were sold to France, / The false revolting Normans thorough thee / Disdain to call us lord, and Picardy / Hath slain their governors, surpris'd our forts, / And sent the ragged soldiers wounded home. / The princely Warwick, and the Nevils all, / Whose dreadful swords were never drawn in vain, / As hating thee are rising up in arms; / And now the house of York, thrust from the crown / By shameful murther of a guiltless king / And lofty proud encroaching tyranny, / Burns with revenging fire, whose hopeful colours / Advance our half-fac'd sun, striving to shine, / Under the which is writ 'Invitis nubibus.' / The commons here in Kent are up in arms; / And, to conclude, reproach and beggary / Is crept into the palace of our king, / And all by thee.—Away! convey him hence.

Pool! Sir Pool! Lord! Yes, gutter, puddle, sewer, whose filth and dirt muddies the clear spring England drinks from. Now I'll stop up your gaping mouth for swallowing the kingdom's treasure. Your lips that kissed the queen will sweep the ground, and you who smiled at good Duke Humphrey's death will grin in vain at the unfeeling winds, which will hiss back at you in contempt. And may you be married to the hags of hell for daring to betroth a mighty lord to the daughter of a worthless king who has no subjects, money or crown. You've grown great by devilish cunning, and like ambitious Sulla gorged yourself on lumps of your mother country's bleeding heart. Because of you Anjou and Maine were sold to France; because of you the false, rebellious Normans refuse to call us lord, and Picardy has killed its governors, captured our forts, and sent our ragged soldiers home wounded. Princely Warwick and all the Nevilles, whose dreaded swords were never drawn for nothing, are rising in arms because they hate you. And now the house of York, pushed from the crown by the shameful murder of an innocent king and by proud, grasping tyranny, burns with avenging fire; its hopeful banners carry our half-hidden sun, struggling to shine, with the motto "In spite of the clouds". The commons here in Kent are up in arms, and, to finish, disgrace and poverty have crept into our king's palace, and all because of you. Away! Take him away.

O that I were a god, to shoot forth thunder / Upon these paltry, servile, abject drudges! / Small things make base men proud; this villain here, / Being captain of a pinnace, threatens more / Than Bargulus the strong Illyrian pirate.— / Drones suck not eagles' blood but rob bee-hives. / It is impossible that I should die / By such a lowly vassal as thyself. / Thy words move rage and not remorse in me. / I go of message from the queen to France; / I charge thee waft me safely cross the Channel.

Oh, if only I were a god, to fire thunderbolts at these worthless, servile, low drudges! Small things make low men proud. This villain here, just because he's captain of a little boat, threatens more than Bargulus, the mighty Illyrian pirate. Drones don't suck eagles' blood; they rob beehives. It's impossible that I should die at the hands of such a low servant as you. Your words make me angry, not sorry. I'm going to France with a message from the queen; I order you to carry me safely across the Channel.
Come, Suffolk, I must waft thee to thy death.
Come, Suffolk, I must carry you to your death.
Gelidus timor occupat artus; it is thee I fear.
"Cold fear seizes my limbs"; it's you I fear.
Thou shalt have cause to fear before I leave thee. / What, are ye daunted now? now will ye stoop?
You'll have reason to fear before I'm done with you. What, are you frightened now? Now will you bow down?
My gracious lord, entreat him, speak him fair.
My gracious lord, beg him, speak kindly to him.

Suffolk's imperial tongue is stern and rough, / Us'd to command, untaught to plead for favour. / Far be it we should honour such as these / With humble suit; no, rather let my head / Stoop to the block than these knees bow to any / Save to the God of heaven and to my king, / And sooner dance upon a bloody pole / Than stand uncover'd to the vulgar groom. / True nobility is exempt from fear; / More can I bear than you dare execute.

Suffolk's royal tongue is stern and rough, used to giving orders, not taught to beg for favours. Far be it from us to honour such men with humble pleas. No, I'd rather let my head bow to the block than let these knees bend to anyone but the God of heaven and my king, and sooner dance on a bloody pole than stand bare-headed before a common servant. True nobility knows no fear. I can bear more than you dare do.
Hale him away, and let him talk no more.
Drag him away, and don't let him talk any more.

Come, soldiers, show what cruelty ye can, / That this my death may never be forgot! / Great men oft die by vile bezonians: / A Roman sworder and banditto slave / Murther'd sweet Tully; Brutus' bastard hand / Stabb'd Julius Caesar; savage islanders / Pompey the Great; and Suffolk dies by pirates.

Come, soldiers, show what cruelty you can, so that my death may never be forgotten! Great men often die at the hands of low ruffians. A Roman swordsman and outlaw slave murdered sweet Cicero; Brutus's bastard hand stabbed Julius Caesar; savage islanders killed Pompey the Great; and Suffolk dies by pirates.
And as for these whose ransom we have set, / It is our pleasure one of them depart, / Therefore come you with us, and let him go.
And as for these whose ransom we've set, we've decided to let one of them go. So you come with us, and let him go.
There let his head and lifeless body lie / Until the queen his mistress bury it.
Let his head and lifeless body lie there until the queen, his mistress, buries it.
O barbarous and bloody spectacle! / His body will I bear unto the king. / If he revenge it not, yet will his friends; / So will the queen, that living held him dear.
Oh, barbaric and bloody sight! I'll carry his body to the king. If he doesn't avenge it, his friends will; and so will the queen, who loved him dearly while he lived.
Come, and get thee a sword, though made of / a lath; they have been up these two days.
Come on, get yourself a sword, even if it's made of wood; they've been up these two days.
They have the more need to sleep now, then.
Then they need sleep all the more now.
I tell thee, Jack Cade the clothier means to dress the / commonwealth, and turn it, and set a new nap upon it.
I tell you, Jack Cade the cloth worker means to dress the country like cloth, turn it inside out and give it a new nap.
So he had need, for 't is threadbare. Well, I say / it was never merry world in England since gentlemen came up.
He needs to, for it's threadbare. Well, I say England has never been a happy place since gentlemen came along.
O miserable age! virtue is not regarded in / handicraftsmen.
Oh, miserable times! Nobody respects the virtue of craftsmen.
The nobility think scorn to go in leather aprons.
The nobles turn their noses up at wearing leather aprons.
Nay, more, the king's council are no good workmen.
What's more, the king's council are no good as workers.
True; and yet it is said, labour in thy vocation, / which is as much to say as, let the magistrates be labouring / men; and therefore should we be magistrates.
True; and yet it's said, "Work hard at your calling", which is as much as to say, let the rulers be working men; and so we should be the rulers.
Thou hast hit it; for there's no better sign of a brave / mind than a hard hand.
You've got it, for there's no better sign of a brave mind than a hard hand.
I see them! I see them! There's Best's son, the / tanner of Wingham,—
I see them! I see them! There's Best's son, the tanner from Wingham—
He shall have the skin of our enemies, to make dog's- / leather of.
He'll take our enemies' skins to make dog-leather from.
Then is sin struck down like an ox, and iniquity's / throat cut like a calf.
Then sin will be struck down like an ox, and wickedness have its throat cut like a calf.
Argo, their thread of life is spun.
Ergo, their thread of life is spun.
Come, come, let's fall in with them.
Come on, come on, let's join them.
We John Cade, so term'd of our supposed father,—
We, John Cade, so called after our supposed father—
[Aside] Or rather, of stealing a cade of herrings.
(Aside) Or rather, from stealing a barrel of herrings.
For our enemies shall fall before us, inspired with the / spirit of putting down kings and princes,—Command silence.
For our enemies shall fall before us, inspired with the spirit of putting down kings and princes— Call for silence.
[Aside] He was an honest man and a good bricklayer.
(Aside) He was an honest man and a good bricklayer.
[Aside] I knew her well; she was a midwife.
(Aside) I knew her well; she was a midwife.
My wife descended of the Lacies,—
My wife descended from the Lacy family—
[Aside] She was, indeed, a pedler's daughter, and sold / many laces.
(Aside) She was indeed a pedlar's daughter, and sold plenty of laces.
[Aside] But now of late, not able to travel with her / furred pack, she washes bucks here at home.
(Aside) But lately, unable to travel with her fur-covered pack, she does washing here at home.
Therefore am I of an honourable house.
So I come from an honourable house.
[Aside] Ay, by my faith, the field is honourable; and / there was he born, under a hedge, for his father had never a / house but / the cage.
(Aside) Yes, by my faith, the field is honourable, and that's where he was born, under a hedge, for his father never had any house but the lock-up.
[Aside] A' must needs; for beggary is valiant.
(Aside) He must be, for beggars are tough.
I am able to endure much.
[Aside] No question of that; for I have seen him whipped / three market-days together.
(Aside) No doubt about that, for I've seen him whipped three market days in a row.
I fear neither sword nor fire.
I fear neither sword nor fire.
[Aside] He need not fear the sword, for his coat is of / proof.
(Aside) He needn't fear the sword, for his coat is sword-proof, it's so tough.
[Aside] But methinks he should stand in fear of fire, / being burnt i' the hand for stealing of sheep.
(Aside) But I think he should be afraid of fire, having been branded on the hand for stealing sheep.

Be brave, then; for your captain is brave, and vows / reformation. There shall be in England seven halfpenny loaves / sold for a penny; the three-hooped pot shall have ten hoops; and / I will make it felony to drink small beer. All the realm shall be / in common; and in Cheapside shall my palfry go to grass; and / when I am king, as king I will be,—

Be brave, then, for your captain is brave and promises reform. In England seven halfpenny loaves will be sold for a penny; the three-hooped beer pot will have ten hoops; and I'll make it a crime to drink weak beer. The whole kingdom will be held in common, and my horse will graze in Cheapside. And when I'm king, as king I will be—
I thank you, good people;—there shall be no money; all shall / eat and drink on my score, and I will apparel them all in one / livery, that they may agree like brothers and worship me their / lord.
Thank you, good people. There will be no money; everyone will eat and drink at my expense, and I'll dress them all in the same uniform, so that they get on like brothers and worship me as their lord.
The first thing we do, let's kill all the lawyers.
The first thing we do, let's kill all the lawyers.

Nay, that I mean to do. Is not this a lamentable thing, that / of the skin of an innocent lamb should be made parchment, that / parchment, being scribbl'd o'er, should undo a man? Some say the / bee stings; but I say 't is the bee's wax, for I did but seal / once to a thing, and I was never mine own man since.—How now! / who's there?

Indeed, I mean to. Isn't it a sad thing that the skin of an innocent lamb should be made into parchment, and that parchment, once scribbled over, should ruin a man? Some say the bee stings; but I say it's the bee's wax, for I put my seal to a document once, and I've never been my own man since. What's this! Who's there?
The clerk of Chatham; he can write and read and cast / accompt.
The clerk of Chatham. He can write and read and do accounts.
We took him setting of boys' copies.
We caught him setting copying exercises for boys.
Has a book in his pocket with red letters in 't.
He has a book in his pocket with red letters in it.
Nay, then, he is a conjurer.
Nay, he can make obligations and write court-hand.
No, he can draw up contracts and write legal script.
I am sorry for 't. / The man is a proper man, of mine honour; / unless I find him guilty, he shall not die.—Come hither, sirrah, / I must examine thee; what is thy name?
I'm sorry for it. The man is a fine fellow, on my honour; unless I find him guilty, he won't die. Come here, you; I must examine you. What's your name?
They use to write it on the top of letters.—'T will go / hard with you.
They usually write that at the top of letters. Things will go badly for you.
Let me alone.—Dost thou use to write thy name? or hast / thou a mark to thyself, like a honest, plain-dealing man?
Leave this to me. Do you usually write your name, or do you have your own mark, like an honest, plain-dealing man?
Sir, I thank God, I have been so well brought up that I / can write my name.
Sir, thank God, I've been well enough brought up that I can write my name.
He hath confess'd; away with him! he's a villain and a / traitor.
He's confessed! Away with him! He's a villain and a traitor.
Away with him, I say! hang him with his pen and inkhorn / about his neck.
Away with him, I say! Hang him with his pen and inkpot round his neck.
Here I am, thou particular fellow.
Here I am, you particular fellow.
Fly, fly, fly! Sir Humphrey Stafford and his brother / are hard by, with the king's forces.
Run, run, run! Sir Humphrey Stafford and his brother are close by with the king's forces.
Stand, villain, stand, or I'll fell thee down. He shall be / encountered with a man as good as himself; he is but a knight, / is a'?
Stand still, villain, stand, or I'll knock you down. He'll be met by a man as good as himself. He's only a knight, isn't he?
To equal him, I will make myself a knight presently.— / [Kneels] Rise up Sir John Mortimer.—[Rises] Now have at him!
To match him, I'll make myself a knight at once. (Kneels) Arise, Sir John Mortimer. (Rises) Now let's at him!
Rebellious hinds, the filth and scum of Kent, / Mark'd for the gallows, lay your weapons down; / Home to your cottages, forsake this groom. / The king is merciful, if you revolt.
Rebellious peasants, the filth and scum of Kent, marked out for the gallows, lay down your weapons. Go home to your cottages and abandon this servant. The king is merciful if you give up your revolt.
But angry, wrathful, and inclin'd to blood, / If you go forward; therefore yield, or die.
But angry, furious and ready to shed blood if you carry on. So surrender, or die.
As for these silken-coated slaves, I pass not; / It is to you, good people, that I speak, / Over whom, in time to come, I hope to reign, / For I am rightful heir unto the crown.
As for these silk-coated slaves, I don't care about them. It's to you, good people, that I'm speaking, over whom I hope to reign in time to come, for I am the rightful heir to the crown.
Villain, thy father was a plasterer; / And thou thyself a shearman, art thou not?
Villain, your father was a plasterer, and you yourself are a cloth-shearer, aren't you?
Marry, this: Edmund Mortimer, Earl of March, / Married the Duke of Clarence' daughter, did he not?
Just this: Edmund Mortimer, Earl of March, married the Duke of Clarence's daughter, didn't he?
By her he had two children at one birth.

Ay, there's the question; but I say 't is true. / The elder of them, being put to nurse, / Was by a beggar-woman stolen away, / And, ignorant of his birth and parentage, / Became a bricklayer when he came to age. / His son am I; deny it, if you can.

Yes, that's the question; but I say it's true. The elder of them was put out to a nurse and stolen away by a beggar woman, and not knowing his birth or parents, he became a bricklayer when he grew up. I'm his son; deny it if you can.
Nay, 't is too true; therefore he shall be king.
No, it's too true; so he will be king.
Sir, he made a chimney in my father's house, and the bricks / are alive at this day to testify it; therefore deny it not.
Sir, he built a chimney in my father's house, and the bricks are alive to this day to prove it; so don't deny it.
And will you credit this base drudge's words, / That speaks he knows not what?
And will you believe the words of this low drudge, who doesn't know what he's saying?
Ay, marry, will we; therefore get ye gone.
Yes, indeed we will; so get out of here.
Jack Cade, the Duke of York hath taught you this.
Jack Cade, the Duke of York has taught you this.

[Aside] He lies, for I invented it myself.—Go to, sirrah, / tell the king from me that, for his father's sake, Henry the / Fifth, in whose time boys went to span-counter for French crowns, / I am content he shall reign; but I'll be protector over him.

(Aside) He's lying, for I made it up myself. Go on, you, tell the king from me that for the sake of his father, Henry the Fifth, in whose time boys played games for French coins as stakes, I'm happy for him to reign, but I'll be his Protector.
And furthermore, we'll have the Lord Say's head for / selling the dukedom of Maine.
And what's more, we'll have Lord Say's head for selling the dukedom of Maine.

And good reason; for thereby is England mained, and fain to go / with a staff, but that my puissance holds it up. Fellow kings, I / tell you that that Lord Say hath gelded the commonwealth and made / it an eunuch; and more than that, he can speak French, and / therefore he is a traitor.

And with good reason, for that has maimed England, and she'd have to walk with a stick if my power didn't hold her up. Fellow kings, I tell you that Lord Say has castrated the country and made it a eunuch; and more than that, he can speak French, and so he's a traitor.
Nay, answer if you can: the Frenchmen are our enemies; / go to, then, I ask but this: can he that speaks with the tongue / of an enemy be a good counsellor, or no?
No, answer if you can. The French are our enemies. Well then, I only ask this: can a man who speaks the enemy's language be a good adviser or not?
No, no; and therefore we'll have his head.
No, no; and so we'll have his head.
Well, seeing gentle words will not prevail, / Assail them with the army of the king.
Well, since gentle words won't work, attack them with the king's army.

Herald, away; and throughout every town / Proclaim them traitors that are up with Cade; / That those which fly before the battle ends / May, even in their wives' and children's sight, / Be hang'd up for example at their doors.— / And you that be the king's friends, follow me.

Herald, go, and in every town proclaim that those who have risen with Cade are traitors, so that those who run away before the battle ends may be hanged at their own doors as an example, even in front of their wives and children. And you who are the king's friends, follow me.

And you that love the commons follow me. / Now show yourselves men; 't is for liberty. / We will not leave one lord, one gentleman; / Spare none but such as go in clouted shoon, / For they are thrifty honest men and such / As would, but that they dare not, take our parts.

And you who love the commons, follow me. Now prove yourselves men; it's for liberty. We won't leave one lord or one gentleman alive. Spare nobody but those who wear patched shoes, for they're thrifty, honest men who'd take our side if they dared.
They are all in order and march toward us.
They're all in order and marching towards us.
But then are we in order when we are most out of / order.—Come, march forward.
But we're most in order when we're most out of order. Come, march on.
Where's Dick, the butcher of Ashford?
Where's Dick, the butcher from Ashford?

They fell before thee like sheep and oxen, and thou / behavedst thyself as if thou hadst been in thine own / slaughter-house; therefore thus will I reward thee: / the Lent shall be as long again as it is, and thou / shalt have a licence to kill for a hundred lacking one.

They fell in front of you like sheep and oxen, and you behaved as if you were in your own slaughterhouse. So I'll reward you like this: Lent will be twice as long as it is, and you'll have a licence to kill meat for a hundred people minus one.

And, to speak truth, thou deservest no less. / This monument of the victory will I bear / [putting on Sir Humphrey's brigandine]; / and the bodies shall be dragged at my horse heels till I do come / to London, where we will have the mayor's sword borne before us.

And to tell the truth, you deserve no less. I'll wear this souvenir of the victory (putting on Sir Humphrey's armour), and the bodies will be dragged at my horse's heels until I get to London, where we'll have the mayor's sword carried before us.
If we mean to thrive and do good, break open the gaols and / let out the prisoners.
If we mean to prosper and do good, let's break open the jails and let the prisoners out.
Fear not that, I warrant thee. Come, let's march towards / London.
Don't worry about that, I promise you. Come, let's march on London.

Oft have I heard that grief softens the mind / And makes it fearful and degenerate; / Think therefore on revenge and cease to weep. / But who can cease to weep and look on this? / Here may his head lie on my throbbing breast; / But where's the body that I should embrace?

I've often heard that grief softens the mind and makes it fearful and weak. So think about revenge and stop weeping. But who can stop weeping who looks at this? Let his head lie here on my throbbing breast; but where is the body I should hold?
What answer makes your grace to the rebels' / supplication?
What answer does your grace give to the rebels' petition?

I'll send some holy bishop to entreat; / For God forbid so many simple souls / Should perish by the sword! And I myself, / Rather than bloody war shall cut them short, / Will parley with Jack Cade their general.— / But stay, I'll read it over once again.

I'll send some holy bishop to plead with them, for God forbid so many simple souls should die by the sword! And rather than let bloody war cut them down, I'll talk with Jack Cade, their general, myself. But wait, I'll read it through again.
Ah, barbarous villains! hath this lovely face / Rul'd, like a wandering planet, over me, / And could it not enforce them to relent / That were unworthy to behold the same?
Ah, savage villains! Has this lovely face ruled over me like a wandering planet, and couldn't it make those who weren't fit even to look at it show mercy?
Lord Say, Jack Cade hath sworn to have thy head.
Lord Say, Jack Cade has sworn to have your head.
Ay, but I hope your highness shall have his.
Yes, but I hope your highness will have his.
How now, madam! / Still lamenting and mourning for Suffolk's death? / I fear me, love, if that I had been dead, / Thou wouldst not have mourn'd so much for me.
What, madam! Still weeping and mourning over Suffolk's death? I fear, my love, that if I had died, you wouldn't have mourned so much for me.
No, my love, I should not mourn, but die for thee.
No, my love, I wouldn't mourn; I'd die for you.
How now! what news? why com'st thou in such haste?
What's this! What news? Why do you come in such a hurry?

The rebels are in Southwark; fly, my lord! / Jack Cade proclaims himself Lord Mortimer, / Descended from the Duke of Clarence' house, / And calls your grace usurper openly, / And vows to crown himself in Westminster. / His army is a ragged multitude / Of hinds and peasants, rude and merciless; / Sir Humphrey Stafford and his brother's death / Hath given them heart and courage to proceed. / All scholars, lawyers, courtiers, gentlemen, / They call false caterpillars, and intend their death.

The rebels are in Southwark; run, my lord! Jack Cade calls himself Lord Mortimer, descended from the Duke of Clarence's house, calls your grace a usurper openly and swears to crown himself in Westminster. His army is a ragged crowd of farm workers and peasants, rough and merciless. The deaths of Sir Humphrey Stafford and his brother have given them heart and courage to carry on. They call all scholars, lawyers, courtiers and gentlemen false caterpillars and mean to kill them.
O graceless men! they know not what they do.
Oh, godless men! They don't know what they're doing.
My gracious lord, retire to Killingworth / Until a power be rais'd to put them down.
My gracious lord, withdraw to Kenilworth until an army is raised to put them down.
Ah, were the Duke of Suffolk now alive, / These Kentish rebels would be soon appeas'd!
Ah, if the Duke of Suffolk were alive now, these Kentish rebels would soon be quieted!
Lord Say, the traitors hate thee; / Therefore away with us to Killingworth.
Lord Say, the traitors hate you, so come away with us to Kenilworth.
So might your grace's person be in danger. / The sight of me is odious in their eyes; / And therefore in this city will I stay / And live alone as secret as I may.
That might put your grace in danger. The sight of me is hateful to them, so I'll stay in the city and live as secretly as I can.

Jack Cade hath gotten London bridge; / The citizens fly and forsake their houses. / The rascal people, thirsting after prey, / Join with the traitor, and they jointly swear / To spoil the city and your royal court.

Jack Cade has taken London Bridge. The citizens are running away and leaving their houses. The rabble, hungry for plunder, are joining the traitor, and they all swear together to loot the city and your royal court.
Then linger not, my lord; away, take horse.
Then don't delay, my lord; go, get on your horse.
Come Margaret; God, our hope, will succour us.
Come, Margaret; God, our hope, will help us.
My hope is gone, now Suffolk is deceas'd.
My hope is gone now Suffolk is dead.
Farewell, my lord; trust not the Kentish rebels.
Farewell, my lord; don't trust the Kentish rebels.
Trust nobody, for fear you be betray'd.
Trust nobody, in case you're betrayed.
The trust I have is in mine innocence, / And therefore am I bold and resolute.
I trust in my innocence, and so I am bold and determined.
How now! Is Jack Cade slain?
What's the news? Is Jack Cade killed?

No, my lord, nor likely to be slain; for they / have won the bridge, killing all those that withstand them. / The lord mayor craves aid of your honour from the Tower / to defend the city from the rebels.
No, my lord, and not likely to be, for they've taken the bridge and are killing everyone who resists them. The Lord Mayor asks your honour for help from the Tower to defend the city from the rebels.

Such aid as I can spare you shall command, / But I am troubled here with them myself; / The rebels have assay'd to win the Tower. / But get you to Smithfield and gather head, / And thither I will send you Matthew Goffe. / Fight for your king, your country, and your lives; / And so, farewell, for I must hence again.

You can have whatever help I can spare, but I'm troubled by them here myself; the rebels have tried to take the Tower. But go to Smithfield and gather a force, and I'll send Matthew Goffe to you there. Fight for your king, your country and your lives. And so farewell, for I must go back.

Now is Mortimer lord of this city. And here, sitting upon / London-stone, I charge and command that, of the city's cost, the / conduit run nothing but claret wine this first year of our reign. / And now henceforward it shall be treason for any that calls me / other / than Lord Mortimer.

Now Mortimer is lord of this city. And here, sitting on London Stone, I order and command that at the city's expense the water fountain will run with nothing but red wine in this first year of our reign. And from now on it will be treason for anyone to call me anything but Lord Mortimer.
If this fellow be wise, he'll never call ye Jack / Cade more; I think he hath a very fair warning.
If this fellow's wise, he'll never call you Jack Cade again; I think he's had a very fair warning.
My lord, there's an army gathered together in Smithfield.
My lord, there's an army gathered in Smithfield.
Come then, let's go fight with them. But first, go and set / London bridge on fire; and, if you can, burn down the Tower too. / Come, let's away.
Come on then, let's go and fight them. But first go and set London Bridge on fire, and if you can, burn down the Tower too. Come, let's go.
So, sirs.—Now go some and pull down the Savoy; others / to the inns of court; down with them all.
So, men. Now some of you go and pull down the Savoy palace; others go to the Inns of Court; down with them all.
I have a suit unto your lordship.
I have a request to your lordship.
Be it a lordship, thou shalt have it for that word.
Even if it's a lordship, you'll have it for that word.
Only that the laws of England may come out of / your mouth.
Only that the laws of England may come out of your mouth.
[Aside] Mass, 't will be sore law, then; for he / was thrust in the mouth with a spear, and 't is not whole yet.
(Aside) By the mass, it'll be sore law, then, for he was stabbed in the mouth with a spear and it hasn't healed yet.
[Aside] Nay, John, it will be stinking law, for his / breath stinks with eating toasted cheese.
(Aside) No, John, it'll be stinking law, for his breath stinks from eating toasted cheese.
I have thought upon it, it shall be so. Away, burn / all the records of the realm. My mouth shall be the parliament / of England.
I've thought about it, and so it will be. Go, burn all the kingdom's records. My mouth will be the parliament of England.
[Aside] Then we are like to have biting statutes, / unless his teeth be pulled out.
(Aside) Then we're likely to have biting laws, unless his teeth are pulled out.
And henceforward all things shall be in common.
And from now on everything will be held in common.
My lord, a prize, a prize! here's the Lord / Say, which sold the towns in France; he that made us pay / one and twenty fifteens, and one shilling to the pound, the / last subsidy.
My lord, a prize, a prize! Here's Lord Say, who sold the towns in France, who made us pay twenty-one fifteenths and a shilling in the pound in the last tax.

Well, he shall be beheaded for it ten times.—Ah, thou say, / thou serge, nay, thou buckram lord! now art thou within point- / blank of our jurisdiction regal. What canst thou answer to my / majesty for giving up of Normandy unto Mounsieur Basimecu, the / dauphin of France? Be it known unto thee by these presence, even / the presence of Lord Mortimer, that I am the besom that must / sweep the court clean of such filth as thou art. Thou hast most / traitorously corrupted the youth of the realm in erecting a / grammar school; and whereas, before, our forefathers had no other / books but the score and the tally, thou hast caused printing to / be used, and, contrary to the king, his crown, and dignity, thou / hast built a paper-mill. It will be proved to thy face that thou / hast men about thee that usually talk of a noun and a verb, and / such abominable words as no Christian ear can endure to hear. / Thou hast appointed justices of peace, to call poor men before / them about matters they were not able to answer. Moreover, thou / hast put them in prison, and because they could not read, thou / hast hanged them; when, indeed, only for that cause they have / been most worthy to live. Thou dost ride in a foot-cloth, dost / thou not?

Well, he'll be beheaded ten times for it. Ah, you say, you serge, no, you buckram lord! Now you're right within range of our royal jurisdiction. What can you answer to my majesty for giving up Normandy to Monsieur Kiss-my-arse, the Dauphin of France? Be it known to you by these presents, that is, the presence of Lord Mortimer, that I am the broom that must sweep the court clean of such filth as you. You have most treacherously corrupted the youth of the kingdom by setting up a grammar school; and whereas before, our ancestors had no books but the notched tally stick, you have brought in printing, and, against the king, his crown and his dignity, you have built a paper mill. It will be proved to your face that you keep men around you who usually talk about nouns and verbs and such abominable words as no Christian ear can bear to hear. You have appointed justices of the peace to summon poor men about matters they couldn't answer. What's more, you've put them in prison, and because they couldn't read, you've hanged them, when for that reason alone they most deserved to live. You ride a horse with a fancy saddlecloth, don't you?
Marry, thou oughtest not to let thy horse wear a cloak / when honester men than thou go in their hose and doublets.
Why, you shouldn't let your horse wear a cloak when more honest men than you go about in their tights and jackets.
And work in their shirt too; as myself, for example, that / am a butcher.
And work in their shirts too, like me, for example, a butcher.
What do you say about Kent?
Nothing but this; 't is 'bona terra, mala gens.'
Only this: it's "a good land, a bad people".
Away with him, away with him! he speaks Latin.
Away with him, away with him! He speaks Latin.

Hear me but speak, and bear me where you will. / Kent, in the Commentaries Caesar writ, / Is term'd the civil'st place of all this isle. / Sweet is the country, because full of riches; / The people liberal, valiant, active, wealthy; / Which makes me hope you are not void of pity. / I sold not Maine, I lost not Normandy, / Yet, to recover them, would lose my life. / Justice with favour have I always done; / Prayers and tears have mov'd me, gifts could never. / When have I aught exacted at your hands / But to maintain the king, the realm, and you? / Large gifts have I bestow'd on learned clerks, / Because my book preferr'd me to the king; / And seeing ignorance is the curse of God, / Knowledge the wing wherewith we fly to heaven, / Unless you be possess'd with devilish spirits, / You cannot but forbear to murther me. / This tongue hath parley'd unto foreign kings / For your behoof,—

Just hear me speak, and then take me where you like. In the Commentaries Caesar wrote, Kent is called the most civilised place in all this island. The country is lovely, being full of riches, the people generous, brave, energetic and wealthy, which makes me hope you are not without pity. I didn't sell Maine, I didn't lose Normandy, but I'd give my life to win them back. I have always done justice with mercy; prayers and tears have moved me, gifts never could. When have I ever demanded anything from you except to support the king, the kingdom and you? I've given large gifts to scholars because my learning got me advancement with the king; and since ignorance is God's curse and knowledge the wing we fly to heaven with, unless you're possessed by devils, you can't help but refrain from murdering me. This tongue has negotiated with foreign kings for your benefit—
Tut, when struck'st thou one blow in the field?
Nonsense, when did you ever strike a blow in battle?
Great men have reaching hands; oft have I struck / Those that I never saw, and struck them dead.
Great men have long arms. I've often struck people I never saw, and struck them dead.
O monstrous coward! what, to come behind folks?
Oh, monstrous coward! What, attacking people from behind?
These cheeks are pale for watching for your good.
These cheeks are pale from staying awake working for your good.
Give him a box o' the ear, and that will make 'em red / again.
Give him a smack round the ear, and that'll make them red again.
Long sitting to determine poor men's causes / Hath made me full of sickness and diseases.
Sitting for long hours deciding poor men's cases has made me full of sickness and disease.
Ye shall have a hempen caudle then, and the help of / hatchet.
Then you'll have a hemp-rope medicine, and the help of a hatchet.
The palsy, and not fear, provokes me.
It's palsy that makes me shake, not fear.
Nay, he nods at us, as who should say, I'll be even with / you. I'll see if his head will stand steadier on a pole or / no. Take him away, and behead him.
No, he's nodding at us, as if to say, "I'll get even with you." I'll see if his head stands steadier on a pole. Take him away and behead him.

Tell me wherein have I offended most? / Have I affected wealth or honour? speak. / Are my chests fill'd up with extorted gold? / Is my apparel sumptuous to behold? / Whom have I injur'd, that ye seek my death? / These hands are free from guiltless bloodshedding, / This breast from harbouring foul deceitful thoughts. / O, let me live!

Tell me, what have I done so wrong? Have I chased after wealth or honour? Speak. Are my chests full of extorted gold? Are my clothes expensive to look at? Whom have I hurt, that you want me dead? These hands are free of innocent blood, this heart of foul, deceitful thoughts. Oh, let me live!

[Aside] I feel remorse in myself with his words, but I'll bridle / it; he shall die, an it be but for pleading so well for his / life.— / Away with him! he has a familiar under his tongue; he speaks not / o' God's name. Go, take him away, I say, and strike off his head / presently; and then break into his son-in-law's house, Sir James / Cromer, and strike off his head, and bring them both upon two / poles hither.

(Aside) His words make me feel sorry, but I'll rein it in. He'll die, if only for pleading so well for his life. Away with him! He has a devil under his tongue; he doesn't speak in God's name. Go, take him away, I say, and cut off his head at once; then break into his son-in-law Sir James Cromer's house and cut off his head, and bring them both here on two poles.
Ah, countrymen! if when you make your prayers, / God should be so obdurate as yourselves, / How would it fare with your departed souls? / And therefore yet relent, and save my life.
Ah, countrymen! If when you pray God were as hard-hearted as you are, how would your souls fare after death? So relent even now, and spare my life.
Away with him! and do as I command ye.—
Away with him, and do as I order you.

The proudest peer in the realm shall not / wear a head on his shoulders unless he pay me tribute; there / shall not a maid be married but she shall pay to me her / maidenhead ere they have it. Men shall hold of me in capite; / and we charge and command that their wives be as free as / heart can wish or tongue can tell.

The proudest lord in the kingdom won't keep his head on his shoulders unless he pays me tribute. No girl will be married unless she gives me her virginity before her husband gets it. Men will hold their lands directly from me; and we order and command that their wives be as free as heart can wish or tongue can tell.
My lord, when shall we go to Cheapside, and take up / commodities upon our bills?
My lord, when shall we go to Cheapside and take goods on credit with our bills?

But is not this braver? Let them kiss one another, / for they loved well when they were alive. Now part them again, / lest they consult about the giving up of some more towns in / France.—Soldiers, defer the spoil of the city until night; for / with these borne before us, instead of maces will we ride / through the streets, and at every corner have them kiss.—Away!

But isn't this more splendid? Let them kiss each other, for they loved each other well when they were alive. Now part them again, in case they plot to give up some more towns in France. Soldiers, put off looting the city until night, for we'll ride through the streets with these carried in front of us instead of maces, and make them kiss at every corner. Away!

Up Fish Street! down Saint Magnus' Corner! kill / and knock down! Throw them into Thames! [Sound a parley] / What noise is this I hear? Dare any be so bold to sound retreat / or parley when I command them kill?

Up Fish Street! Down St Magnus' Corner! Kill and knock them down! Throw them in the Thames! (A trumpet sounds a parley) What's this noise I hear? Does anyone dare to sound retreat or parley when I order them to kill?

Ay, here they be that dare and will disturb thee. / Know, Cade, we come ambassadors from the king / Unto the commons whom thou hast misled, / And here pronounce free pardon to them all / That will forsake thee and go home in peace.

Yes, here are men who dare and will disturb you. Know, Cade, that we come as ambassadors from the king to the commons you have misled, and here we announce a free pardon to all who will abandon you and go home in peace.

What say ye, countrymen? will ye relent / And yield to mercy whilst 't is offer'd you, / Or let a rebel lead you to your deaths? / Who loves the king and will embrace his pardon, / Fling up his cap, and say 'God save his Majesty!' / Who hateth him and honours not his father, / Henry the Fifth, that made all France to quake, / Shake he his weapon at us and pass by.

What do you say, countrymen? Will you give in and accept mercy while it's offered, or let a rebel lead you to your deaths? Whoever loves the king and will accept his pardon, throw up your cap and say "God save his Majesty!" Whoever hates him and doesn't honour his father, Henry the Fifth, who made all France tremble, shake your weapon at us and go past.
God save the king! God save the king!
God save the king! God save the king!

What, Buckingham and Clifford, are ye so brave?— / And you, base peasants, do ye believe him? will you needs be / hang'd with your pardons about your necks? Hath my sword therefore / broke through London gates, that you should leave me at the / White Hart in Southwark? I thought ye would never have given / out these arms till you had recovered your ancient freedom; / but you are all recreants and dastards, and delight to live in / slavery to the nobility. Let them break your backs with burthens, / take your houses over your heads, ravish your wives and daughters / before your faces. For me, I will make shift for one; and so, / God's curse light upon you all!

What, Buckingham and Clifford, are you so bold? And you low peasants, do you believe him? Are you set on being hanged with your pardons round your necks? Did my sword break through London's gates just so you could desert me at the White Hart in Southwark? I thought you'd never lay down these arms till you had won back your old freedom. But you're all deserters and cowards, and love to live as slaves to the nobility. Let them break your backs with burdens, take your houses from over your heads, rape your wives and daughters in front of you. As for me, I'll look after myself; and so, God's curse on you all!
We'll follow Cade, we'll follow Cade!
We'll follow Cade, we'll follow Cade!

Is Cade the son of Henry the Fifth, / That thus you do exclaim you'll go with him? / Will he conduct you through the heart of France, / And make the meanest of you earls and dukes? / Alas, he hath no home, no place to fly to; / Nor knows he how to live but by the spoil, / Unless by robbing of your friends and us. / Were 't not a shame that whilst you live at jar / The fearful French, whom you late vanquished, / Should make a start o'er seas and vanquish you? / Methinks already in this civil broil / I see them lording it in London streets, / Crying 'Villiaco!' unto all they meet. / Better ten thousand base-born Cades miscarry / Than you should stoop unto a Frenchman's mercy. / To France, to France, and get what you have lost; / Spare England, for it is your native coast. / Henry hath money, you are strong and manly; / God on our side, doubt not of victory.

Is Cade the son of Henry the Fifth, that you shout you'll go with him like this? Will he lead you through the heart of France and make the lowest of you earls and dukes? Alas, he has no home, no place to run to, and doesn't know how to live except by plunder, by robbing your friends and us. Wouldn't it be a shame if, while you quarrel among yourselves, the frightened French, whom you recently beat, should suddenly cross the sea and beat you? I can already see them, in this civil chaos, lording it in London's streets, shouting "Villain!" at everyone they meet. Better ten thousand low-born Cades should die than you should bow to a Frenchman's mercy. To France, to France, and win back what you've lost! Spare England, for it's your native land. Henry has money, you are strong and manly; with God on our side, don't doubt we'll win.
A Clifford! a Clifford! we'll follow the king and / Clifford.
A Clifford! A Clifford! We'll follow the king and Clifford.

Was ever feather so lightly blown to and fro as this / multitude? The name of Henry the Fifth hales them to an hundred / mischiefs and makes them leave me desolate. I see them lay their / heads together to surprise me. My sword make way for me, for / here is no staying.—In despite of the devils and hell, have / through the very middest of you! and heavens and honour be / witness / that no want of resolution in me, but only my followers' base and / ignominious treasons, makes me betake me to my heels.

Was any feather ever blown back and forth as easily as this crowd? The name of Henry the Fifth drags them into a hundred kinds of trouble and makes them leave me alone. I see them putting their heads together to seize me. Sword, cut a way for me, for there's no staying here. In spite of devils and hell, I'll go right through the middle of you! And may heaven and honour witness that it's not lack of courage in me but only my followers' low, shameful treachery that makes me run for it.
What, is he fled?—Go some, and follow him; / And he that brings his head unto the king / Shall have a thousand crowns for his reward.—
What, has he fled? Some of you go after him; whoever brings his head to the king will get a thousand crowns as a reward.
Follow me, soldiers; we'll devise a mean / To reconcile you all unto the king.
Follow me, soldiers; we'll find a way to reconcile you all with the king.

Was ever king that joy'd an earthly throne, / And could command no more content than I? / No sooner was I crept out of my cradle / But I was made a king at nine months old. / Was never subject long'd to be a king / As I do long and wish to be a subject.

Was there ever a king who enjoyed an earthly throne and had less happiness than me? I'd hardly crawled out of my cradle before I was made king, at nine months old. No subject ever longed to be a king as much as I long to be a subject.
Health and glad tidings to your majesty!
Health and good news to your majesty!
Why, Buckingham, is the traitor Cade surpris'd? / Or is he but retir'd to make him strong?
Why, Buckingham, is the traitor Cade captured? Or has he only withdrawn to gather strength?
He is fled, my lord, and all his powers do yield, / And humbly thus, with halters on their necks, / Expect your highness' doom, of life or death.
He has fled, my lord, and all his forces are surrendering, and humbly, like this, with nooses round their necks, they await your highness's sentence of life or death.

Then, heaven, set ope thy everlasting gates, / To entertain my vows of thanks and praise!— / Soldiers, this day have you redeem'd your lives / And show'd how well you love your prince and country. / Continue still in this so good a mind, / And Henry, though he be infortunate, / Assure yourselves, will never be unkind. / And so, with thanks and pardon to you all, / I do dismiss you to your several countries.

Then, heaven, open your everlasting gates to receive my vows of thanks and praise! Soldiers, today you've saved your lives and shown how much you love your prince and country. Keep this good attitude, and be sure that Henry, though he's unlucky, will never be unkind. And so, with thanks and pardon to you all, I send you home to your own counties.
God save the king! God save the king!
God save the king! God save the king!

Please it your grace to be advertised / The Duke of York is newly come from Ireland, / And with a puissant and a mighty power / Of gallowglasses and stout kerns / Is marching hitherward in proud array, / And still proclaimeth, as he comes along, / His arms are only to remove from thee / The Duke of Somerset, whom he terms a traitor.

If it please your grace to be told, the Duke of York has just come from Ireland with a powerful army of Irish soldiers, heavy and light, and is marching here in proud formation, announcing as he comes that his only aim is to remove from you the Duke of Somerset, whom he calls a traitor.

Thus stands my state, 'twixt Cade and York distress'd, / Like to a ship that, having scap'd a tempest, / Is straightway calm'd and boarded with a pirate; / But now is Cade driven back, his men dispers'd, / And now is York in arms to second him.— / I pray thee, Buckingham, go and meet him, / And ask him what's the reason of these arms. / Tell him I'll send Duke Edmund to the Tower;— / And, Somerset, we will commit thee thither, / Until his army be dismiss'd from him.

This is how I stand, troubled between Cade and York, like a ship that has escaped a storm and is immediately becalmed and boarded by a pirate. Just as Cade is driven back and his men scattered, York is up in arms to follow him. Please, Buckingham, go and meet him and ask him the reason for this army. Tell him I'll send Duke Edmund to the Tower; and Somerset, we will send you there until he dismisses his army.
My lord, / I'll yield myself to prison willingly, / Or unto death, to do my country good.
My lord, I'll go to prison willingly, or to my death, to do my country good.
In any case, be not too rough in terms, / For he is fierce and cannot brook hard language.
Whatever happens, don't use harsh words, for he is fierce and can't stand rough language.
I will, my lord, and doubt not so to deal / As all things shall redound unto your good.
I will, my lord, and don't doubt I'll handle it so that everything turns out for your good.
Come, wife, let's in, and learn to govern better; / For yet may England curse my wretched reign.
Come, wife, let's go in and learn to govern better, for so far England may well curse my wretched reign.

Fie on ambitions! fie on myself, that have a sword / and yet am ready to famish! These five days have I hid me in / these woods and durst not peep out, for all the country is laid / for me; but now am I so hungry that if I might have a lease of / my life for a thousand years I could stay no longer. Wherefore, / on a brick wall have I climb'd into this garden, to see if I can / eat grass, or pick a sallet another while, which is not amiss to / cool / a man's stomach this hot weather. And I think this word 'sallet' / was born to do me good; for many a time, but for a sallet, my / brain-pain had been cleft with a brown bill; and many a time, / when I have been dry and bravely marching, it hath served me / instead of a quart pot to drink in; and now the word 'sallet' / must serve me to feed on.

Curse ambition! Curse me, who have a sword and yet am starving to death! For five days I've hidden in these woods and haven't dared to peep out, for the whole county is searching for me. But now I'm so hungry that even if I were promised another thousand years of life, I couldn't wait any longer. So I've climbed over a brick wall into this garden to see if I can eat grass or pick a salad, which isn't bad for cooling a man's stomach in this hot weather. And I think this word "sallet" was born to do me good. Many times, if not for a sallet, a helmet, my skull would have been split by a soldier's axe; and many times, when I've been thirsty and marching bravely, it has served me as a pot to drink from; and now the word "sallet" must serve me as food.

Lord, who would live turmoiled in the court, / And may enjoy such quiet walks as these? / This small inheritance my father left me / Contenteth me, and worth a monarchy. / I seek not to wax great by others' waning, / Or gather wealth, I care not with what envy; / Sufficeth that I have maintains my state / And sends the poor well pleased from my gate.

Lord, who would live in the turmoil of the court when he could enjoy quiet walks like these? This small estate my father left me satisfies me and is worth a kingdom. I don't try to grow great by others' falling, or gather wealth regardless of the envy it causes. It's enough that what I have supports my position and sends the poor away from my gate well pleased.

Here's the lord of the soil come to seize me for a / stray, for entering his fee-simple without leave.—Ah, villain, / thou wilt betray me, and get a thousand crowns of the king / by carrying my head to him; but I'll make thee eat iron like / an ostrich, and swallow my sword like a great pin, ere thou / and I part.

Here's the lord of the land come to arrest me as a stray for entering his property without permission. Ah, villain, you'll betray me and get a thousand crowns from the king by carrying my head to him. But I'll make you eat iron like an ostrich and swallow my sword like a big pin before we part.

Why, rude companion, whatsoe'er thou be, I know / thee not! why, then, should I betray thee? / Is 't not enough to break into my garden, / And, like a thief, to come to rob my grounds, / Climbing my walls in spite of me the owner, / But thou wilt brave me with these saucy terms?

Why, rough fellow, whoever you are, I don't know you! Why, then, would I betray you? Isn't it enough to break into my garden and come like a thief to rob my land, climbing my walls against the owner's will, without defying me with these cheeky words?

Brave thee? ay, by the best blood that ever was / broached, and beard thee too. Look on me well: I have eat / no meat these five days; yet, come thou and thy five men, / and if I do not leave you all as dead as a door-nail, I pray / God I may never eat grass more.

Defy you? Yes, by the best blood ever spilled, and insult you to your face too. Take a good look at me. I haven't eaten for five days; yet let you and your five men come, and if I don't leave you all as dead as a doornail, I pray God I may never eat grass again.

Nay, it shall ne'er be said, while England stands, / That Alexander Iden, an esquire of Kent, / Took odds to combat a poor famish'd man. / Oppose thy steadfast-gazing eyes to mine, / See if thou canst outface me with thy looks. / Set limb to limb and thou art far the lesser; / Thy hand is but a finger to my fist, / Thy leg a stick compared with this truncheon; / My foot shall fight with all the strength thou hast; / And if mine arm be heaved in the air, / Thy grave is digg'd already in the earth. / As for words, whose greatness answers words, / Let this my sword report what speech forbears.

No, it will never be said, as long as England stands, that Alexander Iden, a gentleman of Kent, took unfair odds to fight a poor starving man. Set your staring eyes against mine; see if you can outstare me. Compare limb with limb and you're far smaller. Your hand is only a finger next to my fist, your leg a stick compared with this club of mine; my foot alone will fight with all the strength you have. And if my arm is raised in the air, your grave is already dug in the earth. As for words, whose bragging answers words, let this sword of mine say what speech holds back.

By my valour, the most complete champion that / ever I heard!—Steel, if thou turn the edge, or cut not out / the burly-boned clown in chines of beef ere thou sleep in / thy sheath, I beseech God on my knees thou mayst be turn'd / to hobnails.—[Here they fight. Cade falls] O, I am slain! / famine and no other hath slain me; let ten thousand devils / come against me, and give me but the ten meals I have lost, / and I'd defy them all.—Wither, garden; and be henceforth a / burying place to all that do dwell in this house, because / the unconquered soul of Cade is fled.

By my courage, the most perfect champion I ever heard! Steel, if your edge turns, or you don't carve this big-boned peasant into joints of beef before you sleep in your sheath, I pray God on my knees that you may be turned into hobnails. (They fight. Cade falls) Oh, I'm killed! Hunger and nothing else has killed me. Let ten thousand devils come against me, and give me the ten meals I've missed, and I'd defy them all. Wither, garden, and be from now on a graveyard for everyone who lives in this house, because the unconquered soul of Cade has fled.

Is't Cade that I have slain, that monstrous traitor?— / Sword, I will hallow thee for this thy deed, / And hang thee o'er my tomb when I am dead; / Ne'er shall this blood be wiped from thy point, / But thou shalt wear it as a herald's coat, / To emblaze the honour that thy master got.

Is it Cade I've killed, that monstrous traitor? Sword, I'll make you sacred for this deed and hang you over my tomb when I'm dead. This blood will never be wiped from your point; you'll wear it like a herald's coat, to proclaim the honour your master won.

Iden, farewell; and be proud of thy victory. Tell Kent from / me, she hath lost her best man, and exhort all the world to be / cowards; for I, that never feared any, am vanquished by famine, / not by valour.

Iden, farewell, and be proud of your victory. Tell Kent from me that she has lost her best man, and urge the whole world to be cowards; for I, who never feared anyone, am beaten by hunger, not by courage.

How much thou wrong'st me, heaven be my judge. / Die, damned wretch, the curse of her that bare thee; / And as I thrust thy body in with my sword, / So wish I I might thrust thy soul to hell. / Hence will I drag thee headlong by the heels / Unto a dunghill which shall be thy grave, / And there cut off thy most ungracious head, / Which I will bear in triumph to the king, / Leaving thy trunk for crows to feed upon.

Heaven judge how much you wrong me. Die, damned wretch, curse of the woman who bore you! And as I thrust my sword into your body, so I wish I could thrust your soul into hell. From here I'll drag you headlong by the heels to a dunghill, which will be your grave, and there cut off your wicked head, which I'll carry in triumph to the king, leaving your body for the crows to eat.

From Ireland thus comes York to claim his right, / And pluck the crown from feeble Henry's head. / Ring, bells, aloud; burn, bonfires, clear and bright, / To entertain great England's lawful king. / Ah! sancta majestas! who would not buy thee dear? / Let them obey that knows not how to rule; / This hand was made to handle nought but gold. / I cannot give due action to my words / Except a sword or sceptre balance it. / A sceptre shall it have, have I a soul, / On which I'll toss the flower-de-luce of France.—

So York comes from Ireland to claim his right and pluck the crown from feeble Henry's head. Ring loud, bells; burn clear and bright, bonfires, to welcome great England's lawful king. Ah, sacred majesty! Who wouldn't pay dearly for you? Let those obey who don't know how to rule. This hand was made to hold nothing but gold. I can't put my words into action unless a sword or sceptre gives it weight. It will have a sceptre, as surely as I have a soul, and on it I'll toss the fleur-de-lis of France.
Whom have we here? Buckingham, to disturb me? / The king hath sent him, sure: I must dissemble.
Who's this? Buckingham, come to bother me? The king has sent him, surely; I must pretend.
York, if thou meanest well, I greet thee well.
York, if you mean well, I greet you well.
Humphrey of Buckingham, I accept thy greeting. / Art thou a messenger, or come of pleasure?
Humphrey of Buckingham, I accept your greeting. Are you a messenger, or here for your own pleasure?

A messenger from Henry, our dread liege, / To know the reason of these arms in peace; / Or why thou, being a subject as I am, / Against thy oath and true allegiance sworn, / Should raise so great a power without his leave, / Or dare to bring thy force so near the court.

A messenger from Henry, our dread lord, to learn why you are in arms in peacetime, or why you, a subject like me, against your oath and sworn allegiance, should raise such a big army without his permission, or dare to bring your forces so near the court.

[Aside] Scarce can I speak, my choler is so great: / O, I could hew up rocks and fight with flint, / I am so angry at these abject terms; / And now, like Ajax Telamonius, / On sheep or oxen could I spend my fury. / I am far better born than is the king, / More like a king, more kingly in my thoughts; / But I must make fair weather yet a while, / Till Henry be more weak and I more strong.— / Buckingham, I prithee, pardon me, / That I have given no answer all this while; / My mind was troubled with deep melancholy. / The cause why I have brought this army hither / Is to remove proud Somerset from the king, / Seditious to his grace and to the state.

(Aside) I can hardly speak, I'm so angry. Oh, I could hack up rocks and fight with flint, these insulting words make me so furious; and now, like Ajax, son of Telamon, I could spend my fury on sheep or oxen. I'm far better born than the king, more like a king, more kingly in my thoughts. But I must pretend to be friendly a while longer, until Henry is weaker and I'm stronger. Buckingham, please forgive me for not answering all this time; my mind was troubled with deep sadness. The reason I've brought this army here is to remove proud Somerset from the king, since he is a traitor to his grace and the state.
That is too much presumption on thy part; / But if thy arms be to no other end, / The king hath yielded unto thy demand. / The Duke of Somerset is in the Tower.
That's too presumptuous of you. But if your army is for no other purpose, the king has granted your demand. The Duke of Somerset is in the Tower.
Upon thine honour, is he prisoner?
On your honour, is he a prisoner?
Upon mine honour, he is prisoner.
On my honour, he is a prisoner.

Then, Buckingham, I do dismiss my powers.— / Soldiers, I thank you all; disperse yourselves; / Meet me to-morrow in Saint George's field, / You shall have pay and everything you wish.— / And let my sovereign, virtuous Henry, / Command my eldest son, nay, all my sons, / As pledges of my fealty and love, / I'll send them all as willing as I live; / Lands, goods, horse, armour, anything I have, / Is his to use, so Somerset may die.

Then, Buckingham, I'll dismiss my forces. Soldiers, thank you all; break up; meet me tomorrow in St George's Field, and you'll have your pay and everything you want. And let my sovereign, virtuous Henry, demand my eldest son, or all my sons, as pledges of my loyalty and love; I'll send them all as willingly as I live. Lands, goods, horses, armour, anything I have is his to use, as long as Somerset dies.
York, I commend this kind submission; / We twain will go into his highness' tent.
York, I praise this kind submission. We two will go to his highness's tent.
Buckingham, doth York intend no harm to us, / That thus he marcheth with thee arm in arm?
Buckingham, does York mean us no harm, that he walks with you arm in arm like this?
In all submission and humility / York doth present himself unto your highness.
York presents himself to your highness in full submission and humility.
Then what intends these forces thou dost bring?
Then what is the purpose of these forces you bring?
To heave the traitor Somerset from hence, / And fight against that monstrous rebel Cade, / Who since I heard to be discomfited.
To remove the traitor Somerset from here, and to fight that monstrous rebel Cade, who I've since heard has been defeated.
If one so rude and of so mean condition / May pass into the presence of a king, / Lo, I present your grace a traitor's head, / The head of Cade, whom I in combat slew.
If someone so rough and of such low rank may come into a king's presence, look, I present your grace a traitor's head, the head of Cade, whom I killed in a fight.
The head of Cade!—Great God, how just art Thou!— / O, let me view his visage, being dead, / That living wrought me such exceeding trouble. / Tell me, my friend, art thou the man that slew him?
The head of Cade! Great God, how just you are! Oh, let me look at his face, now he's dead, which in life caused me so much trouble. Tell me, my friend, are you the man who killed him?
I was, an 't like your majesty.
I am, if it please your majesty.
How art thou call'd? and what is thy degree?
What is your name, and what is your rank?
Alexander Iden, that's my name; / A poor esquire of Kent, that loves his king.
Alexander Iden is my name, a poor gentleman of Kent who loves his king.
So please it you, my lord, 't were not amiss / He were created knight for his good service.
