If it please you, my lord, it would be fitting to make him a knight for his good service.
Iden, kneel down. [He kneels] Rise up a knight. / We give thee for reward a thousand marks, / And will that thou thenceforth attend on us.
Iden, kneel. (He kneels) Rise up a knight. We give you a thousand marks as a reward, and want you to serve us from now on.
May Iden live to merit such a bounty, / And never live but true unto his liege!
May Iden live to deserve such generosity, and never live except loyal to his lord!
See, Buckingham, Somerset comes with the queen. / Go, bid her hide him quickly from the duke.
Look, Buckingham, Somerset is coming with the queen. Go and tell her to hide him quickly from the duke.
For thousand Yorks he shall not hide his head, / But boldly stand and front him to his face.
He won't hide his head for a thousand Yorks, but will stand boldly and face him.

How now! is Somerset at liberty? / Then, York, unloose thy long-imprisoned thoughts, / And let thy tongue be equal with thy heart. / Shall I endure the sight of Somerset? / False king! why hast thou broken faith with me, / Knowing how hardly I can brook abuse? / King did I call thee? no, thou art not king, / Not fit to govern and rule multitudes, / Which dar'st not, no, nor canst not rule a traitor. / That head of thine doth not become a crown; / Thy hand is made to grasp a palmer's staff, / And not to grace an awful princely sceptre. / That gold must round engirt these brows of mine, / Whose smile and frown, like to Achilles' spear, / Is able with the change to kill and cure. / Here is a hand to hold a sceptre up / And with the same to act controlling laws. / Give place; by heaven, thou shalt rule no more / O'er him whom heaven created for thy ruler.

What's this! Is Somerset free? Then, York, let loose your long-imprisoned thoughts, and let your tongue match your heart. Shall I put up with the sight of Somerset? False king! Why have you broken your word to me, knowing how badly I take being cheated? Did I call you king? No, you're not king, not fit to govern and rule the people, since you don't dare, no, and can't, rule even a traitor. That head of yours doesn't suit a crown. Your hand was made to grip a pilgrim's staff, not to grace an awe-inspiring royal sceptre. That gold must circle these brows of mine, whose smile and frown, like Achilles' spear, can kill or cure as they change. Here is a hand to hold up a sceptre and to enforce laws with it. Make way; by heaven, you'll rule no longer over the man heaven made to rule you.
O monstrous traitor!—I arrest thee, York, / Of capital treason 'gainst the king and crown. / Obey, audacious traitor; kneel for grace.
Oh, monstrous traitor! I arrest you, York, for capital treason against the king and crown. Obey, impudent traitor; kneel for mercy.
Wouldst have me kneel? first let me ask of these / If they can brook I bow a knee to man.— / Sirrah, call in my sons to be my bail.—
Would you have me kneel? First let me ask these men if they can bear to see me bow my knee to any man. You, call my sons in to be my guarantors.
I know, ere thy will have me go to ward, / They'll pawn their swords for my enfranchisement.
I know that before they let me go to prison, they'll pledge their swords to free me.
Call hither Clifford; bid him come amain, / To say if that the bastard boys of York / Shall be the surety for their traitor father.
Call Clifford here; tell him to come at once, to say whether York's bastard boys shall be guarantors for their traitor father.

O blood-bespotted Neapolitan, / Outcast of Naples, England's bloody scourge! / The sons of York, thy betters in their birth, / Shall be their father's bail; and bane to those / That for my surety will refuse the boys!

Oh, blood-stained Neapolitan, outcast of Naples, England's bloody scourge! The sons of York, better born than you, will be their father's bail, and the ruin of those who refuse to accept the boys as my guarantee!
See where they come; I'll warrant they'll make it good.
See, here they come; I promise you they'll make it good.
And here comes Clifford to deny their bail.
And here comes Clifford to refuse their bail.
Health and all happiness to my lord the king!
Health and all happiness to my lord the king!
I thank thee, Clifford; say, what news with thee? / Nay, do not fright us with an angry look. / We are thy sovereign, Clifford, kneel again; / For thy mistaking so, we pardon thee.
Thank you, Clifford. Tell me, what news do you bring? No, don't frighten us with an angry look. We are your sovereign, Clifford; kneel again. We pardon you for your mistake.
This is my king, York, I do not mistake; / But thou mistakes me much to think I do.— / To Bedlam with him! is the man grown mad?
This is my king, York; I'm not mistaken, but you are very mistaken to think I am. Off to the madhouse with him! Has the man gone mad?
Ay, Clifford; a bedlam and ambitious humour / Makes him oppose himself against his king.
Yes, Clifford; a mad, ambitious temper makes him set himself against his king.
He is a traitor; let him to the Tower, / And chop away that factious pate of his.
He's a traitor. Send him to the Tower and chop off that rebellious head of his.
He is arrested, but will not obey; / His sons, he says, shall give their words for him.
He's been arrested, but won't obey. He says his sons will give their word for him.
Ay, noble father, if our words will serve.
Yes, noble father, if our words will do.
And if words will not, then our weapons shall.
And if words won't, then our weapons will.
Why, what a brood of traitors have we here!
Why, what a brood of traitors we have here!

Look in a glass, and call thy image so; / I am thy king, and thou a false-heart traitor.— / Call hither to the stake my two brave bears, / That with the very shaking of their chains / They may astonish these fell-lurking curs. / Bid Salisbury and Warwick come to me.

Look in a mirror and call your reflection that. I am your king, and you a false-hearted traitor. Call my two brave bears to the stake, so that the mere rattle of their chains will terrify these fierce, skulking dogs. Tell Salisbury and Warwick to come to me.
Are these thy bears? we'll bait thy bears to death, / And manacle the bear-herd in their chains, / If thou dar'st bring them to the baiting-place.
Are these your bears? We'll bait your bears to death and chain up the bear-keeper in their chains, if you dare bring them to the bear pit.

Oft have I seen a hot o'erweening cur / Run back and bite because he was withheld, / Who, being suffer'd with the bear's fell paw, / Hath clapp'd his tail between his legs and cried; / And such a piece of service will you do / If you oppose yourselves to match Lord Warwick.

I've often seen a hot-headed, cocky dog run back and bite because he was held back, who, when let loose at the bear's cruel paw, put his tail between his legs and howled. And that's the kind of service you'll do if you set yourselves against Lord Warwick.
Hence, heap of wrath, foul indigested lump, / As crooked in thy manners as thy shape!
Get away, you heap of anger, foul, shapeless lump, as twisted in your manners as in your body!
Nay, we shall heat you thoroughly anon.
No, we'll heat you up thoroughly soon.
Take heed, lest by your heat you burn yourselves.
Be careful you don't burn yourselves with your heat.

Why, Warwick, hath thy knee forgot to bow?— / Old Salisbury, shame to thy silver hair, / Thou mad misleader of thy brainsick son! / What, wilt thou on thy death-bed play the ruffian, / And seek for sorrow with thy spectacles? / O, where is faith? O, where is loyalty? / If it be banish'd from the frosty head, / Where shall it find a harbour in the earth? / Wilt thou go dig a grave to find out war, / And shame thine honourable age with blood? / Why art thou old, and want'st experience? / Or wherefore dost abuse it, if thou hast it? / For shame! in duty bend thy knee to me / That bows unto the grave with mickle age.

Why, Warwick, has your knee forgotten how to bow? Old Salisbury, shame on your silver hair, you mad misleader of your brainsick son! What, will you play the thug on your deathbed and go looking for sorrow with your spectacles on? Oh, where is faith? Where is loyalty? If it's banished from the white-haired head, where on earth will it find a home? Will you dig up war from your grave and shame your honourable old age with blood? Why are you old and lack experience? Or why do you misuse it, if you have it? For shame! Do your duty and bend your knee to me, you who are already bending to the grave with old age.
My lord, I have consider'd with myself / The tide of this most renowned duke, / And in my conscience do repute his grace / The rightful heir to England's royal seat.
My lord, I have thought hard about this famous duke's title, and in my conscience I consider his grace the rightful heir to England's throne.
Hast thou not sworn allegiance unto me?
Haven't you sworn allegiance to me?
Canst thou dispense with heaven for such an oath?
Can you get heaven to release you from such an oath?

It is great sin to swear unto a sin, / But greater sin to keep a sinful oath. / Who can be bound by any solemn vow / To do a murtherous deed, to rob a man, / To force a spotless virgin's chastity, / To reave the orphan of his patrimony, / To wring the widow from her custom'd right, / And have no other reason for this wrong / But that he was bound by a solemn oath?

It is a great sin to swear to commit a sin, but a greater sin to keep a sinful oath. Who can be bound by any solemn vow to commit murder, rob a man, rape a pure virgin, steal an orphan's inheritance, or squeeze a widow out of her lawful rights, and have no other reason for this wrong except that he was bound by a solemn oath?
A subtle traitor needs no sophister.
A clever traitor doesn't need anyone to argue for him.
Call Buckingham, and bid him arm himself.
Call Buckingham and tell him to arm himself.
Call Buckingham, and all the friends thou hast, / I am resolv'd for death or dignity.
Call Buckingham and all the friends you have; I'm determined to have death or the crown.
The first I warrant thee if dreams prove true.
Death, I promise you, if dreams come true.
You were best to go to bed and dream again, / To keep thee from the tempest of the field.
You'd better go to bed and dream again, to keep yourself out of the storm of battle.
I am resolv'd to bear a greater storm / Than any thou canst conjure up to-day; / And that I'll write upon thy burgonet, / Might I but know thee by thy household badge.
I'm determined to face a greater storm than any you can conjure up today, and I'll write that on your helmet, if only I can recognise you by your family badge.

Now, by my father's badge, old Nevil's crest, / The rampant bear chain'd to the ragged staff, / This day I'll wear aloft my burgonet, / As on a mountain top the cedar shows / That keeps his leaves in spite of any storm, / Even to affright thee with the view thereof.

Now, by my father's badge, old Neville's crest, the rearing bear chained to the knotted staff, I'll wear my helmet high today, like the cedar on a mountaintop that keeps its leaves in spite of any storm, just to frighten you with the sight of it.
And from thy burgonet I'll rend thy bear / And tread it under foot with all contempt, / Despite the bear-herd that protects the bear.
And I'll tear your bear off your helmet and trample it underfoot with total contempt, in spite of the bear-keeper who protects the bear.
And so to arms, victorious father, / To quell the rebels and their complices.
And so to arms, victorious father, to crush the rebels and their accomplices.
Fie! charity, for shame! speak not in spite, / For you shall sup with Jesu Christ to-night.
Shame! Be charitable, for shame! Don't speak in spite, for you'll have supper with Jesus Christ tonight.
Foul stigmatic, that's more than thou canst / tell.
Foul, deformed creature, that's more than you can tell.
If not in heaven, you'll surely sup in hell.
If not in heaven, you'll surely have supper in hell.

Clifford of Cumberland, 't is Warwick calls; / And if thou dost not hide thee from the bear, / Now, when the angry trumpet sounds alarum / And dead men's cries do fill the empty air, / Clifford, I say, come forth and fight with me! / Proud northern lord, Clifford of Cumberland, / Warwick is hoarse with calling thee to arms.—

Clifford of Cumberland, it's Warwick calling! If you're not hiding from the bear, now, when the angry trumpet sounds the call to battle and dying men's cries fill the empty air, Clifford, I say, come out and fight me! Proud northern lord, Clifford of Cumberland, Warwick is hoarse from calling you to fight.
How now, my noble lord! what, all afoot?
What's this, my noble lord? What, on foot?
The deadly-handed Clifford slew my steed, / But match to match I have encount'red him, / And made a prey for carrion kites and crows / Even of the bonny beast he lov'd so well.
Deadly Clifford killed my horse, but I've paid him back in kind and made a meal for scavenging kites and crows of the fine animal he loved so well.
Of one or both of us the time is come.
The time has come for one or both of us.
Hold, Warwick, seek thee out some other chase, / For I myself must hunt this deer to death.
Stop, Warwick, find some other quarry, for I must hunt this deer to death myself.
Then, nobly, York; 't is for a crown thou fight'st.— / As I intend, Clifford, to thrive to-day, / It grieves my soul to leave thee unassail'd.
Then fight nobly, York; it's for a crown you're fighting. As I hope to win today, Clifford, it grieves my soul to leave you unattacked.
What seest thou in me, York? why dost thou pause?
What do you see in me, York? Why do you pause?
With thy brave bearing should I be in love / But that thou art so fast mine enemy.
I'd fall in love with your brave bearing if you weren't so firmly my enemy.
Nor should thy prowess want praise and esteem / But that 't is shown ignobly and in treason.
And your courage would deserve praise and respect if it weren't shown dishonourably, in treason.
So let it help me now against thy sword / As I in justice and true right express it!
Then let it help me now against your sword, as surely as I show it for justice and true right!
My soul and body on the action both!
I stake my soul and body on this fight!
A dreadful bet! Get ready at once.
Thus war hath given thee peace, for thou art still. / Peace with his soul, heaven, if it be thy will!
So war has given you peace, for you are still. Heaven, give peace to his soul, if it's your will!

Shame and confusion! all is on the rout; / Fear frames disorder, and disorder wounds / Where it should guard.—O war, thou son of hell, / Whom angry heavens do make their minister, / Throw in the frozen bosoms of our part / Hot coals of vengeance!—Let no soldier fly. / He that is truly dedicate to war / Hath no self-love; nor he that loves himself / Hath not essentially but by circumstance / The name of valour.—[Seeing his dead father] / O, let the vile world end, / And the premised flames of the last day / Knit earth and heaven together! / Now let the general trumpet blow his blast, / Particularities and petty sounds / To cease!—Wast thou ordain'd, dear father, / To lose thy youth in peace, and to achieve / The silver livery of advised age, / And in thy reverence and thy chair-days, thus / To die in ruffian battle?—Even at this sight / My heart is turn'd to stone; and while 't is mine / It shall be stony. York not our old men spares; / No more will I their babes; tears virginal / Shall be to me even as the dew to fire, / And beauty that the tyrant oft reclaims / Shall to my flaming wrath be oil and flax. / Henceforth I will not have to do with pity; / Meet I an infant of the house of York, / Into as many gobbets will I cut it / As wild Medea young Absyrtus did. / In cruelty will I seek out my fame.— / Come, thou new ruin of old Clifford's house: / As did Aeneas old Anchises bear, / So bear I thee upon my manly shoulders; / But then Aeneas bare a living load, / Nothing so heavy as these woes of mine.

Shame and confusion! Everyone is running away. Fear creates disorder, and disorder wounds where it should protect. O war, son of hell, whom the angry heavens use as their servant, throw hot coals of vengeance into the frozen hearts of our side! Let no soldier run away. A man truly devoted to war has no love for himself; and a man who loves himself is not truly brave, only brave by accident. (Seeing his dead father) Oh, let the vile world end, and the promised flames of Judgement Day weld earth and heaven together! Now let the last trumpet blow, and all small, individual sounds stop! Were you destined, dear father, to spend your youth in peace, and to reach the silver uniform of wise old age, and then, in your venerable armchair years, to die like this in a brutal battle? At this sight my heart has turned to stone, and while it's mine it will stay stone. York doesn't spare our old men; no more will I spare their babies. Girls' tears will be to me like dew on fire, and beauty, which often softens a tyrant, will be oil and flax to my flaming anger. From now on I'll have nothing to do with pity. If I meet a baby of the house of York, I'll cut it into as many lumps as wild Medea cut young Absyrtus. I'll seek my fame in cruelty. Come, you new ruin of old Clifford's house. As Aeneas carried old Anchises, so I carry you on my manly shoulders. But Aeneas carried a living load, nothing as heavy as my grief.

So, lie thou there; / For underneath an alehouse' paltry sign, / The Castle in Saint Alban's, Somerset / Hath made the wizard famous in his death. / Sword, hold thy temper; heart, be wrathful still; / Priests pray for enemies, but princes kill.

So, lie there. For under a cheap pub sign, The Castle in St Albans, Somerset has made the wizard famous by his death. Sword, keep your edge; heart, stay angry; priests pray for enemies, but princes kill.
Away, my lord! you are slow; for shame, away!
Away, my lord! You're slow. For shame, away!
Can we outrun the heavens? good Margaret, stay.
Can we outrun the heavens? Good Margaret, stop.
What are you made of? you'll nor fight nor fly; / Now is it manhood, wisdom, and defence, / To give the enemy way, and to secure us / By what we can, which can no more but fly.
What are you made of? You'll neither fight nor run. Now it's manly, wise and the best defence to give way to the enemy and save ourselves however we can, and the only way is to run.

If you be ta'en, we then should see the bottom / Of all our fortunes; but if we haply scape, / As well we may, if not through your neglect, / We shall to London get, where you are lov'd, / And where this breach now in our fortunes made / May readily be stopp'd.

If you're captured, we'll have hit the bottom of all our fortunes; but if we escape, as we may if you don't neglect it, we'll get to London, where you are loved, and where this break in our fortunes can be quickly mended.

But that my heart's on future mischief set, / I would speak blasphemy ere bid you fly. / But fly you must; uncurable discomfit / Reigns in the hearts of all our present parts. / Away, for your relief! and we will live / To see their day and them our fortune give. / Away, my lord, away!

If my heart weren't set on future harm to them, I'd speak blasphemy rather than tell you to run. But run you must; hopeless defeat fills the hearts of everyone still on our side. Away, to save yourselves! We'll live to see them have their day and give them our bad fortune. Away, my lord, away!

Of Salisbury, who can report of him, / That winter lion, who in rage forgets / Aged contusions and all brush of time / And, like a gallant in the brow of youth, / Repairs him with occasion? This happy day / Is not itself, nor have we won one foot, / If Salisbury be lost.

Who can give news of Salisbury, that winter lion, who in his fury forgets the bruises of age and all the wear of time and, like a gallant young man in his prime, renews his strength with the occasion? This happy day isn't happy, and we haven't won a foot of ground, if Salisbury is lost.

My noble father, / Three times to-day I holp him to his horse, / Three times bestrid him; thrice I led him off, / Persuaded him from any further act; / But still, where danger was, still there I met him; / And like rich hangings in a homely house, / So was his will in his old feeble body. / But, noble as he is, look where he comes.

My noble father, three times today I helped him back on his horse, three times stood over him when he was down, three times led him off and persuaded him to fight no more. But wherever there was danger, there I met him again; and like rich tapestries in a plain house, so was his will in his old, weak body. But, noble as he is, look, here he comes.

Now, by my sword, well hast thou fought to-day; / By the mass, so did we all.—I thank you, Richard; / God knows how long it is I have to live, / And it hath pleas'd him that three times to-day / You have defended me from imminent death.— / Well, lords, we have not got that which we have; / 'T is not enough our foes are this time fled, / Being opposites of such repairing nature.

Now, by my sword, you fought well today; by the mass, so did we all. Thank you, Richard. God knows how long I have left to live, and it has pleased him that three times today you saved me from certain death. Well, lords, we haven't secured what we've won. It's not enough that our enemies have run away this time, since they're the kind of opponents who recover quickly.

I know our safety is to follow them; / For, as I hear, the king is fled to London, / To call a present court of parliament. / Let us pursue him ere the writs go forth.— / What says Lord Warwick? shall we after them?

I know our safety lies in following them; for, as I hear, the king has fled to London to call a parliament at once. Let's chase him before the summonses go out. What does Lord Warwick say? Shall we go after them?

After them! nay, before them, if we can. / Now, by my hand, lords, 'twas a glorious day; / Saint Alban's battle won by famous York / Shall be eterniz'd in all age to come.— / Sound drums and trumpets!—and to London all; / And more such days as these to us befall!

After them? No, ahead of them, if we can. Now, by my hand, lords, it was a glorious day. The battle of St Albans, won by famous York, will be remembered for all time to come. Sound the drums and trumpets! And everyone to London; and may more days like this come to us!
